SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it would establish Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Columbus Community Hospital Heliport, Columbus, TX, to support IFR operations at this airport.
Comments Invited
The FAA invites interested persons to participate in this rulemaking by submitting written comments, data, or views. Comments are specifically invited on the overall regulatory, aeronautical, economic, environmental, and energy-related aspects of the proposal. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. To ensure the docket does not contain duplicate comments, commenters should submit only one time if comments are filed electronically, or commenters should send only one copy of written comments if comments are filed in writing.
The FAA will file in the docket all comments it receives, as well as a report summarizing each substantive public contact with FAA personnel concerning this proposed rulemaking. Before acting on this proposal, the FAA will consider all comments it received on or before the closing date for comments. The FAA will consider comments filed after the comment period has closed if it is possible to do so without incurring expense or delay. The FAA may change this proposal in light of the comments it receives.

5 U.S.C. 553(c)
, DOT solicits comments from the public to better inform its rulemaking process. DOT posts these comments, without edit, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov
as described in the system of records notice (DOT/ALL-14FDMS), which can be reviewed at
www.dot.gov/​privacy
.

Class E airspace is published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in
14 CFR 71.1
on an annual basis. This document proposes to amend the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These updates would be published subsequently in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Proposal
The FAA is proposing an amendment to
14 CFR part 71
that would establish Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 7.3-mile radius of Columbus Community Hospital Heliport, Columbus, TX.
(
printed page 75460)
This action is the result of instrument procedures being developed for this airport to support IFR operations.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this proposed regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Policies and Procedures for Rulemakings” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these proposed amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this proposed rule, when promulgated, will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
This proposal will be subject to an environmental analysis in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures” prior to any FAA final regulatory action.

SUMMARY:
This action amends the Class E airspace at Del Rio, TX. This action is the result of a biennial review of the airspace associated with Laughlin Air Force Base (AFB), Del Rio, TX. This proposal also updates the name and geographic coordinates of Laughlin AFB to coincide with the FAA's aeronautical database. This action brings the airspace into compliance with FAA orders and supports instrument flight rule (IFR) procedures and operations.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it amends the Class E airspace at the affected airport to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-12310 in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 60909
; September 25, 2026) proposing to amend the Class E airspace at Del Rio, TX. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. No comments were received.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraphs 6003 and 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in
14 CFR 71.1
on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action amends
14 CFR part 71
by modifying the Class E airspace designated as an extension to a Class C surface area and the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 ft. above the surface at Del Rio, Texas due to a biennial review of the airspace associated with Laughlin AFB, Del Rio, Texas.
For the Laughlin AFB Class E airspace designated as an extension to a Class C surface area, this action: (1) removes the extension north of the airport from the airport legal description as it is no longer required; (2) removes the extension from the 060° radial of the Laughlin VORTAC clockwise to the 195° radial, extending from the 5-mile radius of Laughlin AFB to the 5.5-mile radius as it is no longer required; (3) amends the extension southeast of the airport to extending southeast from the 5-mile radius of Laughlin AFB within 1-mile each side of the line from SWANT to MINNM and 1-mile each side of the 150° bearing from MINNM to 8 miles southeast of MINNM, excluding Mexican airspace (previously, 2.6 miles each side of the 145° radial of the Laughlin VORTAC extending from the 5.5-mile radius of Laughlin AFB to 6.6 miles southeast of the airport); (4) amends the extension northwest of Laughlin AFB to within 2 miles (previously 2.6 miles) each side of the 305° bearing (previously radial) from the Laughlin VORTAC extending from the 5-mile radius of Laughlin AFB to 10.5 miles (previously 6.6 miles) northwest of Laughlin AFB; (4) adds an extension within 1.8 miles each side of the 315° bearing from Laughlin AFB: RWY 13C-LOC extending from the 5-mile radius of Laughlin AFB to 11.5 miles northwest of Laughlin AFB; (5) removes the extension from the 333° radial of Laughlin VORTAC as it is no longer required; (6) removes the city associated with the airport to comply with changes to FAA Order JO 7400.2R, Procedures for Handling Airspace Matters; (7) updates the geographic coordinates of Laughlin AFB to coincide with the FAA's aeronautical database; and (8) updates the outdated term “Airport/Facility Directory” with “Chart Supplement.”
For the Laughlin AFB Class E airspace extending upward from 700 ft. above the surface, this action: (1) reduces the radius to within a 7.4-mile (previously 20 miles) radius of Laughlin AFB, excluding Mexican airspace; (2) adds an extension within 2 miles each side of the 135° bearing from the Laughlin AFB: RWY 31C-LOC extending from the 7.4-mile radius of Laughlin AFB to 11.4 miles southeast of Laughlin AFB; (3) adds an extension within 1.9 miles each side of the 149° bearing from the Laughlin VORTAC extending from the 7.4-mile radius of Laughlin AFB to 11.4 miles southeast of Laughlin AFB; (4) adds an extension extending southeast from the 7.4-mile radius of Laughlin AFB within 1 mile each side of line from SWANT to MINNM to OTULE, excluding Mexican airspace; (5) adds an extension within 2 miles each side of the 305° bearing from the Laughlin VORTAC extending from the 7.4-mile radius of Laughlin AFB to 11.5 miles northwest of Laughlin AFB; (6) adds an extension within 2 miles each side of the 315° bearing from the Laughlin AFB: RWY 13C-LOC extending from the 7.4-mile radius to 11.5 miles northwest of Laughlin AFB; (7) removes the city associated with the airport in the header to comply with changes to FAA Order JO 7400.2R; and (8) updates the name of the airport to Laughlin AFB (previously Laughlin ABF) to coincide with the FAA's aeronautical database.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Policies and Procedures for Rulemakings” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
The FAA has determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” Paragraph B-2.5(a). This airspace action is not expected to cause any potentially significant environmental impacts, and no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of an environmental assessment.

Synopsis
I. Introduction
In this document, consistent with the directives of the Rural Broadband Protection Act of 2025 (RBPA), the Commission initiates a rulemaking to establish a vetting process for applicants for, and other recipients of, certain new funding awards of high-cost USF support.
With this NPRM, the Commission seeks comment on its proposals for implementing the RBPA, including the Commission's proposed interpretation of the Act's definition of “new covered funding awards” under its universal service rules, and what details and documentation an applicant will be required to provide to the Commission to demonstrate that it has the technical, financial, and operational capabilities to deploy and operate a USF-supported network that will meet program requirements. The Commission also invites comment on implementation of the RBPA's penalty framework for pre-authorization defaults.
II. Discussion
In proposing rules to implement RBPA's vetting process and penalties for pre-authorization defaults for future awards of new covered funding, the Commission largely tracks the relevant statutory language. The Commission seeks comment on proposals to implement the statutory language in its rules, generally, and with regard to each specific issue addressed in the following.
The Commission proposes to interpret the statute's definitions of “covered funding” and “new covered funding award” to comprise an award of high-cost support based on an application for funding to support the deployment of a broadband-capable network and the provision of supported services over the network. The Commission seeks comment on the proposal.
The Commission proposes to interpret “application” as used in the RBPA as an application for funding from a specific high-cost mechanism wherein the applicant is required to include information and/or certifications regarding technical, financial, and operational capabilities, including, but not limited to, applications for funding from high-cost mechanisms governed by subpart AA of the Commission's rules. Though the Commission could choose to include an RBPA-compliant vetting process in any future high-cost mechanism, its proposed interpretation of application would not require that of high-cost mechanisms that offer support to a carrier based on its Eligible Telecommunications Carrier (ETC) status and mode of FCC regulation (
i.e.,
rate-of-return or price cap). The Commission seeks comment on the proposal. The Commission's rules distinguish between high-cost mechanisms that require applications from potential funding recipients and other mechanisms. For example, the rules governing the Alternative-Connect America Cost Model (A-CAM) support mechanism state that a rate-of-return carrier receiving support pursuant to
47 CFR part 54, subparts K
(Connect America Fund Broadband Loop Support (CAF-BLS)) or M (High-Cost Loop Support (HCLS)) of the Commission's rules “shall have the opportunity to voluntarily elect, on a state-level basis, to receive Connect America Fund (CAF) A-CAM support as calculated by the A-CAM adopted by the Commission in lieu of support calculated pursuant to subparts K or M.” For rate-of-return carriers that continued receiving support from the CAF-BLS and/or HCLS high-cost mechanism, subparts K and M, respectively, of the Commission's rules detail how the support is calculated, and the information required from the support recipient has nothing to do with demonstrating technical, financial, or operational capabilities or the Commission vetting the recipient. Recipients of these mechanisms are vetted using the ETC designation process, which is not directly tied to receipt of support from any specific high-cost mechanism. In summary, these mechanisms offer support (and in some cases the possibility of electing a different support mechanism) to a class of carriers and do not contemplate an
(
printed page 75484)
“application” or specific applicant vetting, whereas
47 CFR part 1, subpart AA
of the Commission's rules enumerates extensive application requirements for carriers interested in participating in competitive bidding for USF support, and those rules are supplemented by further application requirements for each specific high-cost mechanism that employs competitive bidding.
The Commission further proposes to interpret the phrase “the deployment of a broadband-capable network and the provision of supported services over the network” as clarifying that the statute only applies to awards that include both of the two specified categories of funded activities, with “deployment” referring to construction of a network to serve a previously unserved location or upgrading the network to improve service at an underserved or unserved location and “provision of supported services” referring to maintaining existing service levels at a location. Therefore, funding that is being awarded only to maintain existing service levels would not be considered “covered funding” because it is not funding that supports deployment. Further, the Commission proposes that any new requirements adopted in this proceeding to establish a vetting process for a “new covered funding award” would not apply to any existing high-cost mechanisms for which the Commission had already adopted rules prior to enactment of the RBPA. The Commission seeks comment on its proposal and potential alternatives.
The Commission proposes adopting a new general Part 54 rule that would require new covered funding awards, offered through a competitive bidding mechanism or otherwise, to include a detailed RBPA-compliant vetting process. The RBPA provides the basic structure for the proposed new rule by directing the Commission to only award funding to applicants that can demonstrate through an initial application sufficient detail and documentation for the Commission to ascertain that the applicant possesses the technical, financial, and operational capabilities, and has a reasonable business plan, to deploy the proposed network and deliver services with the relevant performance characteristics and requirements defined by the Commission and as pledged by the applicant. The Commission seeks comment on the effectiveness of past and existing vetting frameworks and how those prior frameworks can inform the RBPA's vetting requirements for new covered funding awards. However, given that the Commission does not know what form a future mechanism for distributing “new covered funding awards” will take, it seeks comment on avoiding the adoption of a rigid, specific framework that must be used for all new covered funding awards. Instead, the Commission tentatively concludes that it is sufficient to require that future new covered funding awards meet the basic requirements of the RBPA. Specific requirements for evaluating applications for such new covered funding awards would instead be proposed and adopted as part of the proceedings to establish the program-specific requirements for such funding.
The plain language of the RBPA applies to an applicant's “initial application” for a new covered funding award, not an application to participate in competitive bidding. In the context of high-cost mechanisms that employ competitive bidding, the Commission seeks comment on whether the long-form application constitutes a winning bidder's “initial application” for a “new covered funding award.”
In the first stage of the Commission's well-established two-stage application process for high-cost mechanisms that use competitive bidding, an entity seeking to participate in the competition must provide information and a series of certifications in a short-form application used by the Commission to determine whether the applicant has the necessary legal, technical, and financial qualifications. A determination that an applicant is qualified to bid based on that application is not a determination of the applicant's eligibility for such support.
After competitive bidding concludes, a winning bidder has a binding obligation to file a timely and sufficient post-auction long-form application before it can be authorized to receive the support associated with its winning bid(s). The long-form application contains more extensive information about the winning bidder's qualifications, funding, and the network it intends to use to meet its public interest obligations and performance requirements, as well as a series of certifications, to demonstrate to the Commission that it is legally, technically, and financially qualified to receive the universal service support associated with its winning bids, which allows for a further in-depth review by the Commission of the winning bidder's qualifications prior to any authorization of support.
The Commission has found that requiring an in-depth review of extensive information only from winning bidders at the long-form stage balances the need to collect essential information from potential auction applicants with administrative efficiency and provides an appropriate screen at the pre-auction stage to ensure serious participation by qualified bidders without being unduly burdensome to potential auction participants. Before there is a known pool of applicants for a given competition, finding the optimal balance between encouraging participation and screening out unqualified applicants is difficult to do with any certainty. The Commission has observed in connection with the use of competitive bidding to award high-cost support “that maximizing the number of qualified participants in the competitive bidding process is likely to improve the overall quality of the process.”
In the interest of facilitating a robust and fulsome discussion of applicant vetting, the Commission seeks comment on whether there are further actions at the short-form application stage that, without contravening the purpose of the two-stage application process, could provide greater insight into an applicant's fitness to participate in competitive bidding for universal service support and its ability to meet the expectations of a support recipient. Would a more thorough application and intense vetting of applicants at the short-form stage prevent unqualified bidders from participating in the auction, and then defaulting prior to authorization, as was seen in the Rural Digital Opportunity Fund (RDOF)? Was that the intent of Congress in enacting the RBPA?
The Commission also seeks comment on whether it should require additional information at the long-form application stage to facilitate the Commission's review of winning bidders applying for new covered funding awards for universal service support. For example, to what extent does the Commission need to obtain information showing a realistic assessment that the provider's plans not only will enable the deployment of a network with the required technical and service capabilities that can be funded from available revenues but also the ability to meet pertinent deadlines specified in the program rules? Does the Commission need more specific and/or detailed information than it has received in the past regarding the provider's plans to address the types of challenges that routinely arise in connection with network deployments, such as weather, permitting, land access, or other considerations? The Commission further seeks comment on whether applicants with less experience providing the service(s) for which
(
printed page 75485)
support will be awarded, or which must be offered as a condition of support, should be required to undergo a more extensive vetting process. If so, how should the Commission categorize applicants based on experience? Could this framework be informed by the prior practice of creating two categories of applicants, those with at least two years of experience providing a voice, broadband, and/or electric transmission or distribution service and those with less than two? What information should be required for each category of applicant, and at what stage in the process?
The most recent use of competitive bidding for high-cost support (Auction 904) benefited from adapting lessons learned from vetting frameworks used by prior mechanisms and should serve as the starting point for discussion. The RDOF vetting framework is summarized in the following.
Applicants to participate in Auction 904 were required to submit:
The applicant's ownership information
Applicant information, including legal classification, jurisdiction of formation, address, contact information, and responsible individual
Information regarding any agreements relating to its participation in the auction
Description of the broadband technology the applicant planned to deploy
Recent audited financials (with more financial statements required from less experienced applicants)
A letter from a qualified bank committing to provide a letter of credit
Various certifications, including certifications regarding:
ETC status, including an acknowledgement that it must be designated as an ETC in the relevant areas prior to being authorized to receive support in those areas
Audited financial statements (applicants with at least two years of operational history that were not audited in the ordinary course of business were allowed to submit unaudited financials and certify that they would submit audited financials at the long-form stage if selected)
Compliance with statutory and regulatory requirements
Financial and technical capability to meet the relevant public interest obligations for each performance tier and latency combination in the geographic areas in which it seeks support
Availability of funds for all project costs that exceed the amount of support to be received for the first two years of its support term
Compliance with the relevant public interest obligations
Access to spectrum, if applicable
Information regarding earth station licenses for satellite technology, if applicable
Prior to being authorized to receive the support already won at auction, each winning bidder in Auction 904 was required to submit during the long-form application process:
Documentation of its designation as an ETC in all areas where it will receive support and ETC certification letter(s) from an officer of the applicant certifying that the ETC designation(s) covers all the areas where the applicant will receive support (submitted with long-form application if ETC designation(s) already obtained or no later than 180 days after the announcement of Auction 904 winning bidders if not yet obtained)
Audited financial statements (if not submitted during the pre-auction short-form process)
A detailed technology and system design description that explains how the design and technologies chosen will meet the relevant performance requirements, including information regarding quality, coverage, voice service, network management, and on-going operations, and a detailed network diagram that is certified by a professional engineer; the engineer must certify that the network is capable of delivering, to at least 95% of the required number of locations in each relevant state, voice and broadband service that meets the requisite performance requirements
A description of how the required construction will be funded in each state, specifying how high-cost support and other funds, if applicable, will be used to complete the project, with financial projections demonstrating that the applicant can cover the necessary debt service payments over the life of any loans
An irrevocable standby letter of credit issued by a qualified bank for each state in which it will be authorized to receive support that covers at least the first year of support to be received for the first-year support term for the state
A letter of credit bankruptcy opinion letter from outside legal counsel regarding the treatment of the letter(s) of credit or its proceeds in a bankruptcy proceeding
Similarly, as explained in this document, where the Commission has used a competitive application process, as opposed to competitive bidding, to award high-cost support to a chosen selectee, it has also used a two-stage application process for a selectee to become authorized to receive support, albeit with the inclusion of more extensive applicant information required at the first phase of the application process. Given the unique circumstances of the Bringing Puerto Rico Together (Uniendo a Puerto Rico) Fund and Connect USVI Fund (PR-USVI Funds) program and because the Commission does not know whether, and if so how, it may choose to implement a competitive application process to award support in a future high-cost program, the Commission seeks comment on what it should consider to be an “initial application” for a “new covered funding award” when using that type of process and the information that applicants should be required to include in the initial application.
For future high-cost programs that do not use a system of competitive bidding or another competitive application process to allocate universal service support, the Commission seeks to develop a record on the appropriate framework and content for an application for a new covered funding award under any such program in order to facilitate vetting of such applications in compliance with the RBPA.
For future high-cost programs covered by the RBPA for which support is not allocated through competitive bidding or another competitive application process, the Commission seeks comment on whether the application process and content used to apply for Auction 904 provide a good starting point for establishing the framework for initial applications for new covered funding awards. The Commission further seeks comment on both the substance and the timing for new covered funding award applications outside of a competitive process. In particular, the Commission seeks comment on whether, and if yes, how, it should modify or build upon the requirements used for Auction 904 to ensure the Commission can sufficiently ascertain an applicant's capabilities and conduct the vetting required under the RBPA. The Commission also seeks comment on whether any of these requirements are overly burdensome or not useful outside of a competitive process and should therefore not be
(
printed page 75486)
required. Commenters are free to use examples from other programs to inform their positions.
The two-phased RDOF vetting process solicits both (i) information that is probative of applicants' technical, financial, and operational capabilities, as well as (ii) additional information that is typically included in prudent business plans. To the extent that future high-cost support mechanisms subject recipients of new covered funding awards to a similarly detailed vetting process, the Commission seeks comment on whether there is a need to also require a business plan on top of the other required submissions. The Commission seeks comment on whether obtaining a substantial amount of information in vetting processes amounts to a “reasonable business plan” as required by the RBPA even if it is not required as part of a separately-labeled portion of the submission. Using the RDOF vetting process as the starting point for discussion, the Commission invites comment and welcomes proposals regarding what applicants should be required to show, if anything, beyond what was required of RDOF program applicants through the two-phased vetting process.
Under the RBPA, the Commission may only award covered funding to applicants that can demonstrate that they meet the qualifications. The RBPA states that the Commission must evaluate the applicant's proposal against “reasonable and well-established technical, financial, and operational standards, including the technical standards adopted by the Commission in orders of the Commission relating to Establishing the Digital Opportunity Data Collection (WC Docket No. 19-195) (or orders of the Commission relating to modernizing any successor collection) for purposes of entities that must report broadband availability coverage.”
Historically, the Commission did not adopt generally applicable standards and assumptions for reviewing information demonstrating a high-cost support applicant's capability given the fact-intensive, case-by-case nature of the review. The Commission benefits from the expertise of Commission engineers and/or other subject matter experts to discuss network plans with each applicant, including engineers and other specialists that support the applicant's operations and/or assisted with the application. Further, given the broad array of broadband technologies that compete in the communications marketplace and diverse terrain of areas needing service, it is difficult to develop one uniform set of evaluation standards for reviewing all applications and also maintain the principles of technology neutrality cited in the RBPA. The Commission invites comment on whether case-by-case evaluation is most appropriate to ensure that eligibility determinations are made consistently across all applications. The Commission welcomes proposals for a set of technical, financial, and operational standards that could be used for evaluating applicants for new covered funding awards in compliance with the RBPA.
The RBPA specifically references technical standards for entities that must report broadband availability coverage. These standards can be found in the Commission`s rules and in the Commission's published guides designed to support entities that must report broadband availability coverage. For example, providers of fixed wired broadband service must not exceed specific maximum buffer distances (which must include the drop distance) from their aggregation points to their served locations when reporting service availability based on their wired technologies, with specific maximum buffer distances for fiber to the premises and hybrid fiber-coax. Similarly, these rules provide certain factors when modeling terrestrial fixed wireless services, including the geographic coordinates of each base station, “the link budget and a description of the other parameters used in the propagation model, including predicted signal strength” and “receiver heights within a range of four to seven meters.” The Commission invites comment on how, for purposes of evaluating applicant technical capability, it could employ these technical standards when evaluating applicants for new covered funding awards.
Under the RBPA, the Commission must also evaluate the applicant's proposal in light of “the applicant's history of complying with requirements in Commission and other government broadband deployment funding programs.” Myriad state and Federal programs could fall under a broad definition of “other government broadband deployment funding programs.” Compliance with some programs may be relatively easier for the Commission to track than others. It may be harder to elicit information about compliance in other programs, such as those with minimal support for network deployment and some state programs. The Commission seeks comment on interpreting “other government broadband deployment funding programs” to mean those programs depicted in the FCC's Broadband Funding Map.
How can the Commission most efficiently and effectively obtain information from administrators of state and other Federal broadband deployment programs that have records of an applicant's compliance history? Should new participants be penalized for having no program compliance history? How should the Commission weigh an applicant's prior history of abiding by, or failure to comply with, program rules? What if the applicant was able to cure its prior non-compliance? How should defaults on awards under other broadband deployment funding programs be addressed? The Commission invites comment on how best to ensure these criteria are fairly and systematically applied across all applicants. The Commission also proposes and invites comment on requiring applicants to disclose if they have been suspended or debarred from other Federal broadband deployment funding programs or are currently subject to an ongoing suspension and debarment action. The Commission further invites comment on how a potential applicant's suspension or debarment status should affect its eligibility to pursue a new covered funding award.
Regarding the Commission's broadband deployment funding programs, applicants that failed to comply with the obligations of high-cost support are subject to the compliance measures in § 54.320 of the Commission's rules, and failure to comply may trigger further action, including suspension or debarment pursuant to rule § 54.8. The Commission invites comment on whether and how a potential applicant previously subject to a non-compliance action under rule § 54.320 should be encumbered in or prevented from pursuing a new covered funding award. For example, Auction 903 participants that subsequently defaulted on their entire award were barred from participating in Auction 904. Should potential applicants that previously substantially defaulted in a universal service program be barred from participating in future competitions for new covered funding awards? How would the Commission determine what constitutes a substantial default, or would it evaluate that default on a case-by-case basis? Should a substantial or complete default result in a ban on participating in all subsequent competitions, or only the next competition? Should a default result in a disadvantage instead of an outright ban? Should these determinations be made when future programs that will
(
printed page 75487)
make new covered funding awards are noticed?
The RBPA requires the Commission to “set a penalty for pre-authorization defaults of at least $9,000 per violation” and stipulates that it “may not limit the base forfeiture to an amount less than 30 percent of the applicant's total support, unless the Commission demonstrates the need for lower penalties in a particular instance.” The Commission believes this RBPA provision addresses defaults after an applicant becomes a winning bidder or is selected by the Commission to receive support, but before it is authorized to receive funding.
Regarding pre-authorization defaults, a winning bidder that fails to file an application by the applicable deadline or that for any reason is not subsequently authorized to receive support has defaulted on its bid. The Commission may dismiss a winning bidder's application with prejudice for failure of the winning bidder to prosecute, failure of the winning bidder to respond substantially within the time period specified in official correspondence or requests for additional information, or failure of the winning bidder to comply with requirements for becoming authorized to receive support. Any such determination by the Bureau shall be final upon public notice of the determination, and a winning bidder or long-form applicant shall have no opportunity to cure through additional submissions, negotiations, or otherwise. The Commission invites comment on retaining these definitions from
47 CFR 1.21004
and Auction 904.
The advent of the Commission's Broadband Serviceable Location Fabric opened new possibilities for defining service areas under new awards of covered funding. The Commission proposes to defer defining “violation” for the purposes of the RBPA until it adopts rules for specific high-cost mechanisms and identifies the geographic areas eligible for support. The Commission invites comment on the proposal.
Auction 904 limited the total base forfeiture to 15% of “the bidder's total assigned support for the Census Block Groups in which it is defaulting” to prevent the base forfeiture amount from being disproportionate to the amount of a winning bidder's bid. In light of Congress's desire to increase penalties for pre-authorization defaults, the Commission invites comment on defining “applicant's total support” as the entire amount of support won at auction, which could potentially increase penalties considerably. The Commission also invites proposals for alternative definitions, such as defining applicant's total support as the total defaulted bid amount. The Commission further invites comment on which factors would demonstrate the need for lower penalties in a particular instance, per section 254(m)(3)(D) of the Communications Act.
In the Commission's experience developing subsidy programs to spur deployment of broadband-capable networks, the Commission recognizes that program design can impact outcomes. Therefore, the Commission invites proposals addressing the design of high-cost support mechanisms that would reduce pre-authorization defaults, possibly through deterring potential applicants that are unlikely to meet program requirements if they receive support. The proposals could include limits on the number of locations an applicant can win relative to the number of locations that it currently serves or the applicant's current revenues—especially applicants that lack any current ETC designation or have not provided a voice, broadband, and/or electric transmission or distribution service for at least two years (or are not a wholly-owned subsidiary of such an entity). Commenters should address potential downsides of design proposals, including potentially hindering competition and rapidly exhausting program budgets. Proposals may also include solutions for expeditiously awarding support for locations that still need service after a winning bidder defaults, and specific penalties for post-authorization defaults when the Commission reasonably believes that the winning bidder did not intend to meet program requirements or otherwise acted in bad faith.

The NPRM seeks comment on proposals for implementing the RBPA, which directs the Commission to initiate a rulemaking proceeding to establish a vetting process for applicants for, and other recipients of, a new covered funding award. The NPRM also seeks comment on proposals for implementing the RBPA's penalties for pre-authorization defaults.
Specifically, the NPRM seeks comment on adopting a rule that would require future high-cost support mechanisms that will make new covered funding awards to include a vetting framework that requires proposals from applicants for funding to contain sufficient detail and documentation for the Commission to ascertain that the applicant possesses the technical, financial, and operational capabilities, and has a reasonable business plan, to deploy the proposed network and deliver services with the relevant performance characteristics and requirements defined by the Commission and as pledged by the applicant. The NPRM also seeks comment on the effectiveness of vetting frameworks used for prior high-cost support competitive bidding mechanisms but allows the details of the vetting framework to be determined when programs for new covered funding awards are noticed in the future.
The RFA directs agencies to provide a description of and, where feasible, an estimate of the number of small entities that may be affected by the proposed rules, if adopted. The RFA generally defines the term “small entity” as having the same meaning as the terms “small business,” “small organization,” and “small governmental jurisdiction.” In addition, the term “small business” has the same meaning as the term
(
printed page 75488)
“small business concern” under the Small Business Act. A “small business concern” is one which: (1) is independently owned and operated; (2) is not dominant in its field of operation; and (3) satisfies any additional criteria established by the Small Business Administration (SBA). The SBA establishes small business size standards that agencies are required to use when promulgating regulations relating to small businesses; agencies may establish alternative size standards for use in such programs, but must consult and obtain approval from SBA before doing so.
Commission actions, over time, may affect small entities that are not easily categorized at present. The Commission therefore describes three broad groups of small entities that could be directly affected by its actions. In general, a small business is an independent business having fewer than 500 employees. These types of small businesses represent 99.9% of all businesses in the United States, which translates to 34.75 million businesses. Next, “small organizations” are not-for-profit enterprises that are independently owned and operated and not dominant their field. While the Commission does not have data regarding the number of non-profits that meet that criteria, over 99 percent of nonprofits have fewer than 500 employees. Finally, “small governmental jurisdictions” are defined as cities, counties, towns, townships, villages, school districts, or special districts with populations of less than fifty thousand. Based on the 2022 U.S. Census of Governments data, the Commission estimates that at least 48,724 out of 90,835 local government jurisdictions have a population of less than 50,000.

The RFA directs agencies to describe the economic impact of proposed rules on small entities, as well as projected reporting, recordkeeping and other compliance requirements, including an estimate of the classes of small entities which will be subject to the requirements and the type of professional skills necessary for preparation of the report or record.
In the NPRM, the Commission seeks comment on proposals that, if adopted, would require future high-cost support program applicants, including small entities, to demonstrate that they possess the technical, financial, and operational capabilities to deploy the proposed network and deliver services with the relevant performance characteristics and requirements defined by the Commission. This includes proposed definitions for “covered funding” and the use of a two-stage application process for competitive bidding for high-cost support. Specifically, the NPRM seeks comment on the effectiveness of vetting frameworks used for prior high-cost support competitive bidding mechanisms while allowing the details of the vetting framework to be determined when programs for new covered funding awards are noticed in the future. The NPRM also seeks comment on proposals for implementing the RBPA's penalties for pre-authorization defaults.
The proposals in the NPRM would require that future high-cost support mechanisms that will make new covered funding awards include a vetting framework that complies with the RBPA, allowing the specifics of the framework to be detailed when the future high-cost mechanisms are noticed. This will allow the Commission to adopt a vetting framework that satisfies the RBPA and also comports with the specifics of a future mechanism that has not yet been proposed. Given that the proposed rules will not adopt the specific vetting framework to be used for future
(
printed page 75489)
programs, the Commission is uncertain of the impact on small entities at this time. However, small carriers that have participated in competitive bidding for high-cost support should be familiar with what is normally required of applicants for proving capabilities, such as audited financial statements, letters of credit, and ETC designation. The same measures have been used consistently across several mechanisms of competitive bidding for high-cost support and will likely be used in the future, perhaps with changes to the timing of the required submission during the competition. Under the RBPA, carriers will have greater certainty regarding the penalties for pre-authorization defaults on new covered funding awards. The proposed rules will only apply to future high-cost support mechanisms that make new covered funding awards. The Commission's previous competitive bidding programs for high-cost support attracted a broad array of applicants, including small entities. Before reaching its final conclusions and taking action in this proceeding, the Commission expects to review the comments filed in response to the
NPRM,
including costs and benefits of these proposed rules, and more fully consider the economic impact on small entities and how any impact can be minimized.
The RFA directs agencies to provide a description of any significant alternatives to the proposed rules that would accomplish the stated objectives of applicable statutes, and minimize any significant economic impact on small entities. The discussion is required to include alternatives such as: “(1) the establishment of differing compliance or reporting requirements or timetables that take into account the resources available to small entities; (2) the clarification, consolidation, or simplification of compliance and reporting requirements under the rule for such small entities; (3) the use of performance rather than design standards; and (4) an exemption from coverage of the rule, or any part thereof, for such small entities.”
In the NPRM, the Commission proposes new rules that may impact small entities and seeks comment on alternatives that may minimize any significant economic impact on small providers. Specifically, the Commission invites comment on alternative approaches for vetting applicants for future, new covered funding awards. This includes whether to request additional information, such as a business plan, with their application. The NPRM also seeks comment on whether small and other applicants that previously defaulted in a universal service program should be eligible to compete in new covered funding awards, and whether a history of compliance with other state and Federal programs should be included with the application. Alternative proposals and approaches from commenters will further develop the record and could help the Commission further minimize the economic impact on small entities. The Commission's evaluation of the comments filed in this proceeding will shape the final conclusions it reaches, the final alternatives it considers, and the actions it ultimately takes to minimize any possible economic impact the final rules may have on small entities.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
This action proposes to amend Class D and Class E airspace over Lebanon, NH. This action would increase the lateral dimensions of the Lebanon, NH, Class D airspace to appropriately contain Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) operations at the Lebanon Municipal Airport. This action would also update verbiage in the Class D airspace legal description to comply with current FAA guidance. This action would also update the geographic coordinates for the airport in both the Class D and Class E5 airspace legal descriptions. This action would also remove the exclusions for adjacent Class E5 airspace from the Lebanon, NH, Class E5 airspace legal description. This action would also remove the Lebanon, NH, Class E4 airspace, which is no longer necessary for IFR operations at the airport.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it would amend Class D and Class E airspace in Lebanon, NH.
(
printed page 75461)
Comments Invited
The FAA invites interested persons to participate in this rulemaking by submitting written comments, data, or views. Comments are specifically invited on the overall regulatory, aeronautical, economic, environmental, and energy-related aspects of the proposal. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. To ensure the docket does not contain duplicate comments, commenters should submit only one time if comments are filed electronically, or commenters should send only one copy of written comments if comments are filed in writing.
The FAA will file in the docket all comments it receives, as well as a report summarizing each substantive public contact with FAA personnel concerning this proposed rulemaking. Before acting on this proposal, the FAA will consider all comments it receives on or before the closing date for comments. The FAA will consider comments filed after the comment period has closed if it is possible to do so without incurring expense or delay. The FAA may change this proposal in light of the comments it receives.

Incorporation by Reference
Class D and Class E airspace designations are published in paragraphs 5000, 6004, and 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in
14 CFR 71.1
on an annual basis. This document proposes to amend the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These updates would be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Proposal
This action proposes to amend
14 CFR part 71
by modifying Class D and Class E airspace over Lebanon, NH. An evaluation of the Lebanon, NH, Class D and Class E airspace revealed a need for an increase to the dimensions of the Class D airspace as well as a removal of the associated Class E4 airspace in order to appropriately contain IFR operations at Lebanon Municipal Airport. This action would increase the lateral dimensions of the Lebanon, NH, Class D airspace to within a 4.8-mile radius of Lebanon Municipal Airport; and within 1.3 miles each side of the 349° bearing from the airport extending from the 4.8-mile radius to 6.4 miles north of the airport; and within 1.1 miles each side of the 058° bearing from the airport extending from the 4.8-mile radius to 6.5 miles northeast of the airport; and within 1.1 miles each side of the 182° bearing from the airport extending from the 4.8-mile radius to 5.6 miles south of the airport; and within 1.2 miles each side of the 225° bearing from the airport extending from the 4.8-mile radius to 5.3 miles southwest of the airport.
This action would also remove the Lebanon, NH, Class E4 airspace. This action would also update the superseded term “Airport/Facility Directory” to “Chart Supplement” in the Lebanon, NH Class D airspace legal description. This action would also update the geographic coordinates of the airport in the Class D and Class E5 airspace legal descriptions from (lat. 43°37′35″ N, long. 72°18′15″ W) to (lat. 43°37′34″ N, long. 72°18′15″ W), which is one second of latitude. This action would also remove the exclusions for the adjacent Class E5 airspace from the Class E5 airspace legal description to comply with current FAA guidance.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this proposed regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore, (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Rulemaking and Guidance Procedure” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these proposed amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this proposed rule, when promulgated, will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
This proposal will be subject to an environmental analysis in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures” prior to any FAA final regulatory action.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
On May 8, 2024, we published a final rule amending the horse protection regulations. The final rule was initially scheduled to go into effect on February 1, 2025, except for § 11.19, which was effective on June 7, 2024. On January 28, 2025, we published a postponement of the effective date of the remaining provisions from February 1, 2025, to April 2, 2025. On March 21, 2025, we published a further delay of the effective date to February 1, 2026, and a request for comment on whether the length of the postponement should be extended. On January 28, 2026, based on developments following the issuance of the March 21, 2025, delay of effective date, we published a document further delaying the effective date of the final rule to December 31, 2026. On November 13, 2026, we published a proposed rule to remove parts of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule that were vacated by Court order from the regulations, as well as proposing to withdraw the non-vacated parts and update the regulations. As a consequence, in this document, we are issuing an extension of the postponement of the effective date of the final rule to December 31, 2027.

), are further delayed until December 31, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Martha Keller, DVM, Director of the Center for Animal Welfare, Animal Care, 2150 Centre Ave. Bldg. B, Mailstop 3W11, Fort Collins, CO 80526; (970) 821-5734.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Under the Horse Protection Act (HPA, or the Act,
15 U.S.C. 1821
et seq.
), the Secretary of Agriculture is authorized to promulgate regulations to carry out the purposes of the Act, which include eliminating the cruel practice of soring horses and promoting fair competition.
The Secretary has delegated responsibility for administering the Act to the Administrator of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS). Within APHIS, the responsibility for administering the Act has been delegated to the Deputy Administrator for Animal Care. Regulations and standards established under the Act are contained in
9 CFR part 11
(referred to below as the regulations), and
9 CFR part 12
lists the rules of practice governing administrative proceedings.
On May 8, 2024, APHIS published in the
Federal Register
(
89 FR 39194-39251
, APHIS-2022-0004)
[
1
]
, a final rule titled “Horse Protection Amendments” (2024 Horse Protection final rule) that was to be effective on February 1, 2025, except for § 11.19, which had an effective date of June 7, 2024.
On January 28, 2025, APHIS published in the
Federal Register
(
90 FR 8253-8254
, APHIS-2022-0004),
[
2
]
a postponement of the regulations in the 2024 Horse Protection final rule, which delayed the effective date of sections 11.1 through 11.18 of that rule until April 2, 2025. In the postponement, we noted that, on July 1, 2024, a complaint was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas and amended on September 23, 2024.
[
3
]
The amended complaint alleged, in part, that the 2024 Horse Protection final rule exceeded APHIS' statutory authority and would have a significant economic impact on the Tennessee Walking Horse industry altogether. The amended complaint requested vacatur of the final rule. The parties completed briefing on their cross motions for summary judgment on December 20, 2024.
In the postponement, we explained that we were taking the action pursuant to section 705 of the Administrative Procedure Act to temporarily preserve the regulatory status quo during the pendency of the litigation.
On January 31, 2025, the U.S. District Court issued its decision.
[
4
]
The Court held that the prohibition on the use of action devices, pads, and substances in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule had exceeded APHIS' statutory authority; that a “Dermatologic Conditions Indicative of Soring” provision intended to replace the “scar rule” failed to provide adequate due process; and that the rule's pre- and post-deprivation reviews failed to provide adequate due process. In the order, the Court vacated the above provisions, found in §§ 11.5, 11.6(c), 11.7, and 11.8(h) of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule. However, the Court held that the final rule's replacement of the Designated Qualified Persons (DQP) program with Horse Protection Inspectors (HPIs) did not exceed the USDA's statutory authority, was not arbitrary and capricious, and did not violate the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Following the Court's decision, on March 21, 2025, APHIS published in the
Federal Register
(
90 FR 13273-13276
)
[
5
]
a document announcing a further delay of the effective date to February 1, 2026, and a request for comment regarding whether the length of the postponement should be extended. In that document, APHIS explained that postponement would allow it the necessary time to identify appropriate next steps regarding the regulations, including whether the length of the postponement
(
printed page 75440)
should be further extended. We also stated that allowing the non-vacated portions of the rule to go into effect on April 2, 2025, the previously scheduled effective date, would be untenable for APHIS and disruptive to the industry. We explained that we were taking the action pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
,
553(d)(1)
and
553(d)(3)
.
We solicited comments concerning the length of the postponement for 60 days ending May 20, 2025. We received 6,124 submissions indicative of 93,734 total comments in response to our request. The comments were from members of Congress; State agricultural agencies and farm bureaus; HIOs; equine veterinarians and veterinary associations; animal welfare advocacy organizations; cattle grower associations; horse owners, trainers, and exhibitors; small business owners; and other interested persons.
After the close of the comment period, on June 30, 2025, a new complaint was filed in the U.S. District for the Northern District of Texas
[
6
]
challenging aspects of the current regulations and associated guidance. Specifically, the complaint challenged USDA's “No-Showback Rule,” (
i.e.,
a policy prohibiting noncompliant horses from participating in any subsequent class of the same show), the scar rule, and the adequacy of the due process protections when management disqualifies a horse based on USDA inspection findings. Plaintiffs sought entry of a preliminary injunction to prevent USDA from enforcing these rules and policies.
On August 19, 2025, the Court granted plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction.
[
7
]
In its decision, the Court determined that the No-Showback Rule likely exceeds the USDA's statutory authority because the HPA requires disqualification only when a horse is found sore at the time of inspection. The Court likewise found that the existing scar rule likely goes beyond the scope of the Act by allowing disqualification based solely on indicators of past soring without evidence of current soreness. Additionally, the Court concluded that the inspection procedures in the current regulations likely fail to provide constitutionally required pre-deprivation review because they do not provide the opportunity for a hearing, or for anyone to contest a USDA inspector's decision, prior to a horse being disqualified from an event.  Due to the then-pending lawsuit and the uncertainty of how it would affect the existing regulations, APHIS published in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 3633-3635
, Docket No. APHIS-2022-0004)
[
8
]
a document further delaying the effective date of the non-vacated portions of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule, to December 31, 2026.
Additionally, in a report (H.R. Rep. 118-583) accompanying the FY 2026 Agriculture Appropriations Act, the House Appropriations Committee expressed concern regarding the 2024 Horse Protection final rule, stating the following: “The Committee has consistently recognized the need for APHIS and the Tennessee Walking Horse industry to communicate and work together to eliminate the soring of horses. The Committee is concerned that the final rule, Horse Protection Amendments, published May 8, 2024 (
89 FR 39194
), ignores the strong concerns of and comments submitted by industry experts, is based on out-of-date and unreliable data, and exceeds the agency's legal authority under the Horse Protection Act. Further, the cost-benefit analysis accompanying the rule relies on data that is over a decade old and severely underestimates the impact the rule will have on the 20,000 jobs supported by the Tennessee Walking Horse industry. The Committee reiterates that an objective, science-based inspection system would provide assurance for both accuracy and fairness. Therefore, the Committee directs APHIS to withdraw the final rule and work with the industry to eliminate soring using objective, science-based protocols.” (H.R. Rep. 118-583, at 37.) In our January 28, 2026, document announcing the further delay of effective date, we stated that postponement would also allow APHIS to complete its ongoing review of the Committee's report.
Consistent with the January 2025 U.S. District Court order vacating the 2024 Horse Protection final rule's prohibitions on action devices, pads, and substances on TWHs and racking horses, the DCIS provision, and APHIS' re-inspection and appeals procedures, on November 13, 2026, APHIS published in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 73380-73421
; Docket No. APHIS-2026-0067)
[
9
]
a proposed rule to remove §§ 11.5, 11.6(c), 11.7, and 11.8(h) of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule from the regulations, as well as proposing to withdraw the remaining parts of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule that were not vacated and to update the current Part 11 regulations to reflect expert recommendations and Congressional direction. We stated in that document that we are soliciting comments on the proposed rule for 30 days, ending on December 14, 2026.
As stated earlier in this document, the 2024 Horse Protection final rule is scheduled to go into effect on December 31, 2026. Because the length of time between the end of the comment period of the November 13, 2026, proposed rule and the effective date of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule does not provide the Agency with enough time to review comments received on the proposed rule, any final rule following the November 13, 2026, proposed rule would be issued after the effective date of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule. Allowing the partially vacated 2024 Horse Protection final rule to go into effect while the Agency is reviewing comments and preparing a final rule following the November 13, 2026, proposed rule, that, among other provisions, proposed withdrawal of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule, would almost certainly have disruptive consequences and result in “regulatory whiplash” that could prove costly to the regulated industry.
For these reasons, we are extending the postponement of effective date of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule to December 31, 2027. Further postponing the effective date will allow APHIS the necessary time to review comments received on the November 13, 2026, proposed rule and, if appropriate, subsequently issue a final rule.
APHIS is taking this action, effective immediately, based on the good cause exceptions in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
and
553(d)(3)
. The need for regulatory clarity in this context satisfies the good-cause requirement. Additionally, APHIS has determined that it would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest to provide notice and comment on this action to postpone the effective date of the non-vacated provisions of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule to December 31, 2027, because there is not sufficient time to conduct an additional notice-and-comment process between now and December 31, 2026. Moreover, we are soliciting notice-and-comment until December 14, 2026 on the November 13, 2026, proposed rule to withdraw the non-vacated provisions and update the regulations.

—Decisions of other IMO bodies
—Amendments to mandatory instruments
—Goal-based new ship construction standards
—Development of a goal-based instrument for maritime autonomous surface ships (MASS)

—Carriage of cargoes and containers (Urgent matters emanating from the twelfth session of the Sub-Committee)
—Application of the Committee's method of work
—Work programme
—Election of Chair and Vice-Chair for 2027
—Any other business
—Consideration of the report of the Committee on its 112th session
Please note:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission has received a complaint and a submission pursuant to § 210.8(b) of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure filed on behalf of New Balance Athletics, Inc. on November 18, 2026. The complaint alleges violations of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (
19 U.S.C. 1337
) in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain athletic footwear. The complaint names as respondents: Wenzhou Zibo Trading Co., Ltd. of China; and Wenzhou Bobo International Trade. Co., Ltd. of China. The complainant requests that the Commission issue a limited exclusion order, cease and desist orders and impose a bond upon respondents' alleged infringing articles during the 60-day Presidential review period pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1337(j)
.
Proposed respondents, other interested parties, members of the public, and interested government agencies are invited to file comments on any public interest issues raised by the complaint or § 210.8(b) filing. Comments should address whether issuance of the relief specifically requested by the complainant in this investigation would affect the public health and welfare in the United States, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, or United States consumers.
In particular, the Commission is interested in comments that:
(i) explain how the articles potentially subject to the requested remedial orders are used in the United States;
(ii) identify any public health, safety, or welfare concerns in the United States relating to the requested remedial orders;
(iii) identify like or directly competitive articles that complainant, its licensees, or third parties make in the United States which could replace the subject articles if they were to be excluded;
(iv) indicate whether complainant, complainant's licensees, and/or third party suppliers have the capacity to replace the volume of articles potentially subject to the requested exclusion order and/or a cease and desist order within a commercially reasonable time; and
(v) explain how the requested remedial orders would impact United States consumers.
Written submissions on the public interest must be filed no later than by close of business, eight calendar days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. There will be further opportunities for comment on the public interest after the issuance of any final initial determination in this investigation. Any written submissions on other issues must also be filed by no later than the close of business (5:15 p.m.)
[
1
]

Federal Register
. Complainant(s) may file replies to any written submissions no later than three calendar days after the date on which the written submissions were due. Notwithstanding § 201.14(a) of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, the deadlines for written submissions and replies shall be counted by calendar days starting with the first calendar day following the
Federal Register
publication date or the due date for written submissions, respectively. The provisions of § 201.14(a) regarding the last day of the period still apply concerning the due date of any filings. No other submissions will be accepted, unless requested by the Commission. Any submissions and replies filed in response to this Notice are limited to five (5) pages in length, inclusive of attachments.
Persons filing written submissions must file the original document electronically on or before the deadlines stated above. Submissions should refer to the docket number (“Docket No. 3954”) in a prominent place on the cover page and/or the first page. (

AGENCY:
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
ACTION:
Notice of public meeting.
SUMMARY:
Under the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), this notice sets forth the announcement of a public meeting of the Consumer Advisory Board (CAB or Board) of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB or Bureau). The notice also describes the functions of the Board.
DATES:
The meeting date is Thursday, December 3, 2026, from approximately 11:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., eastern standard time. This meeting will be held virtually and is open to the general public. Members of the public will receive the agenda and dial-in information when they RSVP.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Kim George, Outreach and Engagement Associate, Advisory Board and Councils, External Affairs Division, at 202-450-8617, or email:
CFPB_CABandCouncilsEvents@cfpb.gov
.
If you require this document in an alternative electronic format, please contact
CFPB_Accessibility@cfpb.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Section 3 of the Charter of the Board states that: The purpose of the CAB is outlined in section 1014(a) of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, which states that the CAB shall “advise and consult with the Bureau in the exercise of its functions under the Federal consumer financial laws” and “provide information on emerging practices in the consumer financial products or services industry, including regional trends, concerns, and other relevant information.”
To carry out the CAB's purpose, the scope of its activities shall include providing information, analysis, and recommendations to the CFPB. The CAB will generally serve as a vehicle for trends and themes in the consumer finance marketplace for the CFPB. Its objectives will include identifying and assessing the impact on consumers and other market participants of new, emerging, and changing products, practices, or services.
II. Agenda
The CAB will discuss broad policy matters related to the Bureau's Unified Regulatory Agenda and general scope of authority. During this meeting, the topic of discussion will be Frauds and Scams Targeting Servicemembers and Older Americans.
If you require any additional reasonable accommodation(s) in order to attend this event, please contact the Reasonable Accommodations team at
CFPB_ReasonableAccommodations@cfpb.gov
48 hours prior to the start of this event.
Written comments will be accepted from interested members of the public and should be sent to
CFPB_CABandCouncilsEvents@cfpb.gov
,
a minimum of seven (7) days in advance of the meeting. The comments will be provided to the CAB members for consideration. Individuals who wish to join this meeting must RSVP via this link
https://events.gcc.teams.microsoft.com/​event/​e6083efe-35a1-4cc4-ac19-2ae585ef7e38@c817bf69-ef41-4ed6-ac5f-1f44da3798c0?​source=​copyLinkLegacyShareEventDialog
.
III. Availability
The Board's agenda will be made available to the public on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, via
consumerfinance.gov.
A recording and summary of this meeting will be available after the meeting on the Bureau's website
consumerfinance.gov.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission instituted this investigation on August 19, 2026, based on a complaint filed on behalf of Ayr Energy, Inc. of Mountain View, California (“Complainant”).
91 FR 53
,
631
(Aug. 19, 2026). The complaint, as supplemented, alleged violations of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended,
19 U.S.C. 1337
, in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain transformers and components thereof by reason of misappropriation of trade secrets, false advertising, unfair competition, trademark infringement, false designation of origin, and common law trademark infringement, the threat or effect of which is to destroy or substantially injure an industry in the United States or to prevent the establishment of such an industry. The Commission's notice of investigation named the following respondents: Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses Private Limited of Bangalore, India; Zetwerk Manufacturing USA Inc. of San Francisco, California; Kryfs Power Components Ltd. of Bandra (W), India; and Unimacts Global, LLC of Lexington, Massachusetts (collectively, “Respondents”). The Office of Unfair Import Investigations (“OUII”) was also named as a party in this investigation.
On September 28, 2026, the Complainant and Respondents filed a joint motion to terminate the investigation in its entirety based on settlement. OUII filed a response in support of the motion.
On October 22, 2026, the ALJ issued the subject ID (Order No. 10), granting the joint motion to terminate the investigation based on settlement. The ID found the motion and the revised public version of the settlement agreement comply with the Commission Rules (
19 CFR 210.21(b)
). ID at 1-2. The motion certifies that “there are no other agreements, written or oral, express or implied, between the parties concerning the subject matter of the Investigation.”
Id.
at 2. The ID also found that termination of this investigation by settlement will not adversely affect the public interest.
Id.
at 3. No petitions for review were filed.
The Commission has determined not to review the subject ID. The investigation is terminated in its entirety.

ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
In this document, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau (Bureau) of the Federal Communications Commission (Commission or FCC) seeks comment on recommendations for the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark (USCTM) program, a voluntary cybersecurity labeling program for wireless consumer Internet of Things (IoT) products. The Bureau seeks comment on the design and placement of the FCC IoT Label, display of product registry information, certification renewal, post-market surveillance, and procedures for complaints, noncompliant products, and program administrators that withdraw or whose authority is terminated. These actions would support the establishment and effective administration of the USCTM program and provide consumers with accessible cybersecurity information about certified IoT products.
DATES:
Comments are due on or before December 23, 2026; reply comments are due on or before January 7, 2027.
