Need for, and Objectives of, the Proposed Rules.
The
IoT Labeling Order
adopted a voluntary cybersecurity labeling program for consumer Internet of Things (IoT) products (U.S. Cyber Trust Mark (USCTM) Program) that will provide consumers with an easy-to-understand indicator of a product's relative cybersecurity and improve consumer confidence and understanding of IoT product cybersecurity. Under the USCTM Program, authorized products will bear the FCC IoT Label, including the Mark and a QR code that links to easily understandable security-related information about the product. While the Commission retains ultimate control and oversight as the USCTM Program owner, the program is supported by a Lead Administrator and Cybersecurity Label Administrators (CLAs). The Lead Administrator acts as the point of contact between CLAs, which are responsible for certifying use of the FCC IoT Label and the day-to-day management of the program, and the Commission. Further, in collaboration with the CLAs and other stakeholders, the Lead Administrator is required to undertake tasks associated with the launch of the program, including identifying or developing certain recommendations.
In June 2025, the USCTM Lead Administrator, in collaboration with stakeholders (Stakeholder Committee), submitted its recommendations for technical requirements, label requirements, and renewal and surveillance requirements, consistent with the IoT Labeling Order. In April 2026, the Bureau selected the ioXt Alliance (ioXt) to serve as the new Lead Administrator following the prior Lead Administrator's withdrawal. On October 26, 2026, ioXt submitted additional recommendations with respect to technical requirements only, as a result of ongoing stakeholder engagement. The Bureau will seek comment on the technical requirements recommendations in a subsequent Public Notice.
However, in this
Notice,
we seek comment on the
Label Standard
and
Renewal and Surveillance Document.
In particular, we seek comment on the design of the FCC IoT Label, certification renewal processes, and procedures for post-market surveillance and auditing of USCTM-certified products. The Bureau also seeks comment on other related aspects of the program, including procedures to address complaints, non-complying products, and administrator withdrawal or termination. The Commission delegated authority to the Bureau to evaluate the recommendations and, if the Bureau approves of the recommendations, subject to any required public notice and comment, adopt them into the Commission's rules.

Description of Projected Reporting, Recordkeeping, and Other Compliance Requirements for Small Entities.
The RFA directs agencies to describe the economic impact of proposed rules on small entities, as well as projected reporting, recordkeeping and other compliance requirements, including an estimate of the classes of small entities which will be subject to the requirements and the type of professional skills necessary for preparation of the report or record.
The USCTM Program will be voluntary, so small entities who do not participate in the program will not be subject to any new or modified reporting, recordkeeping, or other compliance obligations. Small entities that choose to participate in the program will incur recordkeeping, reporting, and other compliance obligations necessary to test their IoT products to demonstrate compliance with the program requirements. Small entities that choose to participate by applying to be a CLA or CyberLAB will also incur recordkeeping, reporting, and other compliance obligations. In this
Notice,
we propose record-related compliance obligations for a Lead Administrator or CLA that intends to withdraw from the program. Specifically, we propose to require CLAs to provide copies of all records relating to applications and authorization to use the FCC IoT Label, the use of the FCC IoT Label, post-market surveillance, and complaints with respect to rules of the USCTM Program to the Lead Administrator upon request by the Lead Administrator, including but not limited to, when they withdraw from the program and which may be requested before or after the effective date of the CLA's withdrawal. We propose to require each CLA to cooperate with the Lead Administrator with transferring responsibilities to the manufacturer's new CLA of choice, including the transfer of USCTM Program records even if such transfer occurs after the effective date of the CLA's withdrawal. We propose that the records the CLA would be required to transfer to the new CLA include (but would not be limited to) those associated with the CLA's processing of manufacturer applications to include approved, denied, and pending applications; complaints (pending and completed); audits; renewals; and Trademark Use Agreements. We propose to require CLAs to retain these records for a minimum of the term of their Trademark Use Agreement, plus five years thereafter. We also propose to require CLAs to provide the Bureau with a copy of the grantee's records no later than five business days after receiving a request to do so. Administrators will also be required to comply with the timeframes applicable for any federal records as to preservation and disposal of such records.
We propose the same for Lead Administrators, in their capacity as a CLA, including cooperating with the Bureau to transfer responsibilities to a new Lead Administrator, including the transfer of USCTM Program records, even if such transfer occurs after the effective date of the Lead Administrator's withdrawal. We seek comment on these requirements and any additional information that should be provided by outgoing CLAs to new CLAs, as well as any additional actions the outgoing CLA should take for a smooth transition, without interruption to the program.
Discussion of Significant Alternatives Considered That Minimize the Significant Economic Impact on Small Entities.
The RFA directs agencies to provide a description of any significant alternatives to the proposed rules that would accomplish the stated objectives of applicable statutes, and minimize any
(
printed page 75478)
significant economic impact on small entities. The discussion is required to include alternatives such as: “(1) the establishment of differing compliance or reporting requirements or timetables that take into account the resources available to small entities; (2) the clarification, consolidation, or simplification of compliance and reporting requirements under the rule for such small entities; (3) the use of performance rather than design standards; and (4) an exemption from coverage of the rule, or any part thereof, for such small entities.”
For the USCTM Program to be meaningful to consumers, the requirements for an IoT product to be granted authority to use the FCC IoT Label must be uniform for small businesses and other entities. The Bureau maintains the view expressed in the
IoT Labeling Order
that the significance of Mark integrity, and building confidence among consumers that devices and products bearing the FCC IoT Label can be trusted to be cyber secure, necessitates adherence by all entities participating in the program to the same rules, regardless of size. Accordingly, in the
Notice,
the Bureau takes steps to minimize the economic impact on participants in the program of all sizes, including small entities. Specifically, we seek comment on labeling and post-market surveillance requirements, based on recommendations in the
Label Standard
and
Renewal and Surveillance Document.
With respect to the label, we propose to allow manufacturers to print the label directly on product packaging or apply it as an adhesive sticker. We also propose and seek comment on details related to the layout and sizing of the physical label, as well as marketing and advertising of products that bear the label. For each of these proposals, we invite the public, including small businesses, to comment.
Regarding renewal and surveillance, we seek comment on the initial and renewal application information, the renewal period and process, post-market surveillance requirements, and follow-up actions. We propose a three-year renewal cycle to balance consumer protection concerns with the burden on manufacturers and request comment on whether there are modifications or opportunities to streamline the process that might further reduce burdens on manufacturers, including small entities. We also seek comment on the USCTM “Qualified Professional,” that the
Renewal and Surveillance Document
recommends. In particular, we ask whether the expected benefits of such a role outweigh the costs and whether there are alternatives to such a role that may be less costly for manufacturers, many of whom may be small businesses, or whether we should decline to adopt this recommendation. We propose a 90 calendar day deadline for manufacturers to complete renewal evaluations, which we believe provides added flexibility to manufacturers and CLAs and seek comment on this proposal. For post-market surveillance, we seek comment on the format and content of annual reports that CLAs must submit to the Lead Administrator. We invite commenters to make recommendations that minimize the economic impact on CLAs that may be small entities. We also seek comment on post-termination or disqualification procedures that may be more or less burdensome for manufacturers, including small businesses, that fail to comply with program requirements or are otherwise disqualified.
In comments, small entities can identify which of the proposals raised in this
Public Notice
are particularly difficult or costly for them and how different, simplified, or consolidated requirements would address those burdens. They can also propose any modifications to the proposals that would minimize their anticipated economic impact. The Bureau expects to consider more fully the economic impact on small entities following its review of any comments filed in response to the
Public Notice,
including any costs and benefits information we receive. The Bureau's evaluation of the comments filed in this proceeding will shape the final alternatives we consider, the final conclusions we reach, and any final actions we ultimately take in this proceeding to minimize any significant economic impact that may occur on small entities.

(6) Date(s) on which each grantee received each authorization to use the Trust Mark;
(7) The authorizing CLA (if different);
(8) A description of changes to the IoT product since it was last evaluated;
(9) A copy of all document(s) related to the granting of authorization to the grantee to use the Trust Mark, including the original application and all CyberLAB report(s); and
(10) A test report conducted by a CyberLAB testing the product against any new or revised USCTM Program requirements and 70% of the remaining requirements (those that are not new or revised).
(d) The CLA shall evaluate the product certification renewal as follows:
(1) Evaluate the product against all new and revised requirements published by the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program since the product's certification or previous renewal;
(2) Re-evaluate at least 70% of all remaining applicable program requirements (those that are not new or revised) and re-evaluate 100% of all remaining applicable program requirements if at least one instance of non-compliance is found;
(3) Verify that certification for each Backend component that supports the IoT Product is current according to the respective program's validity periods;
(4) Conduct an in-person or remote audit to confirm that the grantee continues to maintain the documents required by § 8.XXX of this part. In addition, review implementation proofs as defined in § 8.XXX of this part performed within the last three months and information regarding the latest security/patch updates shall be provided as verification that processes continue to be implemented.
(5) Confirm the grantee has maintained a U.S. Cyber Trust Mark Qualified Professional for the duration of the grantee's certification period or since the date of last renewal, whichever is more recent.
(d)
USCTM Qualified Professional.
Grantees must notify the CLA who performed the original assessment of any changes to the product or relevant documentation that impact compliance to applicable program requirements. To provide for the consistent identification of compliance-relevant changes, grantee organizations must appoint and maintain a U.S. Cyber Trust Mark Qualified Professional on staff.
(1) The grantee shall appoint the USCTM Qualified Professional(s), ensuring that the designee has obtained, and continues to maintain, appropriate qualifications. If the designated USCTM Qualified Professional leaves the grantee's organizations or is no longer serving in the role, the grantee must notify the CLA(s) that issued the grantee's product certification of the vacancy. The grantee must fill the vacancy for the USCTM Qualified Professional within six months.
(2) To be designated as a grantee organization's USCTM Qualified Professional, the staff member must have:
(i) Completed an approved course on the requirements of the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark Program including the program's scheme requirements;
(ii) Successfully passed the exam associated with the approved course; and
(iii) Confirmed receipt of information from the FCC and the Lead Administrator regarding major changes to the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program that impact the USCTM Qualified Professional's roles and activities.
(3) To maintain status as a USCTM Qualified Professional an individual shall:
(i) Confirm receipt of information from the FCC and the Lead Administrator regarding major changes to the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program that impact the USCTM Qualified Professional's role and activities; and
(ii) Repeat course and exam requirements every three years.
Note 1 to paragraph (d)(4): These placeholders are for technical requirements that the Bureau will seek comment on in a subsequent Public Notice.
§ 8.225
Post-Market Surveillance and Ad-Hoc Surveillance.
(a)
Post-Market Surveillance.
CLAs shall apply the following processes to fulfill their post-market surveillance obligations under § 8.220(g).
(1)
Sample Test Plan.
CLAs shall develop a written plan describing how they will ensure that the proper percentage of representative certificated products are tested. CLAs shall submit a Sample Test Plan specific for a given 12-month period to the Lead Administrator annually in September. The Lead Administrator in its role as a CLA will submit its Sample Test Plan to the Bureau annually in September. The Lead Administrator, and the Bureau for the Lead Administrator's Sample Test Plan, will review the Sample Test Plan to ensure it is sufficiently robust to identify and mitigate evolving vulnerabilities throughout a product's life cycle and to ensure consistency among test plans. Lead Administrator will provide CLAs' Sample Test Plan to the Bureau upon request.
(2)
CLA Notification to Grantees.
CLAs shall provide their grantees with a copy of the Lead Administrator approved Sample Test Plan. CLA will also notify grantees in writing that:
(i) CLAs must conduct post-market surveillance sampling.
(ii) The grantee must ensure the availability of production samples at least until the longer of either the end
(
printed page 75481)
date of the support period communicated on the product registry or no less than one year after the last production date, whichever period is longer.
(iii) The grantee may be required to submit the product for post-market surveillance testing, and that these samples may be requested, at any time, by either the CLA or the Bureau.
(iv) The failure to provide samples within 30 days of the request may result in withdrawal of certification.
(3)
Sample Selection.
Samples audited by a CLA shall be selected from the products certified or renewed by that CLA over the current year or the two-year period directly preceding submission of the sampling plan to the Lead Administrator. A specific product shall only be selected once for audit within its three-year certification period unless requested by the Bureau. When selecting the samples to be audited, a CLA shall prioritize the following:
(i) Broad grantee and laboratory representation;
(ii) Representation of the full range of product types certified;
(iii) Recent security events;
(iv) Representation across the previous four years of certificates issued;
(v) New grantees;
(vi) Grantees with a history of non-compliance; and
(vii) Requests from the Bureau for an audit to be performed on specific product or a group of products.
(4)
Sample Rate, Selection Timeframe, and Report.
A CLA shall adhere to the following sampling, selection, and report requirements:
(i) The total number of products selected for surveillance by a CLA shall be at least three percent of the total number of products certified or renewed by the CLA during the prior calendar year. A “product” is each grant of certification issued.
(ii) When calculating the total number of products to be selected for surveillance, the number of products shall be rounded up to the nearest whole number.
(iii) Products selected for surveillance by the CLA shall be selected from the devices certified or renewed by the CLA over the current calendar year or previous 2 calendar years.
(iv) A product certified in a prior surveillance year, but tested in the present surveillance year, will be credited as surveillance in the present surveillance year.
(v) A CLA must submit an annual report of their post-market surveillance activities for the surveillance year to the Lead Administrator by June 30th of the year following submission of the sampling plan. The post-market surveillance report is for all audits performed by the CLA in the previous calendar year.
(vi) The Bureau may request a specific product or products be subject to post-market surveillance. The CLA may count any such surveillance conducted under a Bureau request toward their annual sampling requirement.
(5)
Obtain Sample.
The CLA shall obtain a sample by the following method:
(i) Request the grantee submit a sample of the certified product either from their latest production line stock or by purchasing a sample of the product from the marketplace for delivery to the CLA or the CLA's designated CyberLAB.
(ii) The CLA shall notify the Lead Administrator if a grantee refuses, or fails to comply with, a request for a sample within 30 days of the CLA request. The Lead Administrator shall notify the Bureau if it is unable to resolve the failure to comply in a reasonable period of time. All grantees shall have received a copy of the Sample Test Plan from the CLA and should be aware that stating that a product is no longer manufactured or that the product will not be marketed in the United States will not serve as sufficient justification for failing to provide a product sample upon request of the CLA or to the Bureau upon request.
(iii) The grantee shall provide justification to the CLA if it would be overly burdensome for it to keep a production sample on hand or if the production run for the product is limited (
i.e.,
10 items or fewer). The CLA will determine whether this justification is acceptable and retain this determination within the grantee's record.
(6)
Evaluation.
The sample shall be evaluated by the CLA to determine compliance with the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program requirements in accordance with the following procedures and requirements:
(i) The CLA shall perform sufficient testing to a provide a high level of confidence that the sample complies with the FCC IoT Labeling Program requirements. Complete testing to all program requirements is not required; however, testing shall be performed on those requirements most likely to be in non-compliance.
(ii) The CLA may perform the testing through either a CLA-run lab or another recognized CyberLAB. In-house manufacturer labs may not be used. Post market surveillance testing should be performed by the same CLA-run lab or CyberLAB that performed the original evaluation whenever possible. The CLA shall inform the grantee of the name of the CLA-run lab or CyberLAB when the sample is obtained.
(iii) The CLA shall compare the test data and sample specifications obtained in the post-market surveillance evaluation with the information submitted in the application filing, verifying consistency. The CLA shall confirm that the grantee has made no changes to the device, applications, or backend/cloud services that impact compliance to the grantee's existing certification to the applicable program requirements. All information shall be consistent.
(iv) [Reserved]
(v) [Reserved]
(vi) The CLA shall examine the sample packaging to determine compliance with the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program's Labeling requirements.
(vii) The test report documenting surveillance shall be signed by the person(s) performing the tests.
(viii) A review by the certification body personnel shall be made after completion of the evaluation, as to whether the sample complies with the applicable FCC requirements.
(b)
Ad-Hoc Surveillance.
Each CLA shall participate in the ad-hoc surveillance evaluation when initiated by the FCC.
(1) Within 30 days of Bureau initiation, the Lead Administrator will convene a committee consisting of representatives from each CLA, which shall:
(i) Create a decision tree as an objective basis for determining if an ad-hoc surveillance audit is justified (Scope, Logistics Limitations & Risk Model);
(ii) If the Committee determines an audit is not justified, the Lead Administrator will submit the decision tree and its associated justification to the Bureau; and
(iii) If the Committee determines an audit is justified, the Lead Administrator will submit a surveillance plan to the Bureau detailing the types of products to be sampled, the sample rate by CLA, testing to be performed, timeline, and reporting details.
(iv) The Bureau shall be the final arbiter of whether an ad-hoc surveillance audit is conducted.
(2) Once the surveillance plan is approved by Bureau:
(i) Samples shall be obtained as defined in paragraph (a) of this section;
(ii) Evaluation shall be performed in testing facilities as defined in paragraph (a) of this section;
(
printed page 75482)
(iii) Reporting shall be created and communicated to the Bureau as described in the Bureau-approved ad-hoc surveillance plan; and
(iv) The Bureau will communicate the ad-hoc surveillance plans to all approved accreditation bodies.
(3) [Reserved]
(c)
Lead Administrator.
The Lead Administrator shall manage post-market surveillance and ad-hoc surveillance for the UCSTM program and carry out the following responsibilities:
(1) Receive annual CLA Sample Test Plans and review them for consistency and compliance with the USCTM program rules and submit its own Sample Test Plan to the Bureau for review;
(2) Convey updates on requirements to the CLAs;
(3) Organize committee of CLA representatives to conduct ad-hoc surveillance;
(4) Reassign post-market surveillance responsibilities in response to changes to CLAs (
e.g.,
CLA withdraws from USCTM Program, conflict of interest);
(5) Monitor and review CLA performance and develop recommendations to the FCC to improve CLA performance (
e.g.,
delays and time to process evaluations, excessive complaints against products tested);
(6) Create and administer the Qualified Professional training and certification, in collaboration with CLAs; and
(7) File annual post-market surveillance, ad hoc and post-audit surveillance reports with the Bureau.
§ 8.226
Complaints.
Complaints can be submitted against U.S. Cyber Trust Mark labeled products to any CLA through their standard complaints management process.
(a) In response to the complaint, the receiving CLA shall notify the Lead Administrator, who will notify the Bureau of the complaint.
(b) The Lead Administrator will determine if the complaint is within the scope of the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program requirements pursuant to rules adopted by the Commission; confirm the certification status of the product; and assign the complaint to the certifying CLA. The Lead Administrator will notify the Bureau of any product that bears the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark but is not certified. The Commission, via its Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, shall resolve any disputes that exceed the functions of the administrator.
(c) The certifying CLA shall follow the procedures outlined in § 8.225(a)(6) (Evaluation).
§ 8.227
Trademark Use and Branding Guidance.
(a) CLAs shall enter into a Trademark Use Agreement and agree to abide by the terms of the USCTM Branding Guidance, which may be updated from time to time at the sole discretion of the agency. The Trademark Use Agreement outlines the rights and expectations of CLAs related to their use of the USCTM and their limited right to authorize certain third-party sub-licensees to use the USCTM, including sub-licensing to authorized manufacturers or other agents, such as advertising agencies, sales agents, and retailers.
(b) CLAs shall maintain complete information about each sub-licensee including (at a minimum) the name, address, telephone number(s), email address(es), and website(s) of each sub-licensee; the date(s) on which each sub-licensee received authorization from the CLA to use any of the licensed marks; the names of any contact personnel for each sub-licensee; and a copy of all document(s) related to the vetting of and granting of the sublicense.
(c) CLAs shall maintain this information for a minimum of the term of the Trademark Use Agreement, plus five years thereafter.
(d) CLAs shall provide the Bureau with these records within five business days of receipt of a request to do so.
(e) CLAs shall provide the Bureau or its designated authorized representatives, with samples and/or relevant documentation regarding any product, commercial item, package, brochure, advertisement, or any other item that has been prepared by or is in the possession of CLA that the FCC reasonably believes uses, misuses, or incorporates any part or whole of a Cyber Trust Mark.
(f) CLAs shall assist the Bureau in policing unauthorized use of the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark through post-market surveillance and auditing activities, and by notifying the Lead Administrator and FCC as soon as it becomes aware of any use by any other person of a name, trade name, trademark, domain name, email address, metatag, AdWords (or similar search term), mode of advertising, or anything that may reasonably constitute (i) infringement of, (ii) unfair competition with, or (iii) passing off as, any of the Cyber Trust Marks. In addition to promptly reporting the improper usage, the CLAs shall provide relevant material, if available, to the Lead Administrator.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of information collection, request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), invites the general public and other Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. The purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public comment preceding submission of the collection to OMB.
DATES:
To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed information collection must be received on or before January 22, 2027.

Interested persons are invited to submit written comments to Adrienne Thomas, NOAA PRA Officer, at
NOAA.PRA@noaa.gov
.

(

laura.oremland@noaa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Abstract
This request is for an extension of a currently approved collection. NOAA is amending the title to “Generic Clearance for Economic Surveys of the Commercial and Charter Fishing Sectors of U.S. Marine Fisheries” to more accurately reflect NOAA's responsibility for managing marine fisheries within the U.S. exclusive economic zone.
The Office of Science and Technology is sponsoring this collection. Economic surveys will be conducted for the commercial and charter fishing sectors of marine fisheries of the United States.
The requested information will include different components of operating costs/expenditures, earnings, employment, ownership, vessel characteristics, effort/gear descriptors, employment, and demographic information. The information will be collected from the owners and operators of fishing vessels that participated in the commercial and/or charter fishing sectors, where the vessels that participated in the charter sector include guide boats, 6-pack boats, charter boats, commercial passenger fishing vessels, and party/head boats.
A variety of laws, Executive Orders (EOs), and NOAA Fisheries strategies and policies include requirements for economic data and the analyses they support. When met adequately, those requirements allow better-informed conservation and management decisions on the use of living marine resources and marine habitat in marine fisheries of the United States. Obtaining these data improves the ability of NOAA Fisheries and the Regional Fishery Management Councils (Councils) to monitor, explain and predict changes in the economic performance and impacts of U.S. marine fisheries. Measures of economic performance include costs, earnings, and profitability (net revenue); productivity and economic efficiency; capacity; economic stability; the level and distribution of net economic benefits to society; and market power. The economic impacts include sector, community, or region-specific and national employment, sales, value-added, and income impacts. Economic data is required to support more than a cursory effort to comply with or support the following laws, EOs, and NOAA Fisheries strategies and policies:
1. The Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (MSA)
2. The Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA)
3. The Endangered Species Act (ESA)
4. The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
5. The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
6.
E.O. 12866
Regulatory Planning and Review
7.
E.O. 14192
Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
8.
E.O. 14276
Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness
9.
E.O. 13840
Ocean Policy to Advance the Economic, Security, and Environmental Interests of the United States
10. The NOAA Fisheries Guidelines for Economic Reviews of Regulatory Actions
11. The NOAA Fisheries Ecosystem-Based Fishery Management (EBFM) Road Map
12. The NOAA Fisheries National Bycatch Reduction Strategy
13. NOAA's Catch Share Policy
Data collections will focus each year on a different set of fisheries. This cycle of data collection will facilitate economic data being available and updated for all federally managed fisheries.
There will be an effort to coordinate the data collections in order to reduce the additional burden for those who participate in multiple fisheries. To further reduce the burden, the requested information for a specific fishery will be limited to that which is not available from other sources. Participation in these data collections will be voluntary.
II. Method of Collection
The information will be collected by mail, internet, phone, video call, and in-person interviews. Where feasible, survey respondents will have the option to respond to an on-line survey. If phone and in-person interviews are not feasible or not desired by the potential respondents, the information will be collected by mail or internet.
III. Data

IV. Request for Comments
We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department/Bureau to: (a) Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is necessary for the proper functions of the Department, including whether the information will have practical utility; (b) Evaluate the accuracy of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (c) Evaluate ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (d) Minimize the reporting burden on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology.
Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of public record. We will include or summarize each comment in our request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment—including your personal identifying information—may be made publicly available at any time. While you may ask us in your comment to withhold your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so.

Department of Commerce
International Trade Administration
[C-580-882]
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that countervailable
(
printed page 75497)
subsidies were provided to Hyundai Steel Company (Hyundai Steel) and POSCO for the production of certain cold-rolled steel flat products (cold-rolled steel) from the Republic of Korea (Korea). The period of review (POR) is January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. In addition, Commerce is rescinding this review, in part, with respect to 46 companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable November 23, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christopher Doyle or Seth Brown, AD/CVD Operations, Office IX, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-5882 or (202) 482-0029, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.
[
1
]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.
[
2
]
On December 8, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i)
, we initiated an administrative review of the countervailing duty (CVD) order on cold-rolled steel from Korea.
[
3
]
On January 8, 2026, Commerce selected Hyundai Steel and POSCO as the mandatory respondents in this review.
[
4
]
On March 5, 2026, Nucor Corporation, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., Steel Dynamics Inc., and United States Steel Corporation (collectively, the petitioners) timely withdrew their request for review with respect to 46 companies.
[
5
]
On July 27, 2026, we extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review until November 18, 2026.
[
6
]
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
7
]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is provided as Appendix I to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Order
The product covered by the
Order
is cold-rolled steel from Korea. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
, Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if all parties that requested the review withdraw their requests within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation. As noted above, Commerce received timely-filed withdrawal requests with respect to the companies listed in Appendix II, and no other parties requested a review of these companies.
[
8
]
Therefore, we are rescinding this administrative review with respect to these companies, pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
.
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(3)
, it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of a CVD order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.
[
9
]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the CVD assessment rate calculated for the POR.
[
10
]

11

12

.

Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with 751(a)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). For each of the subsidy programs found countervailable, Commerce preliminarily determines that there is a subsidy,
i.e.,
a financial contribution by an “authority” that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific.
[
13
]
For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.

, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, filed electronically via ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice. Consistent with section 751(a)(1) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.212(b)(2)
, upon issuance of the final results, Commerce shall determine, and CBP shall assess, countervailing duties on all appropriate entries covered by this review.

. Commerce intends to issue rescission instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
.

. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (

Cash Deposit Requirements
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.107(e)
, Commerce intends to instruct CBP to collect cash deposits of estimated countervailing duties with regard to shipments of subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication of the final results of this review, as follows: (1) the cash deposit rate for the companies listed above will be equal to the company-specific estimated individual countervailable subsidy rates determined in the final results of this review, except if the rate is less than 0.50 percent and, therefore,

within the meaning of

AGENCY:
Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), this notice announces that the Information Collection Request (ICR)
(
printed page 75502)
abstracted below has been forwarded to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and comment. The ICR describes the nature of the information collection and its expected costs and burdens.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be submitted within 30 days of this notice's publication to OIRA, at
https://www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
Please find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the website's search function. Comments can be entered electronically by clicking on the “comment” button next to the information collection on the “OIRA Information Collections Under Review” page, or the “View ICR—Agency Submission” page. A copy of the supporting statement for the collection of information discussed herein may be obtained by visiting
https://www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
In addition to the submission of comments to
https://Reginfo.gov
as indicated above, a copy of all comments submitted to OIRA may also be submitted to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (Commission or CFTC) by any of the following methods:
Regulations.gov:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and press the “Search” button, then proceed as follows:
1. Under Refine Documents Results—check the box to “Only show documents open for comment”;
2. Under Agency—select “See More” and check the box for “Commodity Futures Trading Commission,” then press the Apply button;
3. Identify this notice in the list of CFTC documents open for comment, press the “Comment” button to open the submission form, and follow the instructions on the form.
Alternatively, if you are viewing this notice on
www.federalregister.gov
,
click the “Submit A Public Comment” button at the top of the page to open the comment form. Follow the instructions on the form to submit your comment to
Regulations.gov
.
Mail:
Send to—Christopher Kirkpatrick, Secretary of the Commission, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Three Lafayette Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581.
Hand Delivery/Courier:
Address to—CFTC Comment Submission, Attn: Christopher Kirkpatrick, Secretary of the Commission, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Three Lafayette Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581.
Please submit your comments using only one of these methods. To avoid possible delays with mail or in-person deliveries, submissions through
Regulations.gov
are encouraged.
All comments must be submitted in English or, if not, accompanied by an English translation. Do not include in your comment text or attachments any personal identifying information or business information that you do not want published online. Comments (regardless of submission method) will be published without review for, and without removal of, any personal identifying information or information your business may consider confidential.
If you wish to submit confidential information for the Commission's consideration, please contact the CFTC personnel listed in this Notice under
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
before making any submission. Please also carefully review the Commission's procedures in
17 CFR 145.9
for requesting confidential treatment under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of information submitted to the Commission.
The CFTC reserves the right, but shall have no obligation, to review, pre-screen, filter, or redact all or any part of your comment submission. The CFTC also reserves the right, without further notification, to refuse to publish or to remove from public view all or any part of your submission to the extent it contains content inappropriate for publication in a comment file, such as—without limitation—obscene language, threats of violence, solicitations for commercial sales or illegal activity, or obvious spam. If a submission that is refused for or withdrawn from publication because of inappropriate content also contains comments on the merits of this notice, such submission will be retained in the record for the matter and will be considered as required under the Administrative Procedure Act, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and other applicable laws, and may be accessible under the FOIA.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Elizabeth Groover, Special Counsel, (202) 418-5985,
egroover@cftc.gov
,
or Michael Ehrstein, Special Counsel, (202) 418-5957,
mehrstein@cftc.gov
,
Market Participants Division, Commodity Futures Trading Commission, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581, and refer to OMB Control No. 3038-0005.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Rules Relating to the Operations and Activities of Commodity Pool Operators and Commodity Trading Advisors and to Monthly Reporting by Futures Commission Merchants (OMB Control No. 3038-0005). This is a request for extension of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
The various collections of information required by part 4 of the Commission's regulations were previously approved by OMB in accordance with the PRA and assigned OMB control number 3038-0005.
[
1
]
The Commission offers the following summary of the renewal and the resulting impact on existing burden hour estimates associated with this information collection. The Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) empowers the Commission with the authority to require commodity pool operators (CPOs) and commodity trading advisors (CTAs) to maintain books and records and to file reports as required by the Commission.
[
2
]
The Commission also has the power to promulgate such regulations as it deems necessary to implement the purposes of the CEA.
[
3
]
It is pursuant to this authority that the Commission has promulgated the various compliance requirements for CPOs and CTAs in
17 CFR part 4
. The reporting, filing, and recordkeeping requirements within part 4 of the Commission's regulations were adopted to assist and inform customers, to establish customer protection initiatives for investors, to facilitate monitoring intermediary compliance with part 4 regulations by the Commission and its delegee, the National Futures Association (NFA), and to enable the Commission to better monitor the market risks posed by its registrants. The information collections are necessary to enable the Commission and NFA to accomplish the purposes of both the CEA and the compliance regime set forth in part 4 of the Commission's regulations.
An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. On August 14, 2026, the Commission published in the
Federal Register
notice of the proposed extension of this information collection and provided 60 days for public comment on the proposed extension,
91 FR 52677
(60-Day Notice). The Commission received one comment, submitted anonymously, asserting that
(
printed page 75503)
the 60-Day Notice “omits monetized public labor costs and operating expenses.” The Commission, however, provides detailed burden estimates in its Supporting Statement including estimated time spent to complete each reporting, recordkeeping, and filing requirement, with along with estimated labor costs and operating expenses associated with each information collection requirement. The commenter did not otherwise comment on the Commission's burden estimates or the utility of the information collected. Accordingly, the Commission is retaining its burden estimates as proposed.
Burden Statement:
The respondent burden for this collection is estimated to be as follows:
Respondents/Affected Entities:
(1) All persons filing reports required by
17 CFR part 4
, and (2) all principals of such persons.
Estimated number of respondents:
49,083.
Estimated number of exempt pools/reports per respondent:
8.8.
Estimated total annual burden on respondents:
432,325 hours.
(Authority:
44 U.S.C. 3501
,
et seq.
)
Dated: November 19, 2026.
Robert Sidman,
Deputy Secretary of the Commission.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Part 41 Relating to Security Futures Products (OMB Control No. 3038-0059). This is a request for extension of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
Section 4d(c) of the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”),
7 U.S.C. 6d(c)
, requires the CFTC to consult with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) and issue such rules, regulations, or orders as are necessary to avoid duplicative or conflicting regulations applicable to firms that are fully registered with the SEC as brokers or dealers and the CFTC as futures commission merchants, involving provisions of the CEA that pertain to the treatment of customer funds. The CFTC, jointly with the SEC, issued regulations requiring such dually-registered firms to make choices as to how its customers' transactions in security futures products will be treated, either as securities transactions held in a securities account or as futures transactions held in a futures account. How an account is treated is important in the unlikely event of the insolvency of the firm. Only securities accounts receive insurance protection under provisions of the Securities Investor Protection Act. By contrast, only futures accounts are subject to the protections provided by the segregation requirements of the CEA.
An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
[
1
]
On August 19, 2026, the Commission published in the
Federal Register
notice of the proposed extension of this information collection and provided 60 days for public comment on the proposed extension,
91 FR 53610

AGENCY:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Request for information.
SUMMARY:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), in the Department of Health and Human Services, requests public input on research priorities and prevention needs related to humanoid robots in workplaces. Through its Center for Occupational Robotics Research (CORR), NIOSH conducts research and provides scientific leadership to improve the safety, health, and well-being of workers who use, wear, or work near robots. NIOSH seeks information on workplace applications, human-robot interaction, performance measurement and validation, and ways to prevent injuries and illnesses throughout design, deployment, and use. This request is for information-gathering purposes only and does not propose new regulations, requirements, or policies.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before February 22, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Submit comments by either of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
Mail:
NIOSH Docket Office, Robert A. Taft Laboratories, MS C-34, 1090 Tusculum Avenue, Cincinnati, Ohio 45226-1998.
Instructions:
All written submissions received in response to this document must include the agency name and docket number (CDC-2026-1882 NIOSH-366) for this activity. All relevant comments, including any personal information provided, will be posted without change to
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Do not submit comments by email.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Emily Haas, 626 Cochran Mills Rd. Pittsburgh, PA 15236; Telephone (412) 386-4627 (this is not a toll-free number); Email
NIOSHregs@cdc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NIOSH established the Center for Occupational Robotics Research (CORR) in 2017 to address the safety of workers who use, wear, or work near robots. CORR works with partners to monitor robot-related injury trends; evaluate robotic technologies as potential sources of, and interventions for, work-related injuries and illnesses; develop risk profiles; identify and conduct research; support consensus safety standards; and develop best practices, guidance, and training for safe human-robot interaction. CORR's portfolio includes traditional industrial robots as well as collaborative and mobile robots, wearable robotics and powered exoskeletons, remotely controlled or autonomous vehicles and drones, and other emerging robotic technologies. Additionally, NIOSH's Center for Direct Reading and Sensor Technologies (CDRST) informs research and guidance related to selecting, evaluating, using, and interpreting direct-reading and sensor technologies for occupational safety and health. This
(
printed page 75514)
expertise may be relevant to questions about robot-mounted sensors, workplace monitoring, worker-worn sensors, alarm performance, sensor data quality, and the interpretation and use of those data. Current and recent NIOSH work includes:
Surveillance of robot-related injury claims and studies of how robot motion and design can affect perceived safety, trust, workload, worker behavior, and task performance.
Human-robot interaction studies including robot-arm and mobile-robot studies that examine how movement speed, trajectory, design, and interaction geometry shape perceived safety, trust, workload, worker behavior, and task performance.
Various approaches to visibility, separation, and collision avoidance.
Research in application areas such as construction that also considers how changing work conditions, sensing, communication, software, and work organization can affect safe implementation.
NIOSH is exploring occupational safety and health applications of humanoid robots. Humanoid robots may combine bipedal or other human-like mobility with manipulation, perception, remote operation, autonomous functions, and software that can be updated or adapted. These characteristics may create questions that are not fully answered by experience with fixed industrial robots or other established robot types. NIOSH is interested in evidence about both potential worker-safety benefits and potential hazards, including how robot capabilities, work organization, and workplace conditions affect risk. Please consider addressing these questions or provide other comments you deem relevant.
(1) What tasks could humanoid robots perform, and how might their safety risks and benefits differ from those of other robots?
(2) How might humanoid robots affect workers' awareness, trust, workload, training, and safety behaviors?
(3) What hazards should be prioritized, and what injury, near-miss, or exposure data would help identify risks to workers?
(4) What tests or measures are needed to assess humanoid robot safety in realistic work conditions?
(5) What factors help or hinder organizations in adopting and sustaining effective safety practices for humanoid robots?
(6) How could sensors or wearables support worker safety around humanoid robots?
(7) Which robot design features and safety controls should be prioritized?
(8) What research, standards, or partnerships should NIOSH prioritize to support safe human-robot interaction?

Director, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Department of Health and Human Services.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NIOSH is requesting public comment on a draft document,
Proposed Short-Term Exposure Limit for Occupational Exposure to Carbon Monoxide,
available in the dockets for this activity. NIOSH's existing recommendations for limiting carbon monoxide exposure in the workplace were published in 1972. This draft document details NIOSH's reassessment of the original recommended exposure limits and proposes updating the ceiling limit recommendation to a short-term exposure limit. This is being done in consideration of improvements to the science and technologies, including instrumentation and monitoring methods, involved in the recognition and control of workplace carbon monoxide health hazards since the publication of NIOSH's original recommendations in 1972. The final publication, which will address public comments, will be available on the NIOSH website and in the dockets for this activity (NIOSH-357 and CDC-2026-1849).
Background:
NIOSH develops recommended occupational exposure limits (RELs) to protect workers from the risk of adverse health effects from acute and repeated exposures to chemicals. These include RELs, short-term exposure limits (STELs), or ceiling values depending on the length of exposure time the recommendation is intended to apply to. NIOSH bases its occupational exposure limits on detailed reviews of available human and animal toxicity data to identify health hazards, determine the level at which
(
printed page 75513)
they are likely to occur in workers, and characterize the point at which the risk to health becomes unreasonable. The analytical feasibility of putting these recommendations into practice using available methods and measurement technologies is also factored into NIOSH's decisions. The Current Intelligence Bulletin (CIB) 69:
NIOSH Practices in Occupational Risk Assessment
details the information and methods used to develop NIOSH RELs [NIOSH 2020].
The bases for NIOSH's current REL for carbon monoxide are detailed in the
Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Exposure to Carbon Monoxide
[NIOSH 1972]. The recommendations at that time included a REL applicable to a whole-day average and a ceiling limit meant not to be exceeded at any point. These recommendations considered the workplace exposure data that were available at the time and the capacity to put the recommendations into practice using available methods and technologies. As technologies and data availability have improved over the years, NIOSH has reassessed the original carbon monoxide exposure limit recommendations and proposes this update to ensure consistency with the current state-of-science and applicability to the modern workplace. This is consistent with NIOSH risk assessment practices [NIOSH 2020].
To facilitate the review of this document, NIOSH requests comment on the following specific questions for this draft proposed workplace short-term exposure limit for carbon monoxide:
1. Does this document clearly describe NIOSH's proposed update for short-term workplace exposure to carbon monoxide and its justification? If not, what specific information is missing from the document?
2. Are the scientific rationale and logic behind the proposed update to the short-term exposure limit clearly explained? If not, what specific information is needed to clarify the basis of the short-term exposure limit?
3. Does the scientific evidence and modeling support replacing the 1972 NIOSH 200-parts per million (ppm) ceiling limit with a 200-ppm, 10-minute time-weighted average (TWA) STEL? Does the proposed STEL adequately protect workers from acute carbon monoxide effects associated with short-term exposures over the 10-minute averaging period? Does the proposed STEL adequately protect workers from acute carbon monoxide effects associated with short-term exposures over the course of a work day?
4. Are the tables, figures, and equations clearly presented? Are the analyses clearly explained in support of the proposed STEL? If not, what specific improvements would be helpful?
5. Are you aware of any additional scientific information reported in government publications, databases, peer-reviewed journals, or other sources that should be considered in this document? If yes, please provide the full reference citation of any additional information or publications that would be helpful to consider.
References
NIOSH [1972]. Criteria for a recommended standard: occupational exposure to carbon monoxide. Cincinnati, OH: U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, Health Services and Mental Health Administration, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, DHEW (NIOSH) Publication No. 73-11000.
NIOSH [2020]. Current intelligence bulletin 69: NIOSH practices in occupational risk assessment. By Daniels RD, Gilbert SJ, Kuppusamy SP, Kuempel ED, Park RM, Pandalai SP, Smith RJ, Wheeler MW, Whittaker C, Schulte PA. Cincinnati, OH: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 2020-106 (revised 03/2020).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Presidential Advisory Council on Combating Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria (PACCARB), established by
Executive Order 13676
, is continued by Section 505 of
Public Law 116-22
, the Pandemic and All-Hazards Preparedness and Advancing Innovation Act of 2019 (PAHPAIA). Activities and duties of the PACCARB are governed by the provisions of the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), Public Law 92-463, as amended (5 U.S.C. App.), which sets forth standards for the formation and use of federal advisory committees.
The PACCARB shall advise and provide information and recommendations to the Secretary of Health and Human Services (Secretary) regarding programs and policies intended to reduce or combat antibiotic-resistant bacteria that may present a public health threat and improve capabilities to prevent, diagnose, mitigate, or treat such resistance. The PACCARB shall function solely for advisory purposes.
Such advice, information, and recommendations may be related to improving: the effectiveness of antibiotics; research and advanced research on, and the development of, improved and innovative methods for combating or reducing antibiotic resistance, including new treatments, rapid point-of-care diagnostics, alternatives to antibiotics, including alternatives to animal antibiotics, and antimicrobial stewardship activities; surveillance of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections, including publicly available and up-to-date information on resistance to antibiotics; education for health care providers and the public with respect to up-to-date information on antibiotic resistance and ways to reduce or combat such resistance to antibiotics related to humans and animals; methods to prevent or reduce the transmission of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections; including stewardship programs; and coordination with respect to international efforts in order to inform and advance the United States capabilities to combat antibiotic resistance.
The focus of the December 2, 2026, meeting will assess the current State of the Threat that antimicrobial resistance possesses. It will include presentations, review, and analysis of recently released data and reports from the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and HHS. Written public comments can be emailed to
CARB@hhs.gov
by midnight December 30, 2026, and should be limited to no more than one page. All public comments received prior to December 30, 2026, will be provided to the subcommittee members.

The Food and Nutrition Administration administers the National School Lunch Program, the School Breakfast Program, and the Special Milk Program as mandated by the Richard B. Russell National School Lunch Act (NSLA), as amended (

The eligibility burden of the Child and Adult Care Food Program and the Summer Food Service Program is reported in information collections under OMB Control Numbers 0584-0055 and 0584-0280, respectively.
Per
7 CFR part 245
, schools participating in these meal and milk programs must make free and reduced price meals and free milk available to eligible children. This information collection obtains eligibility information for free and reduced-price meals and free milk and also incorporates verification procedures as required to confirm eligibility. For households, the most significant change is that fewer households now submit applications for benefits. Increased LEA and school participation in CEP has some impact on state agency and LEA reporting and public notification burden. U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This document amends U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations to reflect the extension of import restrictions on certain categories of archaeological and ethnological material from the Arab Republic of Egypt (Egypt), which were originally published in CBP Decision (CBP Dec.) 16-23, and subsequently extended and amended in CBP Dec. 21-17. The CBP regulations are being amended to reflect this further extension through November 30, 2031.
DATES:
Effective on November 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For legal aspects, W. Richmond Beevers, Chief, Cargo Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, Regulations and Rulings, Office of Trade, (202) 325-0084,
ot-otrrculturalproperty@cbp.dhs.gov
.
For operational aspects, Christopher Mabelitini, Director, Intellectual Property Rights Policy & Programs, Trade Programs Directorate, Office of Trade, (571) 296-1269,
1USGBranch@cbp.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The Convention on Cultural Property Implementation Act (Pub. L. 97-446,
19 U.S.C. 2601
et seq.
) (CPIA), which implements the 1970 United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Convention on the Means of Prohibiting and Preventing the Illicit Import, Export and Transfer of Ownership of Cultural Property (823 U.N.T.S. 231 (1972)) (the Convention), allows for the conclusion of an agreement between the United States and another party to the Convention to impose import restrictions on eligible archaeological and ethnological material. Under the CPIA and the applicable U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations, found in § 12.104 of
title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(
19 CFR 12.104
), the restrictions are effective for no more than five years beginning on the date on which an agreement enters into force with respect to the United States (
19 U.S.C. 2602(b)
). This period may be extended for additional periods, each extension not to exceed five years, if it is determined that the factors justifying the initial agreement still pertain and no cause for suspension of the agreement exists (
19 U.S.C. 2602(e)
;
19 CFR 12.104g(a)
).
On November 30, 2016, the United States and the Arab Republic of Egypt (Egypt) entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) entitled “Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Arab Republic of Egypt Concerning the Imposition of Import Restrictions on Categories of Archaeological Material of the Arab Republic of Egypt” (2016 MOU). The 2016 MOU reflected an agreement to impose import restrictions on certain archaeological material representing Egypt's cultural heritage ranging from
(
printed page 75452)
approximately 5,200 B.C. to A.D. 1517. On December 6, 2016, CBP published CBP Decision (CBP Dec.) 16-23 in the
Federal Register
(
81 FR 87805
), which amended
19 CFR 12.104g(a)
to indicate the imposition of these restrictions and included a list designating the types of archaeological material covered by the restrictions.
Import restrictions listed at
19 CFR 12.104g(a)
are effective for no more than five years beginning on the date on which the agreement enters into force with respect to the United States. This period may be extended for additional periods of not more than five years if it is determined that the factors which justified the initial agreement still pertain and no cause for suspension of the agreement exists. Since the initial notice was published on December 6, 2016, the import restrictions have been extended once. On November 30, 2021, the Governments of the United States and Egypt entered into a new MOU, superseding the 2016 MOU, agreeing to amend the existing import restrictions on archaeological material and impose additional import restrictions on certain categories of ethnological material. Subsequently, CBP published a final rule (CBP Dec. 21-17) in the
Federal Register
(
86 FR 68546
) to reflect the 2021 MOU and extend the restrictions until November 30, 2026. To fulfill the terms of the new MOU, the Designated List of cultural property was amended in this document to reflect the addition and revision of categories of archaeological material of Egypt ranging in date from approximately 300,000 B.C. to A.D. 1750, and to include certain ethnological material ranging from A.D. 1517 to 1914.
On January 26, 2026, the United States Department of State proposed in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 3294
), to extend the 2021 MOU between the United States and Egypt concerning the import restrictions on certain categories of archeological and ethnological material of Egypt. On August 6, 2026, the Assistant Secretary for Educational and Cultural Affairs, United States Department of State, after consultation with and recommendations by the Cultural Property Advisory Committee, made the necessary determinations to extend the 2021 Agreement for an additional five years.
Subsequently, on November 9, 2026, the Governments of the United States and Egypt entered into a new bilateral agreement to extend the import restrictions on archaeological and ethnological material of Egypt. Pursuant to the new agreement, the import restrictions will remain in effect for an additional five-year period through November 30, 2031.
Accordingly, CBP is amending
19 CFR 12.104g(a)
to reflect the extension of these import restrictions. The restrictions on the importation of certain archaeological and ethnological material from Egypt are to continue in effect until November 30, 2031. Importation of such material from Egypt continues to be restricted through that date unless the conditions set forth in
19 U.S.C. 2606
and
19 CFR 12.104c
are met.
The Designated List, which includes archaeological material from Egypt ranging in date from approximately 300,000 B.C. to A.D. 1750, and certain ethnological material from Egypt ranging in date from A.D. 1517 to 1914, is set forth in CBP Dec. 21-17. The Designated List of restricted material and additional information may also be found at the following website address:
https://www.state.gov/​current-agreements-and-import-restrictions
,
by selecting the material for “Egypt.”
Inapplicability of Notice and Delayed Effective Date
This amendment involves a foreign affairs function of the United States and is, therefore, being made without notice or public procedure under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
. For the same reason, a delayed effective date is not required under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
.
Executive Order 12866
Executive Order 12866
(Regulatory Planning and Review) directs agencies to assess the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if a regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, disruptive impacts, and equity). CBP has determined that this document is not a regulation or rule subject to the provisions of
Executive Order 12866
because it pertains to a foreign affairs function of the United States, as described above, and therefore is specifically exempted by section 3(d)(2) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
), as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, requires an agency to prepare and make available to the public a regulatory flexibility analysis that describes the effect of a proposed rule on small entities (
i.e.,
small businesses, small organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions) when the agency is required to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking for a rule. Because a general notice of proposed rulemaking is not necessary for this rule, CBP is not required to prepare a regulatory flexibility analysis for this rule.
Signing Authority
In accordance with Treasury Order 100-20, the Secretary of the Treasury has delegated to the Secretary of Homeland Security the authority related to the customs revenue functions vested in the Secretary of the Treasury as set forth in
6 U.S.C. 212
and
215
, subject to certain exceptions. This regulation is being issued in accordance with Department of Homeland Security Delegation 07010.3, Revision 03.2, which delegates to the Commissioner of CBP the authority to prescribe and approve regulations related to cultural property import restrictions.
Rodney S. Scott, Commissioner, having reviewed and approved this document, has delegated the authority to electronically sign this document to Susan S. Thomas, the Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Trade, for purposes of publication in the
Federal Register
.

AGENCY:
United States Section, USMCA Secretariat, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice of USMCA request for panel review.
SUMMARY:
Two Requests for Panel Review were filed in the matter of Certain Softwood Lumber Products from Canada: Final Results of Countervailing Duty Administrative Review, 2024 with the U.S. Section of the USMCA Secretariat on November 18, 2026. The USMCA Secretariat has assigned case number USA-CDA-2026-10.12-01 to this request. The first Request for Panel Review was filed on behalf of the Government of Canada, the Governments of Alberta, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Ontario, and Québec; Alberta Softwood Lumber Trade Council, British Columbia Lumber Trade Council; Canfor Corporation, Interfor Corporation, Interfor Sales & Marketing Ltd., EACOM Timber Corporation, Chaleur Forest Products Inc., Chaleur Forest Products LP, J.D. Irving, Limited, Tolko Marketing and Sales Ltd. and Tolko Industries Ltd., Gilbert Smith Forest Products, as well as West Fraser Mills Ltd. The second Request for Panel Review was filed on behalf of Resolute FP Canada Inc., the Conseil de l'industrie forestière du Québec, the Ontario Forest Industries Association, and each association's respective individual members listed in Attachment A of the Request for Panel Review (collectively “Central Canada”); Plaster Rock Lumber Corporation; as well as CHAP Alliance Inc.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Vidya Desai, United States Secretary, USMCA Secretariat, Room 2061, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230, 202-482-5438.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The final results of the investigation under review were determined by the United States Department of Commerce and were published in the
Federal Register
on October 19, 2026 (
91 FR 66
,
092
).
Article 10.12 of Chapter 10 of USMCA provides a dispute settlement mechanism involving trade remedy determinations issued by the Government of the United States, the Government of Canada, and the Government of Mexico. Following a Request for Panel Review, a Binational Panel is composed to review the trade remedy determination being challenged and issue a binding Panel Decision. There are established USMCA
Rules of Procedure for Article 10.12 (Binational Panel Reviews),
which were adopted by the three governments for panels requested pursuant to Article 10.12(2) of USMCA which requires Requests for Panel Review to be published in accordance with Rule 40. For the complete Rules, please see
https://can-mex-usa-sec.org/​secretariat/​agreement-accord-acuerdo/​usmca-aceum-tmec/​rules-regles-reglas/​article-article-articulo_​10_​12.aspx?​lang=​eng
.
The Rules provide that:
(a) A Party or interested person may challenge the final determination in whole or in part by filing a Complaint in accordance with Rule 44 no later than 30 days after the filing of the first Request for Panel Review (the deadline for filing a Complaint is December 18, 2026);
(b) A Party, an investigating authority or other interested person who does not file a Complaint but who intends to participate in the panel review shall file a Notice of Appearance in accordance with Rule 45 no later than 45 days after the filing of the first Request for Panel Review (the deadline for filing a Notice of Appearance is January 4, 2027);
(c) The panel review will be limited to the allegations of error of fact or law, including challenges to the jurisdiction of the investigating authority, that are set out in the Complaints filed in the panel review and to the procedural and substantive defenses raised in the panel review.
Dated: November 19, 2026.
Vidya Desai,
United States Secretary, USMCA Secretariat.
