RIN 1235-AA46
(
printed page 75646)
AGENCY:
Wage and Hour Division, Department of Labor.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule rescinds the analysis for determining employee or independent contractor status under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA or Act) set forth in the Department of Labor's (Department) regulations and replaces it with an analysis similar to what it published in a final rule promulgated in 2021, with several modifications and enhancements. In addition, this final rule amends provisions in the Department's regulations implementing the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act (MSPA) to provide that employee or independent contractor status under those laws should be determined using the Department's FLSA analysis, as the FMLA and MSPA both incorporate the FLSA's scope of employment.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on January 22, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Daniel Navarrete, Director, Division of Regulations, Legislation, and Interpretation, Wage and Hour Division (WHD or Division), U.S. Department of Labor, Room S-3502, 200 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20210; telephone: (202) 693-0406 (this is not a toll-free number). Alternative formats are available upon request by calling 1-866-487-9243. If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
Questions of interpretation or enforcement of the agency's existing regulations may be directed to the nearest WHD district office. Locate the nearest office by calling the WHD's toll-free help line at (866) 4US-WAGE ((866) 487-9243) between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. in your local time zone, or log onto WHD's website at
https://www.dol.gov/​agencies/​whd/​contact/​local-offices
for a nationwide listing of WHD district and area offices.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Executive Summary
This final rule sets forth the analysis that the Department will apply to determine whether a worker is properly classified as an employee or independent contractor under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA, as the various requirements and worker protections established by these laws apply only to employees. None of these laws defines the term “independent contractor.” However, the FMLA and MSPA both incorporate the FLSA's statutory definitions governing employment, suggesting that the analysis applied under the FLSA to determine whether an employment relationship exists should likewise determine whether an employment relationship exists under the FMLA and MSPA.
In relevant part, the FLSA defines the term “employer” as “any person acting directly or indirectly in the interest of an employer in relation to an employee,”
[
1
]
“employee” as “any individual employed by an employer,”
[
2
]
and “employ” as “includ[ing] to suffer or permit to work.”
[
3
]
Courts and the Department have long interpreted the phrase “suffer or permit” as requiring a multifactor test to analyze whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the FLSA. The ultimate inquiry is whether, as a matter of economic reality, the worker depends on a particular individual, business, or organization for work (and is thus an employee) or is in business for him- or herself (and is thus an independent contractor). The supporting analysis for answering this question, that is determining employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA, is commonly known as the economic reality test.
On January 7, 2021, the Department published a final rule (2021 Rule) which—for the first time—organized and distilled the longstanding economic reality factors into practical regulatory guidance for workers and businesses in any industry to aid the proper classification of employees and independent contractors under the FLSA.
[
4
]
While reaffirming the overarching concepts of economic reality and economic dependence, the 2021 Rule set forth a sharpened economic reality test with five distinct factors, instead of the six used by most courts. The 2021 Rule designated two of the five identified factors—the nature and degree of control over the work and the worker's opportunity for profit or loss—as “core factors,” which are the most probative and carry greater weight in the analysis.
[
5
]
The 2021 Rule stated that if these two core factors point towards the same status (
i.e.,
employee or independent contractor), there is a substantial likelihood that the indicated outcome is the worker's accurate status.
[
6
]
The 2021 Rule also identified three less probative non-core factors: the amount of skill required for the work, the degree of permanence of the working relationship between the worker and the potential employer, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.
[
7
]
The 2021 Rule stated that it is “highly unlikely” that these three non-core factors could outweigh the combined probative value of the two core factors.
[
8
]
In addition to providing guidance for each of the five factors, the 2021 Rule advised as a general matter that the actual practice of the parties involved is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible. Finally, the 2021 Rule provided six fact-specific examples applying the rule's factors.
[
9
]
The Department explained that the 2021 Rule was intended to combine longstanding legal and judicial frameworks in a practicable package that could be broadly applied in workplaces across the nation—promoting certainty for stakeholders, reducing litigation, and encouraging innovation in the economy.
In early 2021, the Department engaged in a pair of rulemakings to delay the effective date of and subsequently withdraw the 2021 Rule before it took effect.
[
10
]
On March 14, 2022, in response to a legal challenge against the Department alleging that the Delay Rule and Withdrawal Rule violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a district court in the Eastern District of Texas issued a decision vacating the Delay and Withdrawal Rules, concluding that the 2021 Rule “became effective as of March 8, 2021, the rule's original effective date, and remains in effect.”
[
11
]
WHD applied
(
printed page 75647)
the 2021 Rule in its enforcement actions for the next 2 years.
Following publication of a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking in October 2022, on January 10, 2024, the Department published a new final rule (2024 Rule) which rescinded the 2021 Rule and replaced it with a new analysis at
29 CFR part 795
.
[
12
]
While sharing some features with the 2021 Rule, the 2024 Rule set forth a six-factor economic reality test where “no one factor or subset of factors is necessarily dispositive” and “the weight to give each factor may depend on the facts and circumstances of the particular relationship.”
[
13
]
Explanatory guidance provided for several of the factors differed from the 2021 Rule in ways that made the analysis less likely to indicate independent contractor status.
[
14
]
And unlike the 2021 Rule, the 2024 Rule's regulatory text did not include any illustrative examples or address the relevance of parties' actual practice as compared to what may be contractually or theoretically possible (examples were included in the 2024 Rule's preamble). The 2024 Rule took effect on March 11, 2024. Five lawsuits were filed challenging the legality of the 2024 Rule; four of these lawsuits remain pending, though proceedings have been stayed by the presiding courts. On May 1, 2025, the Department issued a field assistance bulletin announcing that WHD would no longer apply the 2024 Rule's analysis in its enforcement actions.
[
15
]
On February 27, 2026, the Department published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) proposing to rescind the 2024 Rule and replace it with an analysis similar to the 2021 Rule.
[
16
]
The Department explained in the NPRM that, upon further consideration, the Department has concerns that the 2024 Rule failed to distill longstanding judicial precedent into an analysis for workers and employers properly to distinguish between independent contractors and employees under the FLSA that is both sufficiently clear to apply and results in legally reliable and predictable outcomes. The NPRM stated that the Department is separately concerned that the 2024 Rule's amorphous description of several economic reality factors could be viewed as so vague and expansive that it operates to set a higher bar to find independent contractor status than required by law. Among other harms, an analysis which is overly nebulous can improperly deter businesses from engaging with bona fide independent contractors or cause them unnecessarily to classify such individuals as employees—concerns emphasized by many self-identified independent contractors who participated in the Department's recent rulemakings on this topic.
The Department invited comments on its proposal and received approximately 16,500 timely comments after a 60-day comment period which ended on April 28, 2026. While the Department received many unique comments, the Department also received 14,244 similar “campaign” comment submissions (86.3 percent) in response to seven different organized initiatives—all of which expressed support for the rulemaking. After considering the feedback from commenters, the Department is finalizing its proposed rule with a few modifications and enhancements.
For the reasons initially explained in the NPRM and further detailed in section III, the Department concludes that it is appropriate to rescind the 2024 Rule and, to a significant degree, return to the 2021 Rule. Accordingly, the Department is finalizing at
29 CFR part 795
the proposed analysis for determining employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA, but has made several changes in response to commenter feedback. Specifically, the Department is revising some of the illustrative examples in proposed § 795.115 and adopting six additional examples to demonstrate how particular factors from the readopted analysis properly apply in factual scenarios involving digital platform workers, farm labor contractors, and truck drivers. These changes to the proposed rule are explained in greater detail below. Additionally, the Department is finalizing its proposal to amend its regulations addressing employee or independent contractor status under MSPA and the FMLA so that the analysis in part 795 applies when determining employee or independent contractor status under those statutes too.
The Department believes that this rule is likely to improve the welfare of workers, businesses, and other interested parties. With a clearer test drawn and distilled from federal case law to distinguish between employees and independent contractors, businesses may more confidently engage with independent contractors, which could increase opportunities for individuals who wish to work—whether primarily or in addition to other employment—as independent entrepreneurs. Consumers and the public, in general, will benefit from the rule's clarification that certain requirements in work arrangements regarding compliance with specific legal obligations, health and safety standards, and quality control measures do not constitute control that makes an individual more or less likely to be an employee. At the same time, this final rule provides a robust standard to guard against the misclassification of employees as independent contractors, including added clarity about the factors and common business practices that are most likely to establish that a worker is an employee because they are economically dependent on an employer for work. Relatedly, the Department expects that this rule will lead to fewer misclassification disputes and more consistent outcomes when such disputes are investigated or adjudicated, as a clearer economic reality test will be easier for all to understand and apply. In this way, the rule will be a valuable resource not only for employers and workers, but also for courts and the Department's enforcement personnel, who often evaluate classification decisions in matters that cross judicial districts and circuits.
The Department emphasizes that it remains committed to preventing the misclassification of employees as independent contractors. Such misclassification undermines the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA by depriving employees of the protections established by those laws. It also cheats competing businesses that comply with those laws, ultimately harming consumers.
[
17
]
However, it is well established that these laws do not cover every work arrangement and were not intended to deter legitimate contracting. Upon reflection, the Department believes that returning to the analysis previously adopted in the 2021 Rule will strike a better balance by promoting the interests of employees and independent contractors alike.
(
printed page 75648)
II. Background
A. Relevant FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA Definitions
Enacted in 1938, the FLSA requires covered employers to pay their nonexempt employees at least the federal minimum wage for every hour worked and overtime pay for every hour worked over 40 in a workweek, and it mandates that employers keep certain records regarding their employees.
[
18
]
Among other protections, the Act regulates the employment of minors,
[
19
]
governs the work and wages of tipped employees,
[
20
]
requires employers to provide reasonable break time and a place for covered employees who are nursing to express breast milk at work,
[
21
]
and prohibits retaliation for protected activity.
[
22
]
The FLSA's many protections apply only to employees.
Although the Act's definitions do not include the term “independent contractor,” it defines “employer” in section 3(d) to “include[ ] any person acting directly or indirectly in the interest of an employer in relation to an employee”; “employee” in section 3(e)(1) to mean, subject to certain exceptions, “any individual employed by an employer”; and “employ” in section 3(g) to include “to suffer or permit to work.”
[
23
]
The Supreme Court has recognized that “no definition . . . solves problems as to the limits of the employer-employee relationship under the Act.”
Rutherford Food Corp.
v.
McComb,
331 U.S. 722, 728 (1947).
The Supreme Court has interpreted the phrase “suffer or permit” broadly, extending the phrase to encompass more than the common law standard of employment. In
Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co.
v.
Darden,
the Court explained that section 3(g)'s “suffer or permit” language “stretches the meaning of `employee' to cover some parties who might not qualify as such under a strict application of traditional agency law principles.”
[
24
]
However, the Court also recognized that the FLSA's “statutory definition[s] . . . have [their] limits.”
Tony & Susan Alamo Found.
v.
Sec'y of Labor,
471 U.S. 290, 295 (1985) (internal citation omitted);
see also Walling
v.
Portland Terminal Co.,
330 U.S. 148, 152 (1947) (“The definition `suffer or permit to work' was obviously not intended to stamp all persons as employees[.]”). The Supreme Court specifically recognized that “[t]here may be independent contractors who take part in production or distribution who would alone be responsible for the wages and hours of their own employees.”
Rutherford Food,
331 U.S. at 729. Accordingly, federal courts of appeals have long and uniformly held, and the Department has consistently maintained, that independent contractors are not “employees” for purposes of the Act.
[
25
]
Enacted in 1983, MSPA protects migrant and seasonal agricultural workers by establishing employment standards related to wages, housing, transportation, disclosures and recordkeeping.
[
26
]
Agricultural employers, agricultural associations, and farm labor contractors (as those terms are defined in MSPA) must comply with such applicable standards in their employment of migrant and seasonal agricultural workers.
[
27
]
MSPA also requires farm labor contractors to register with the Department and obtain a certificate of registration.
[
28
]
It is a violation of MSPA to threaten, discharge, or in any manner discriminate against any migrant or seasonal agricultural worker because such worker, with just cause, files a complaint, institutes a proceeding, testifies or is about to testify in a proceeding, or exercises any right under MSPA.
[
29
]
Because MSPA's worker protections apply only to migrant and seasonal agricultural workers who are “
employed
in agricultural
employment
of a seasonal or other temporary nature,”
[
30
]
they do not apply to agricultural workers who are independent contractors. MSPA expressly adopts the FLSA's definition of “employ” as MSPA's definition of “employ” and thus incorporates the “suffer or permit” standard for determining the scope of employment relationships.
[
31
]
Enacted in 1993, the FMLA entitles eligible employees of covered employers to take unpaid, job-protected leave for specified family and medical reasons with continuation of group health insurance coverage under the same terms and conditions as if the employee had not taken leave.
[
32
]
Eligible employees who take such leave must generally be restored to the same or an equivalent position when they return to work after FMLA leave.
[
33
]
An employer cannot interfere with, restrain, or deny an employee's exercise of or attempt to exercise any rights under the FMLA.
[
34
]
As with the FLSA and MSPA, the FMLA's protections and employer requirements do not apply to workers who are independent contractors. The FMLA adopts the FLSA's definitions of “employ” and “employee” and thus incorporates the FLSA's standard for determining the scope of employment relationships.
[
35
]
B. Economic Dependence and the Economic Reality Test
1. Supreme Court Development of the Economic Reality Test
Less than a decade after the FLSA was enacted, the U.S. Supreme Court explored the limits of the employer-employee relationship in a series of cases from 1944 to 1947 under three different federal statutes: the FLSA, the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), and the Social Security Act (SSA). These cases established an “economic reality” test to distinguish between employees and independent contractors that is still used today in FLSA cases. Although the longstanding “economic reality” descriptor is often repeated and is the lens through which the individual worker's relationship with the employer is viewed, the ultimate inquiry focuses on an individual's “economic dependence” for work.
In the first of these cases,
NLRB
v.
Hearst Publications, Inc.,
322 U.S. 111 (1944), the Supreme Court held that the NLRA's definition of employment, which merely defined “employee” to “include any employee,”
id.
at 113 n.1,
(
printed page 75649)
was broader than that of the common law.
Id.
at 123-25. Congress responded by amending the definition of employment under the NLRA on June 23, 1947, with the “obvious purpose of . . . hav[ing] the [National Labor Relations] Board and the courts apply general agency principles in distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the [NLRA].”
[
36
]
On June 16, 1947, a week before Congress amended the NLRA in response to
Hearst,
the Supreme Court decided
United States
v.
Silk,
331 U.S. 704 (1947), which addressed the distinction between employees and independent contractors under the SSA (which did not define “employee”). In that case, the Court relied on
Hearst
to hold that “economic reality,” as opposed to “technical concepts” of the common law, such as master and servant, determines a worker's employment status.
Id.
at 712-14. Although the Court found it to be “quite impossible to extract from the [SSA] a rule of thumb to define the limits of the employer-employe[e] relationship,” it identified five factors as “important for decision”: “degrees of control, opportunities for profit or loss, investment in facilities, permanency of relation[,] and skill required in the claimed independent operation.”
Id.
at 716. The Court added that “[n]o one [factor] is controlling nor is the list complete.”
Id.
Nevertheless, based on the factors that it identified, the Court found that the coal unloaders were employees by referencing, among other things, the employer's supervision and the workers' lack of opportunity for profit based on initiative and investment.
[
37
]
In addition, the Court held that the truck drivers in that case were independent contractors by emphasizing facts related to control, opportunity for profit, initiative and investment.
[
38
]
One week after
Silk
and on the same day Congress amended the NLRA, the Court reiterated these five factors in
Bartels
v.
Birmingham,
332 U.S. 126 (1947), another case involving employee or independent contractor status under the SSA. In
Bartels,
the Court explained that under the SSA, employee status “was not to be determined solely by the idea of control which an alleged employer may or could exercise over the details of the service rendered to his business by the worker”; instead, employees are “those who as a matter of economic reality are dependent upon the business to which they render service.”
Id.
at 130. The Court held that a dance hall's contractual right of control was insufficient to establish an employment relationship with a band leader that it hired.
Id.
at 132.
The same day as it decided
Silk,
the Court ruled in
Rutherford Food
that certain workers at a slaughterhouse were employees under the FLSA, and not independent contractors, by examining facts pertaining to most of the five factors identified in
Silk.
[
39
]
The Court also considered whether the work was “a part of the integrated unit of production” (meaning whether the putative independent contractors were integrated into the assembly line alongside the company's employees) to assess whether they were employees or independent contractors under the FLSA.
Id.
at 729-30.
In November 1947, nearly half a year after
Silk
and
Rutherford Food
were decided, the Department of the Treasury proposed regulations defining when an individual was an independent contractor or employee under the SSA, which used a test that balanced the following factors: (1) degree of control of the individual, (2) permanency of relation, (3) integration of the individual's work in the business to which he renders service, (4) skill required by the individual, (5) investment by the individual in facilities for work, and (6) opportunity of the individual for profit or loss.
[
40
]
Factors one, two, and four through six corresponded directly with the five factors identified as being “important for decision” in
Silk,
331 U.S. at 716, and the third factor corresponded with
Rutherford Food'
s consideration of the fact that the workers were “part of an integrated unit of production.” 331 U.S. at 729. The Treasury proposal further relied on
Bartels,
332 U.S. at 130, to apply these factors to determine whether a worker was “dependent as a matter of economic reality upon the business to which he renders services.”
[
41
]
Congress rejected the interpretations of the definitions of “employee” adopted in
Hearst
for the NLRA and in
Silk
and
Bartels
for the SSA by amending both acts “to demonstrate that the usual common-law principles were the keys to meaning.”
Darden,
503 U.S. at 324-25. Congress did not, however, similarly amend the FLSA following
Rutherford Food.
In 1961, in
Goldberg
v.
Whitaker House Cooperative, Inc.,
the Supreme Court revisited independent contractor status under the FLSA and reaffirmed that “the `economic reality' rather than `technical concepts' ” is “the test of employment” under the FLSA.
[
42
]
It found that certain homeworkers were “not self-employed . . . [or] independent, selling their products on the market for whatever price they can command,” but instead were “regimented under one organization, manufacturing what the organization desires and receiving the compensation the organization dictates,” and thus employees.
[
43
]
Finally, in
Darden,
the Supreme Court reiterated that the FLSA's test for employee status comes from its definition of “employ” in
29 U.S.C. 203(g)
as including to “suffer or permit” to work and is thus broader than the common law test.
[
44
]
2. Application of the Economic Reality Test by WHD and Federal Courts of Appeals
a. WHD's Early Guidance Applying Economic Reality Test Under the FLSA
Since the
Silk, Rutherford Food,
and
Whitaker House
decisions, WHD has applied variations of the economic reality analysis when considering whether a worker is an employee under the FLSA or an independent contractor, with an eye to facilitating its real-world application by workers and businesses.
For example, on June 23, 1949, WHD issued an opinion letter distilling six “primary factors which the Court considered significant” in
Rutherford
(
printed page 75650)
Food
and
Silk:
“(1) the extent to which the services in question are an integral part of the `employer[']s' business; (2) the amount of the so-called `contractor's' investment in facilities and equipment; (3) the nature and degree of control by the principal; (4) opportunities for profit and loss; . . . (5) the amount of initiative judgment or foresight required for the success of the claimed independent enterprise[;] and [(6)] permanency of the relation.”
[
45
]
The 1949 opinion letter cautioned that no single factor is controlling, and “[o]rdinarily a definite decision as to whether one is an employee or an independent contractor under the [FLSA] cannot be made in the absence of evidence as to [the worker's] actual day-to-day working relationship with [their] principal. Clearly a written contract does not always reflect the true situation.”
[
46
]
Subsequent WHD opinion letters addressing employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA have provided similar recitations of the factors, sometimes omitting one or more of the six factors described in the 1949 opinion letter, and sometimes adding (or substituting) a seventh factor: the worker's “degree of independent business organization and operation.”
[
47
]
In 1964, WHD stated: “The Supreme Court has made it clear that an employee, as distinguished from a person who is engaged in a business of his own, is one who as a matter of economic reality follows the usual path of an employee and is dependent on the business which he serves.”
[
48
]
Indeed, the various factors are directed to evaluating the nature of an individual's “dependence” for work.
In 1962, the Department revised the regulations in
29 CFR part 788
, which generally provides interpretive guidance on the FLSA's exemption for employees in small forestry or lumbering operations, and added a provision addressing the distinction between employees and independent contractors.
[
49
]
Citing to
Silk, Rutherford Food,
and
Bartels,
the regulation advised that “an employee, as distinguished from a person who is engaged in a business of his own, is one who `follows the usual path of an employee' and is dependent on the business which he serves.”
[
50
]
To “aid in assessing the total situation,” the regulation then identified a partial list of “characteristics of the two classifications which should be considered,” including “the extent to which the services rendered are an integral part of the principal's business; the permanency of the relationship; the opportunities for profit or loss; the initiative, judgment or foresight exercised by the one who performs the services; the amount of investment; and the degree of control which the principal has in the situation.”
[
51
]
In 1972, the Department added similar guidance on independent contractor status at
29 CFR 780.330(b)
, in a provision addressing the employment status of sharecroppers and tenant farmers under the FLSA.
[
52
]
This regulation was nearly identical to the independent contractor guidance for the logging and forestry industry previously promulgated at
29 CFR 788.16(a)
, including an identical description of the same six economic reality factors.
[
53
]
Both provisions—
29 CFR 780.330(b)
and
788.16(a)
—remained unchanged until 2021.
b. Federal Appellate Courts' Application of the Economic Reality Test
In the 1970s and 1980s, federal courts of appeals began to adopt versions of a multifactor “economic reality” test based on
Silk, Rutherford Food,
and
Bartels
and similar to WHD's early guidance to analyze whether a worker was an employee or an independent contractor under the FLSA. Drawing on the Supreme Court precedent discussed above, courts have recognized that the heart of the inquiry is whether “as a matter of economic reality” the workers are “dependent upon the business to which they render service.”
Usery
v.
Pilgrim Equip. Co.,
527 F.2d 1308, 1311 (5th Cir. 1976) (quoting
Bartels,
332 U.S. at 130);
see also Mednick
v.
Albert Enters., Inc.,
508 F.2d 297, 299-300 (5th Cir. 1975). Courts have clarified that this question of economic dependence may be boiled down to asking “whether, as a matter of economic reality, the workers depend upon someone else's business for the opportunity to render service or are in business for themselves.”
Saleem,
854 F.3d at 139 (internal quotation marks and citations omitted).
[
54
]
Courts have also explained that a non-exhaustive set of factors—derived from
Silk
and
Rutherford Food
—frame and guide this inquiry.
See, e.g., Usery,
527 F.2d at 1311 (identifying “[f]ive considerations [which] have been set out as aids to making the determination of dependence, vel non”);
Real
v.
Driscoll Strawberry Assocs., Inc.,
603 F.2d 748, 754 (9th Cir. 1979) (articulating a six-factor test).
In
Driscoll,
the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals described its six-factor test as follows: (1) the degree of the alleged employer's right to control the manner in which the work is to be performed, (2) the alleged employee's opportunity for profit or loss depending on his managerial skill, (3) the alleged employee's investment in equipment or materials required for his task, or his employment of helpers, (4) whether the service rendered requires a special skill, (5) the degree of permanency of the working relationship, and (6) whether the service rendered is an integral part of the alleged employer's business. 603 F.2d at 754.
Most courts of appeals articulate a similar test, but application between courts may vary.
Compare, e.g., Sec'y of Labor
v.
Lauritzen,
835 F.2d 1529, 1534-35 (7th Cir. 1987) (applying six-factor economic reality test to hold that pickle pickers were employees under the FLSA),
with Donovan
v.
Brandel,
736 F.2d 1114, 1117 (6th Cir. 1984) (applying the same six-factor economic reality test to hold that pickle pickers were not employees under the FLSA). Courts of appeal also vary somewhat in their articulation of the factors. For example, the Second Circuit has analyzed opportunity for profit or loss and investment (the second and third factors listed above) together as one factor.
See, e.g., Brock
v.
Superior Care, Inc.,
840 F.2d 1054, 1058 (2d Cir. 1988). The Fifth Circuit has not adopted the sixth factor listed above, which analyzes the integrality of the work, as part of its standard,
see, e.g., Usery,
527 F.2d at 1311, but has at times assessed integrality as an additional factor,
see, e.g., Hobbs
v.
Petroplex Pipe & Constr., Inc.,
946 F.3d 824, 836 (5th Cir. 2020).
(
printed page 75651)
Some courts of appeals have made noteworthy modifications to the economic reality factors as originally articulated in 1947 by the Supreme Court.
[
55
]
First, the “skill required” factor identified in
Silk,
331 U.S. at 716, is now articulated more expansively by some courts to include “initiative.”
See, e.g., Parrish,
917 F.3d at 379 (considering “the skill and initiative required in performing the job”);
Karlson,
860 F.3d at 1093 (same);
Superior Care,
840 F.2d at 1058-59 (considering “the degree of skill and independent initiative required to perform the work”).
Second,
Silk
analyzed workers' investments, 331 U.S. at 717-19. However, the Fifth Circuit has revised the “investment” factor to instead consider “the extent of the relative investments of the worker and the alleged employer.”
Hopkins
v.
Cornerstone America,
545 F.3d 338, 343 (5th Cir. 2008). Some other circuits also apply this “relative investment” approach but continue to use the phrase “worker's investment” to describe the factor.
See, e.g., Keller,
781 F.3d at 810;
Snell,
875 F.2d at 805, 810.
Third, although the permanence factor under
Silk
was understood to mean the continuity and duration of working relationships,
see
12 FR 7967
, some courts of appeals have expanded this factor to also consider the exclusivity of such relationships.
See, e.g., Scantland,
721 F.3d at 1319;
Keller,
781 F.3d at 807.
Finally,
Rutherford Food'
s consideration of whether work is “part of an integrated unit of production,” 331 U.S. at 729, has now been replaced by many courts of appeals by consideration of whether the service rendered is “integral,” which those courts have applied as meaning important or central to the potential employer's business.
See, e.g., Verma
v.
3001 Castor, Inc.,
937 F.3d 221, 232 (3rd Cir. 2019) (concluding that workers' services were integral because they were the providers of the business's “primary offering”);
Acosta
v.
Off Duty Police Servs., Inc.,
915 F.3d 1050, 1055 (6th Cir. 2019) (concluding that services provided by workers were “integral” because the potential employer “built its business around” those services);
McFeeley
v.
Jackson St. Ent., LLC,
825 F.3d 235, 244 (4th Cir. 2016) (considering “the importance of the services rendered to the company's business”).
Courts of appeals have cautioned against the “mechanical application” of the economic reality factors.
See, e.g., Saleem,
854 F.3d at 139. “Rather, each factor is a tool used to gauge the economic dependence of the alleged employee, and each must be applied with this ultimate concept in mind.”
Cornerstone Am.,
545 F.3d at 343. Further, courts of appeals make clear that the analysis should draw from the totality of circumstances, with no single factor being determinative by itself.
See, e.g., Keller,
781 F.3d at 807 (“No one factor is determinative.”);
Baker
v.
Flint Eng'g & Constr. Co.,
137 F.3d 1436, 1441 (10th Cir. 1998) (“None of the factors alone is dispositive; instead, the court must employ a totality-of-the-circumstances approach.”).
c. The Department's More Recent Application of the Economic Reality Test Under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA
In 1995, the Department promulgated a regulation at
29 CFR 825.105(a)
addressing employee status under the FMLA and the distinction between employees and independent contractors.
[
56
]
The regulation explains that “[t]he definition of employ for purposes of FMLA is taken from the Fair Labor Standards Act, § 3(g),
29 U.S.C. 203(g)
,” meaning a broader scope of employment than at the common law.
[
57
]
The regulation further explains that determining employee status “depends `upon the circumstances of the whole activity' including the underlying `economic reality.' ”
[
58
]
The regulation adds that: “In general an employee, as distinguished from an independent contractor who is engaged in a business of his/her own, is one who `follows the usual path of an employee' and is dependent on the business which [he or she] serves.”
[
59
]
The regulation does not provide any specific economic reality factors to apply. A separate regulation,
29 CFR 825.102
, defines various terms under the FMLA, and consistent with the FMLA's adoption of the FLSA's statutory definitions, defines “employ” to mean “to suffer or permit to work” and “employee” to generally mean “any individual employed by an employer.”
In 1997, the Department promulgated a regulation applying a multifactor economic reality analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under MSPA, which—like the FMLA—statutorily adopts the FLSA's “suffer or permit” definition of employment by reference.
[
60
]
The regulation explains that “[t]he definition of the term
employ
may include consideration of whether . . . an
independent contractor
or
employment
relationship exists under the Fair Labor Standards Act.”
[
61
]
The regulation advises that in determining if the farm labor contractor or worker is an employee or an independent contractor, the ultimate question is the economic reality of the relationship—whether there is economic dependence upon the agricultural employer/association or farm labor contractor, as appropriate.
[
62
]
The regulation elaborates that “[t]his determination is based upon an evaluation of all of the circumstances, including the following: (i) The nature and degree of the putative employer's control as to the manner in which the work is performed; (ii) The putative employee's opportunity for profit or loss depending upon his/her managerial skill; (iii) The putative employee's investment in equipment or materials required for the task, or the putative employee's employment of other workers; (iv) Whether the services rendered by the putative employee require special skill; (v) The degree of permanency and duration of the working relationship; (vi) The extent to which the services rendered by the putative employee are an integral part of the putative employer's business.”
[
63
]
This description of six economic reality factors is very similar to the earlier description of the six-factor test to evaluate the economic reality, that is an individual's economic dependence for work, on a putative employer, provided in
29 CFR 780.330(b)
and
788.16(a)
.
Also in 1997, WHD issued Fact Sheet #13, “Employment Relationship Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA).”
[
64
]
Like WHD opinion letters, Fact Sheet #13 advises that an employee, as distinguished from a person who is engaged in a business of their own, is one who, as a matter of economic reality, follows the usual path of an employee and is dependent on the business which he or she serves. The fact sheet identifies six familiar economic realities factors, as well as consideration of the worker's degree of independent business organization and operation.
(
printed page 75652)
On July 15, 2015, WHD issued Administrator's Interpretation No. 2015-1, “The Application of the Fair Labor Standards Act's `Suffer or Permit' Standard in the Identification of Employees Who Are Misclassified as Independent Contractors” (AI 2015-1).
[
65
]
AI 2015-1 explained that, “under the FLSA, courts use the multi-factorial `economic realities' test, which focuses on whether the worker is economically dependent on the employer or in business for him or herself,” and it identified and provided guidance regarding the application of six economic reality factors. AI 2015-1 further explained that its FLSA analysis “should also be applied in determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor in cases arising under [MSPA] and the [FMLA]” because both statutes adopt the FLSA's definition of “employ.”
In 2019, WHD issued an opinion letter, FLSA2019-6 (later redesignated as FLSA2025-2),
[
66
]
addressing whether service providers who used a “virtual marketplace” company to be referred to end-market consumers were employees or independent contractors of the virtual marketplace company under the FLSA. The opinion letter generally applied principles and factors similar to those described in the prior opinion letters and the 2008 version of Fact Sheet #13, but not the “independent business organization” factor because it did not add to the analysis as a separate factor and was “[e]ncompassed within” the other factors. WHD Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2 at 5. It also stated that the investment factor should focus on the “amount of the worker's investment in facilities, equipment, or helpers.”
Id.
Based on the facts provided, WHD concluded that the service providers at issue appeared to be independent contractors and not employees of the virtual marketplace company. WHD found that it was “inherently difficult to conceptualize the service providers' `working relationship' with [the virtual marketplace company], because as a matter of economic reality, they are working for the consumer, not [the company].”
Id.
at 7-8. Because “[t]he facts . . . demonstrate economic independence, rather than economic dependence, in the working relationship between [the virtual marketplace company] and its service providers,” WHD opined that they were not employees of the company under the FLSA but rather were independent contractors.
Id.
at 11.
C. The 2021 Rule
In the 2021 Rule, the Department affirmed the “economic reality” test under the FLSA to determine whether a worker is in business for himself or herself (an independent contractor) or is instead economically dependent on an employer for work, as an employee conventionally depends on his employer for work.
[
67
]
Specifically, it organized and distilled the longstanding legal analysis and factors in a practical and accessible way, so that workers and businesses could properly apply them, thereby accurately classifying workers in any industry as employees or independent contractors under the FLSA.
The Department framed five familiar factors, drawn from the longstanding approach articulated by the Supreme Court and courts of appeals, to guide the determination of workers' “economic reality.” Like the components of those tests, the Department explained that the “factors are not exhaustive” and “no single factor is dispositive.”
[
68
]
The Department further identified two of those factors (the nature and degree of control over the work and the individual's opportunity for profit or loss) as “core” factors that, across a wide spectrum of work arrangements, are “the most probative as to whether or not an individual is an economically dependent `employee' ” and “therefore typically carr[y] greater weight in the analysis than any other factor.”
[
69
]
The Department added that, “[g]iven these two core factors' greater probative value, if they both point towards the same classification, whether employee or independent contractor, there is a substantial likelihood that is the individual's accurate classification.”
[
70
]
Similarly, the Department explained that other factors are “less probative and, in some cases, may not be probative at all” in answering the ultimate “economic reality” inquiry to which these tests are directed. Typically, these other factors “are highly unlikely, either individually or collectively, to outweigh the combined probative value of the two core factors.”
[
71
]
Ultimately, the Department aimed to combine longstanding judicial frameworks in a practical package—one that could be reliably applied in workplaces across the nation and, therefore, promote certainty for stakeholders, reduce litigation, and encourage economic innovation.
The Department provided guidance in the 2021 Rule on how to apply the control and opportunity for profit or loss factors, including that an individual's opportunity for profit or loss could be based on “his or her exercise of initiative (such as managerial skill or business acumen or judgment) or management of his or her investment in or capital expenditure on, for example, helpers or equipment or material to further his or her work.”
[
72
]
The Department identified three other factors to be considered with the two core factors and provided guidance on each: the amount of skill required for the work, the degree of permanence of the working relationship between the individual and the potential employer, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.
[
73
]
The Department added that “[a]dditional factors may be relevant in determining whether an individual is an employee or independent contractor for purposes of the FLSA, but only if the factors” are directly material to the “economic reality” inquiry that determines whether an individual's relationship with a potential employer is more akin to that of another business or an employee.
[
74
]
The Department further advised that, when applying the factors, “the actual practice of the parties involved is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible.”
[
75
]
The Department also provided six “illustrative examples” of how the factors may be applied in certain factual situations.
[
76
]
And, the Department included a severability provision explaining that the Department would still give “maximum effect” to the rule in the event that any of its provisions are enjoined or invalidated.
[
77
]
In the 2021 Rule, the Department also revised the industry-specific guidance provided at
29 CFR 780.330(b)
(addressing the employment status of sharecroppers and tenant farmers) and 788.16(a) (workers in forestry or logging). The Department replaced the recitation of the six economic reality factors identified in those regulatory subsections with cross-references to the
(
printed page 75653)
2021 Rule's updated and generally applicable guidance.
[
78
]
Finally, the 2021 Rule noted that the Department had received several comments addressing the possibility of applying that rule's analysis to determining employee or independent contractor status under MSPA, including by revising
29 CFR 500.20(h)(4)
.
[
79
]
The Department recognized in the 2021 Rule that “MSPA adopts by reference the FLSA's definition of `employ,'
see
29 U.S.C. 1802(5)
, and that
29 CFR 500.20(h)(4)
considers `whether or not an independent contractor or employment relationship exists under the Fair Labor Standards Act' to interpret independent contractor status under MSPA.”
[
80
]
The Department added that “the regulatory standard for determining an individual's classification status under MSPA is generally consistent with the FLSA guidance finalized in this rule.”
[
81
]
The Department determined at the time that it did “not see a compelling need to revise” the MSPA regulation because it was “unsure whether application of the six factor economic reality test described in that regulation has resulted in confusion and uncertainty in the more limited MSPA context similar to that described in the FLSA context.”
[
82
]
The Department concluded that it “prefers to proceed incrementally at this time by leaving the MSPA regulation at
29 CFR 500.20(h)(4)
unchanged.”
[
83
]
The effective date of the 2021 Rule was March 8, 2021.

84

The Delay Rule stated that it took effect immediately upon its publication in the
Federal Register
.

85

v.
Walsh,

at *9,

88

failed to show “good cause for making the [Delay Rule] effective immediately upon publication,”

at *11, and acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner in its Withdrawal Rule by “fail[ing] to consider potential alternatives to rescinding the [2021] Rule,”

at *13. Accordingly, the district court vacated the Delay and Withdrawal Rules and ruled that the 2021 Rule “became effective as of March 8, 2021, the rule's original effective date, and remains in effect.”

E. The 2024 Rule
On January 10, 2024, the Department published the 2024 Rule, which rescinded the 2021 Rule and replaced it by adopting a modified analysis for determining employee or independent contractor classification under the FLSA in
29 CFR part 795
.
[
89
]
Like the 2021 Rule, the 2024 Rule advised that the FLSA's “definitions are meant to encompass as employees all workers who, as a matter of economic reality, are economically dependent on an employer for work,” elaborating that “[a] worker is an independent contractor, as distinguished from an `employee' under the [FLSA], if the worker is, as a matter of economic reality, in business for themself.”
[
90
]
The 2024 Rule identified six factors as “tools or guides to conduct a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis”: (1) opportunity for profit or loss depending on managerial skill, (2) investments by the worker and the potential employer, (3) degree of permanence of the work relationship, (4) nature and degree of control, (5) extent to which the work performed is an integral part of the potential employer's business, and (6) skill and initiative.
[
91
]
The 2024 Rule did not identify any core factors or otherwise elaborate on the relative importance of these factors, advising instead that “no one factor or subset of factors is necessarily dispositive” and “the weight to give each factor may depend on the facts and circumstances of the particular relationship.”
[
92
]
The 2024 Rule noted that the six factors “are not exhaustive” and “[a]dditional factors may be relevant in determining whether the worker is an employee or independent contractor for purposes of the FLSA, if the factors in some way indicate whether the worker is in business for themself, as opposed to being economically dependent on the potential employer for work.”
[
93
]
The 2024 Rule commented that the outcome of its analysis “does not depend on isolated factors but rather upon the circumstances of the whole activity to answer the question of whether the worker is economically dependent on the potential employer for work or is in business for themself.”

94
]
In addition, the Department made minor revisions to the industry-specific guidance provided at
29 CFR 780.330(b)
and
788.16(a)
by updating the cross-references to
29 CFR part 795
that the 2021 Rule had added.
[
95
]
Also, like the 2021 Rule, the Department included a severability provision in the 2024 Rule.
[
96
]

[
97
]
The Department explained
(
printed page 75654)
that the guidance provided in the MSPA regulation is “substantially similar” to the economic reality test adopted by the 2024 Rule, the comments received did not address MSPA, and the Department “is not revising the MSPA regulation at this time.”

Unlike the 2021 Rule, the 2024 Rule's regulatory text did not include any illustrative examples of how to apply the economic reality test or address the relevance of parties' actual practice as compared to what may be contractually or theoretically possible. G. The 2026 NPRM
On February 27, 2026, the Department published an NPRM proposing to rescind the 2024 Rule's analysis of employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA set forth in
29 CFR part 795
and to replace it with a version of the analysis similar to that which it published in the 2021 Rule.
[
101
]
Moreover, unlike either the 2021 or 2024 Rules, the NPRM proposed to revise the Department's regulations addressing employee or independent contractor status under the FMLA and MSPA so that the FLSA analysis in part 795 would apply when determining employee or independent contractor status under the FMLA and MSPA as well. The Department added that its proposed rescission of the 2024 Rule would operate independently of any regulatory guidance adopted in its place, as the Department intended for its proposed rescission of the 2024 Rule to be independent and severable from its proposal to readopt guidance from the 2021 Rule.
In the NPRM, the Department expressed concern that the 2024 Rule failed to provide an analysis for distinguishing between independent contractors and employees under the FLSA that was sufficiently clear and led to predictable outcomes. The Department expressed a separate concern that the 2024 Rule's description of several “economic reality” factors could be viewed as setting a higher bar to find independent contractor status than required under longstanding judicial precedent, and that an analysis which is ambiguous or perceived as too restrictive of independent contracting could deter businesses from engaging with bona fide independent contractors. The Department explained that replacing the 2024 Rule with a modified and updated analysis from the 2021 Rule would avoid this outcome and facilitate the more accurate and reliable classification of individuals, with a
(
printed page 75655)
familiar and clear analysis drawn from established case law that is more amenable to the modern economy and fully effective in preventing the misclassification of employees.
[
102
]
H. Commenter Feedback
The Department received approximately 16,500 comments during the NPRM's 60-day comment period.
[
103
]
These came from a diverse array of stakeholders, including workers, self-identified independent contractors, businesses, trade associations, labor unions, advocacy groups, law firms, policy experts, members of Congress, and various officials from state and local governments. Of the approximately 16,500 comments submitted, 14,244 (86.3 percent) were either identical or constituted highly similar submissions grouped in seven different comment campaigns—all of which expressed support for the proposal. The Department did not identify any comment campaigns expressing opposition to the proposal.
Apart from the supportive campaign comments, commenter feedback on the proposed rule generally split into three groups. In one camp, numerous businesses, business advocacy groups, management-side law firms, self-identified independent contractors, and some elected officials expressed strong support for the NPRM, asserting that it would better facilitate legitimate independent contracting arrangements by increasing clarity and reducing legal risk as compared to the 2024 Rule. Among this group of commenters, many requested modifications or additions to the proposed analysis, including additional “safe harbor” provisions for certain business practices or illustrative examples specific to particular industries or occupations.
By contrast, many labor unions, worker advocacy groups, plaintiff-side law firms, some individual workers, and other elected officials expressed strong opposition to the NPRM, asserting that it would increase the misclassification of employees as independent contractors and disadvantage businesses that hire workers as employees. Many of these commenters criticized specific features of the NPRM, including its identification of two core factors, its description of particular economic reality factors, and its emphasis on the actual practice of the parties over contractual abilities.
Some commenters—including several truck drivers and digital platform workers—were neutral or generally supportive of the NPRM but requested the Department to address certain business practices they believe to be coercive or exploitative.

Like the legal frameworks from which they are derived, the independent contractor and joint employer proposed rules each provide a separate legal standard and distinct reasons for adopting the respective standards. Neither the standards nor reasoning in either is dependent on or otherwise tied to the other; the public did not need to be aware of both to comment on this NPRM. III. Need for Rulemaking
As a general matter, this rulemaking achieves three objectives: (1) rescission of the 2024 Rule, which the Department ceased applying in its enforcement actions; (2) restoration of the streamlined analysis distilled from federal case law for both workers and businesses more easily and accurately to determine employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA adopted in the 2021 Rule, with a few enhancements; and (3) clarification that the analysis used to determine employee or independent contractor status under the Act also should be
(
printed page 75656)
applied to make that determination under the FMLA and MSPA, which incorporate the FLSA's scope of employment provisions. The NPRM provided an extensive explanation of the need to achieve—and value of achieving—these objectives, highlighting:
concerns that the 2024 Rule failed to provide an analysis for determining independent contractor and employee status under the FLSA that is sufficiently clear and amenable to application by workers and businesses, thus failing to produce predictable outcomes;
concerns that the 2024 Rule's description of several economic reality factors could have been viewed as setting a higher bar to find independent contractor status than required under the law;
concerns over the 2024 Rule's compatibility with the modern economy, including that the predictive accuracy of certain economic reality factors may be waning due to the evolution of work in America;
concerns over negative effects if the 2024 Rule were left in place, including the unnecessary classification of economically independent workers as employees and the deterrence of bona fide independent contracting and related efficiencies and innovations in the broader economy; and
the need for uniformity and consistency in the analysis of employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA.
The subheadings below summarize the NPRM's discussion of these policy concerns and respond to commenter feedback on them, as well as commenter views on other issues relevant to the need for this rulemaking. The Department's response to commenter feedback on the analysis proposed to replace the 2024 Rule appears in section IV, while the potential economic consequences of this final rule are discussed in greater detail in the regulatory impact analysis in section VI.
A. Concerns That the 2024 Rule Failed To Provide a Clear Analysis for Workers and Businesses Properly To Classify Workers as Employees or Independent Contractors
As explained in the NPRM, the Department believes that the principal flaw of the 2024 Rule was its failure to provide effective guidance on how different factors in its multifactor balancing test should be weighed or applied together. In the absence of such guidance, engaging individuals as independent contractors was both confusing and potentially posed significant legal risk, especially when different factors arguably pointed to different classification outcomes. One can frame a myriad of scenarios involving workers who are in business for themselves (and thus are bona fide independent contractors), but where two or more factors from the 2024 Rule arguably indicate an employment relationship, particularly in industries where those workers are “integral” to the businesses in those industries. As Judge Frank Easterbrook noted, “ `[economic] reality' encompasses millions of facts, and unless we have a legal rule with which to sift the material from the immaterial, we might as well examine the facts through a kaleidoscope. Which facts matter, and why? A legal approach calling on judges to examine all of the facts, and balance them, avoids formulating a rule of decision.”
[
107
]
Indeed, it was this very ambiguity that initially motivated the Department to propose regulations in 2020 for analyzing employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA. In that rulemaking, after reviewing decades of judicial decisions applying
Silk
and
Rutherford Food,
the Department determined that federal courts tend to focus on two of the economic reality factors—control and the opportunity for profit or loss. The Department concluded that courts tended to treat the direction in which they pointed as a reliable indicator of employee or independent contractor status, effectively—if not formally—giving them more weight and an elevated status as reliable indicators of employment or independent contractor status. As the Department explained, this is because control and opportunity “strike at the core of what it means to be in business for oneself.”
[
108
]
It is logical that those factors would and should have primacy in position and weight in assessing the legality of an independent contractor arrangement over ancillary considerations regarding the skill of the individual worker at issue, the permanency of the individual's relationship with a particular business, and whether the work is an “integral part” of that business.
[
109
]
In recent rulemakings, numerous independent contractors and business stakeholders that engage independent contractors asserted that the 2021 Rule's identification of core factors brought helpful clarity and assurance.
[
110

While the Department disagreed with such views in the 2024 Rule and the Withdrawal Rule,
[

the Department acknowledged in the NPRM that, upon reflection, the need for added clarity on how different factors from the economic reality test should be balanced in a consistent and predictable fashion is compelling. As explained in greater detail in section IV.F. below, the Department can apply an economic reality test grounded in federal case law that provides more clear, reliable, and predictable results to interested stakeholders than an unguided “totality-of-the-circumstances analysis” in which “the weight to give each factor may depend on the facts and circumstances of the particular relationship.”
[
112
]
In advising the public on how it intends to weigh the different economic reality factors, the Department—taking its lead from the outcomes of decades of federal appellate court decisions—can and should do better than “it depends.”
See Grossbaum

Indianapolis-Marion Cnty. Bldg. Auth.,
100 F.3d 1287, 1299 (7th Cir. 1996) (noting Judge Easterbrook's observation that real world actors need guidance ahead of time rather than critiques afterward).
The Department is additionally concerned that the 2024 Rule featured numerous redundancies in its description of the different factors in its economic reality test. For example, the phrases “managerial skill (including initiative or business acumen or judgment),” “business-like initiative,” and “independent business initiative” appeared in the guidance provided for three different factors in the 2024 Rule.
[

[

Finally, the “permanence” factor stated in circular fashion that an impermanent work arrangement is only indicative of independent contractor status if it is “based on the worker being in business for themself,”

[

The Department acknowledged in the preamble of the 2024 Rule that “certain relevant facts may overlap among the factors,” but explained that it “does not wish to be overly prescriptive” about such overlap for fear of establishing “a formulaic or rote analysis” that would not be “flexible enough to apply to all kinds of work, and all kinds of workers.”
[

While some degree of factual overlap may be inevitable in a multifactor analysis, the Department now believes that the 2024 Rule crossed the line from natural overlap into unhelpful repetition—particularly where the same concepts (such as “business initiative”) were presented as required elements of multiple factors but applied for different purposes. These redundancies risked confusing businesses and workers alike, creating uncertainty about whether the same considerations must be counted multiple times or weighed differently depending on the factor in which they appear. Indeed, the 2024 Rule not only added unnecessary and unhelpful elements to the tests employed by federal circuit courts, but it also emphasized the breadth of potential considerations in each while at the same time declining to explain—much less demonstrate—how they should be applied. As explained in the NPRM, the Department concludes that a clear articulation and deduplication of the elements of each factor together with unambiguous direction regarding their application and several examples will not only enhance the utility of the Department's regulations on the economic reality test but also make it more likely that workers will be properly classified.

Indeed, several commenters seemed to question the value of any rulemaking in the absence of formal judicial deference. As the Department has previously explained,
[
128
]
the value of a regulation such as this one does not stem from a binding command of deference. To the contrary, regulations should reliably explain, clarify, and assist individuals and entities in efforts to follow the law's requirements. Here, the analysis adopted in this rule will facilitate the proper classification of workers at the outset of a work arrangement, which has always remained the Department's objective. Merely pointing to or parroting circuit law as a regulation is not helpful for most workers and businesses, much less the Division's enforcement personnel, who often must apply standards in investigations that bridge multiple circuits. Judicial tests, developed in multiple cases over time, are designed and applied by judges on a factual record compiled via the adversarial process in pleadings, discovery, and trial. Asking lay workers and businesses to correctly identify, understand, interpret, remain current with, and correctly apply federal circuit law to classify workers without a legal record is a recipe for widespread misclassification. Instead, this rule sets forth a test which is distilled from federal circuit law but framed in an accessible way, allowing workers and businesses to apply it in clear, reliable, and predictable ways with accurate and proper classification outcomes that would stand up in court. At the very least, the rule is more calibrated to achieve reliable classification outcomes from workers and businesses than the 2024 Rule.

Unlike the former, the latter featured an economic reality test with

The Department concludes that an economic reality test with excessive redundancy and no guidance for how the different factors should be weighed, compared, and applied against or in concert with each other is unacceptably opaque,
[

The Department does not share commenter concerns over whether courts will adopt the analysis in this final rule or arrive at different classification outcomes than those produced by this rule. As the Department explained in the NPRM (and in section IV of this rule), this rule's analysis is derived from existing judicial precedent and, as a general matter, the Department does not believe it will result in different outcomes.

That the regulation would not bind or control the courts—only Department investigators—is unremarkable. Courts have always been the final word on the meaning and application of the law. Workers, businesses, courts, and the economy benefit from the proper classification of employees and independent contractors at the outset of a working relationship—not after the fact, years later upon litigation to final judgment. B. Concerns That the 2024 Rule's Description of the Factors Could Have Been Perceived as Too Restrictive of Independent Contracting and a Departure From the Supreme Court's Application
In addition to concerns about the 2024 Rule's lack of clarity, the Department expressed a separate concern in the NPRM that the 2024 Rule could be viewed as more restrictive of independent contracting than the law requires. Specifically, several of the economic reality factors in the 2024 Rule were framed in ways that depart from the Supreme Court's articulation of the factors, effectively distorting the analysis. By expanding the test to include additional considerations that must be satisfied, but only for the factor to indicate independent contractor status, the 2024 Rule stacked the analysis so that it could be viewed as more likely to point to employee classification than a conventional application of judicial tests. The Department noted that by making the proper classification of independent contractors more difficult than the law requires, the 2024 Rule could deter businesses from engaging with bona fide independent contractors or induce them to unnecessarily classify such contractors as employees.
The “investments” factor at
29 CFR 795.110(b)(2)
in the 2024 Rule is instructive. Before the 2024 Rule, when the Department would enumerate the multifactor economic reality test for assessing independent contractor arrangements, the Department's description of the investments factor would generally focus on any investments (or lack thereof) made by the individual worker.
[
138
]
However, the 2024 Rule expanded this factor to examine “investments by the worker
and the potential employer,”
with guidance elaborating that “the worker's investments should be considered on a relative basis with the potential employer's investments in its overall business.”
[
139
]
The Department recognizes that this additional consideration of comparing the worker's investment to the potential employer's investment is applied by some courts, but that approach finds no support in Supreme Court cases. Moreover, comparing investments diminishes the probative value of the investment, if any, by the worker. For example, a worker's investments will almost invariably be smaller than the potential employer's “investments in its overall business,”
[
140
]
so comparing their investments is unbalanced in favor of employee status and fails to offer any insight into distinguishing between employee and independent contractor status. In response to commenter concerns on this point, the Department recognized this problem and sought to address it in the 2024 Rule's regulatory text by stating that the “worker's investments need not be equal to the potential employer's investments and should not be compared only in terms of the dollar values of investments or the sizes of the worker and the potential employer.”
[
141
]
Nevertheless, the 2024 Rule's “investments” factor still undertook this comparative approach, which departed from
Silk
and significantly reduced the probative value of the worker's investments.
The 2024 Rule's “permanence” factor (in § 795.110(b)(3)) is another example. The operative text advised that “[t]his factor weighs in favor of the worker being an employee when the work relationship is indefinite in duration, continuous, or exclusive of work for other employers,” while it “weighs in favor of the worker being an independent contractor when the work relationship is definite in duration, non-exclusive, project-based, or sporadic based on the worker being in business for themself and marketing their services or labor to multiple entities.”
[
142
]
Here, the conditional language following the word “sporadic” seemed to add further considerations than the law requires in order for an impermanent relationship to indicate independent contractor status. Adding to the perception that it could be more difficult to find that this factor weighed in favor of independent contractor status, the 2024 Rule additionally advised, as some courts have, that “this [permanence] factor is not necessarily indicative of independent contractor status” where “a lack of permanence is due to operational characteristics that are unique or intrinsic to particular businesses or industries and the workers they employ . . . unless the worker is exercising their own independent business initiative.”
[
143
]
But there was no corresponding language in the other direction, categorically discounting industries where lengthy professional relationships between businesses and independent contractors might be commonplace. The result was a factor framed in a way that could indicate an FLSA employment relationship when permanence existed but unnecessarily require additional considerations to indicate independent contractor status when permanence did not exist.
The 2024 Rule's “skill and initiative” factor operated in a similar fashion. The regulatory text began with straightforward guidance that a lack of skills indicated that a worker was an employee: “This factor indicates employee status where the worker does not use specialized skills in performing the work or where the worker is dependent on training from the potential employer to perform the work.”
[
144
]
However, the text did not correspondingly state that specialized skills indicated that the worker is an independent contractor and instead included an additional consideration that had to be met for this factor to indicate that a worker with specialized skills is an independent contractor: “Where the worker brings specialized skills to the work relationship, this fact is not itself indicative of independent contractor status because both employees and independent contractors may be skilled workers. It is the worker's use of those specialized skills in connection with business-like initiative that indicates that the worker is an independent contractor.”
[
145
]
Here
(
printed page 75661)
again, the Department recognizes that some form of this approach is applied by some courts, but the 2024 Rule articulated this factor in a way that made it more difficult than the law requires to establish that a worker might be an independent contractor rather than an employee. While it is true that “both employees and independent contractors may be skilled workers,” the converse is also true, as other workers who may not possess “specialized skills” are both employees and independent contractors. Moreover, although the 2024 Rule's consideration of initiative as part of the skill factor is supported by some courts, the Supreme Court has not considered initiative in terms of skill. Instead, and as discussed in section IV.G.1, it has consistently analyzed whether initiative contributes to the success or profitability of the claimed independent business.
[
146
]
The 2024 Rule's “integral” factor departed from
Rutherford Food's
consideration of whether a worker is part of an “integrated unit,” instead examining whether work is “critical, necessary, or central to the potential employer's principal business.”
[
147
]
This framing may have unreasonably frustrated a finding of independent contractor status because, in some sense, all work performed is in some way necessary to the employer's business. If not, the business would not pay for it to be performed.
[
148
]
Finally, in its descriptive guidance for the “control” factor, the 2024 Rule gave several examples of facts relevant to a potential employer's control over workers but did not provide similar examples of facts relevant to a worker's control, further implying that this factor was not a balanced aid in determining proper classification.
[
149
]
Taken together, these aspects of the 2024 Rule appeared to be misaligned with Supreme Court precedent and may have created the perception of an economic reality test with a number of considerations that would make it harder to conclude that an individual who is in business for him- or herself is an independent contractor. While the Department maintains that preventing the misclassification of FLSA-covered employees as independent contractors is an important policy goal, it is equally important that the Department's guidance not be viewed as chilling independent contracting arrangements that comply with the Act.
These features were lost on the regulated community. Numerous commenters asserted that the 2024 Rule's analysis was “slanted,” “tilted,” or “biased” against findings of independent contractor status.
See
CWI; Financial Services Institute (FSI); Landmark Legal Foundation; U.S. Chamber;
see also, e.g.,
Institute for the American Worker (asserting that the 2024 Rule “presented a thumb on the scale in favor of employment status rather than clear lines between employment and independence”). Commenters who opposed the NPRM defended the 2024 Rule by asserting its consistency with longstanding judicial precedent.
See, e.g.,
GFI; Nichols Kaster; United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America (UBC). Some of these commenters seemed to embrace the difficulty of classifying workers as independent contractors under the 2024 Rule, quoting from (withdrawn) AI 2015-1 to assert that “most workers” should be FLSA-covered employees under the economic reality test. see also
SMART & SMACNA (asserting that AI 2015-1 “effectively created a presumption that workers are employees under the FLSA” and recommending the Department to endorse a rebuttable presumption for workers in the construction industry). See
