See, e.g.,
Farmworker Justice (“It is clear that the Proposed Rule, like the 2021 IC Rule, aims to classify more workers as independent contractors, by narrowing the test for employment in a way that Congress had explicitly rejected when enacting the FLSA[.]”); Nichols Kaster (asserting that the NPRM's “[e]mployer-[f]riendly” interpretations of the factors will narrow the scope of FLSA coverage).
The Department reiterates that the goal of this rulemaking is to establish a clear and appropriate analysis for determining employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA—not to favor one status over the other. Given that the 2024 Rule could have been viewed as significantly favoring classification of workers as employees, this final rule, like any middle-of-the-road proposal, could result in
comparatively
more workers being classified as independent contractors.
[
150
]
But that does not mean the Department's rule favors contractors in ways that the 2024 Rule favored employees. To the contrary, it returns to the test derived from decades of federal case law that no more favors contractors than it does employees. While courts and the Department have long interpreted the FLSA's “suffer or permit” language as establishing a broader scope of employment than what exists under the common law, neither the FLSA nor any of the Supreme Court cases addressing the classification of independent contractors require an economic reality test that is perceived to lead to an employee rather than independent contractor outcome. For
(
printed page 75662)
example, to the extent that an individual's lack of specialized skills is correlated with employee status and thus indicative of an employment relationship, the converse should also be true—
i.e.,
an individual's possession of specialized skills should be indicative of independent contractor status, regardless of whether his or her skills are exercised “in connection with business-like initiative.” Similarly, if an indefinite or continuous work relationship with a particular hiring party is indicative of an employment relationship, a definite or sporadic work relationship with a hiring party should be indicative of independent contractor status, regardless of whether such impermanence is attributable to “operational characteristics that are unique or intrinsic to particular businesses or industries.” Notably, the Department's 1997 MSPA regulation did not feature this kind of language in its application of the “skill” and “permanence” factors,
[
151
]
underscoring that the 2024 Rule represented a departure from the Department's prior application of the economic reality test. Ultimately, the Department's place is not to pick favorites, but rather provide a clear analysis that workers and businesses alike may use to properly classify employees and contractors.
While some commenters defended the 2024 Rule's comparative approach to investment,
[
152
]
no commenter disputed the Department's central concern—shared by many commenters—that this approach risks indicating the existence of an employment relationship in many cases simply because the worker's investments are smaller than the potential employer's “investments in its overall business.” Here again, as with the “skill” and “permanency” factors, the 2024 Rule's formulation of the “investment” factor departed from the Department's longstanding application of the economic reality test in a way that made a finding of independent contractor status harder than what is required by the law.
[
153
]
Thus, having considered commenter feedback, the Department concludes that the 2024 Rule's description of the investment factor could have been perceived as unduly restrictive of independent contracting.
The Department acknowledges that the 2024 Rule's “integral part” factor was generally consistent with the Department's pre-2021 guidance and the way most courts apply this factor today.
See, e.g.,
AFL-CIO; Coalition of State Officials; Farmworker Justice. However, as explained in the 2021 Rule and in the NPRM, the Supreme Court in
Rutherford Food
originally examined whether the workers at issue were part of the hiring party's “integrated unit,”
[
154
]
which is more probative of employee or independent contractor status than an inquiry into whether services are “integral” (
i.e.,
“critical, necessary, or central”) to the hiring party. Upon reconsideration, the Department believes that the 2024 Rule's “integral part” factor was a missed opportunity to return to
Rutherford Food's
original focus on integration.
The Department notes that many commenters who opposed the NPRM objected that its proposed analysis would “make it easier” to classify workers as independent contractors. Center for WorkLife Law; Farmworker Justice; North America's Building Trades Unions (NABTU); Sen. Elizabeth Warren. As the Department has noted repeatedly, the objective is the proper classification of workers under the law—not to make classification in any direction more or less
easy
or
difficult
than another. Indeed, the Department believes that the clearer distillation of the legal analysis will be easier for entities to apply than a confusing one; in this respect, the Department expects that this rule will make it easier for entities to appropriately classify all workers, including employees. More fundamentally, it is not the Department's role to encourage, discourage, expand, or restrict independent contracting any more or less than employment. The law allows—and workers, businesses, and the economy benefit from—the diversity of opportunities and protects those workers who are employees. Indeed, the Department recognized in the 2024 Rule that “independent contractors and small businesses play an important role in our economy,”
[
155
]
expressing at the time that the 2024 Rule was “not intended to disrupt the businesses of independent contractors who are, as a matter of economic reality, in business for themselves.”
[
156
]
Upon reconsideration, the Department shares the expressed concerns of many commenters that retaining the 2024 Rule would have such a disruptive effect, in part because the 2024 Rule's description of various economic reality factors appeared to be more restrictive of independent contractor classification than the Department's pre-2021 guidance, or the Supreme Court's application of the economic reality test. Ensuring that the Department's enforcement of federal wage and hour law does not deter or inhibit legitimate independent contracting or result in the unnecessary or mistaken classification of economically independent workers as employees are appropriate policy considerations.
C. Concerns Over the 2024 Rule's Compatibility With the Modern Economy
In the 2021 Rule, the Department explained that certain technological and social changes have made the traditional articulation of the economic reality test more difficult to apply in the modern economy. For example, it highlighted the effects of several types of change, including societal transition from a predominantly industrial-based to a more knowledge-based economy and shorter job tenures among employees.
[
157
]
In 2024, the Department disagreed with its past statements and arguments from some commenters that the 2021 Rule was better suited to the modern economy, asserting that “[m]odern work arrangements . . . are best addressed using the [2024 Rule's] economic reality test, which considers the totality of the circumstances in each working arrangement and offers a flexible, comprehensive, and appropriately nuanced approach which can be adapted to disparate industries and occupations.”
[
158
]
However, as discussed earlier in section III.A., generalizing an already complicated legal analysis in ways that expand “flexibility” injects further ambiguity and can undermine the utility of a rule—namely to clarify the proper application of statutory provisions, which provides regulated entities with the reasonable certainty and predictability they need to do business. This is particularly true for practices which might be novel and innovative. Moreover, in the 2024 Rule, the Department did not address, much less refute, the points made by the 2021 Rule that the predictive accuracy of certain economic reality factors
(
printed page 75663)
(investments, permanence, and integrality) may be waning due to recent workplace trends. These trends are no less true today than they were in 2021, reinforcing the need for prioritization among the factors of the economic reality test.
Numerous self-identified independent contractors and business organizations asserted that the 2024 Rule is ill-suited for the modern economy. Many of these commenters emphasized that, instead of a “flexible” standard, businesses need regulatory certainty to plan, invest, and innovate.
See
Christine Byrne (“I need to be able to rely on a consistent and predictable standard when making decisions about how to structure my business.”); CPAC Foundation Center for Regulatory Freedom (“When the classification standard is unclear, firms may be reluctant to experiment with new approaches . . . [and] potential entrants may delay or abandon new ventures due to concerns about compliance risk.”). Several commenters asserted that regulatory uncertainty imposes a disproportionate burden on independent contractors and small businesses, which lack the resources of larger firms.
See
American Society of Travel Advisors; Institute for the American Worker; National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB); Small Business Administration (SBA) Office of Advocacy. Many commenters emphasized the critical role that independent contracting plays in their industries, which they believed would be harmed if the 2024 Rule were left in place.
See, e.g.,
American Association of Advertising Agencies; Direct Selling Association; National Association of Home Builders; National Association of Realtors; National Council of Agricultural Employers; Truckload Carriers Association. Relatedly, several commenters criticized the 2024 Rule's retention of an “integral part” economic reality factor, asserting that the factor fails to recognize the degree to which independent contractors are critical, necessary, or central.
See, e.g.,
National Association of Home Builders; ShiftKey; Transportation Intermediaries Association.
As with the “integral part” factor, several commenters asserted that changes in the economy have diminished the predictive accuracy of the skill and permanence factors, which the 2024 Rule places on equal footing with control and opportunity. For example, in questioning the need for a factor examining a worker's amount of skill, CWI asserted that “[t]oday's expansive independent work opportunities encompass a far wider array of individuals who may not possess a `skill' that is a part of a traditional learned profession or trade” and that “almost anyone [can] enter into distribution and other service industries and design their own opportunity, often by accessing platforms that connect workers with business opportunities.”
See also
U.S. Chamber; Littler WPI. Similarly, several commenters questioned the probative value of the “permanence” factor, noting that many independent contractors choose to voluntarily reengage with particular entities in the context of a successful business relationship.
See, e.g.,
CWI; FedEx; Scopelitis, Garvin, Light, Hanson & Feary P.C. (Scopelitis); U.S. Chamber.
Some commenters defended the 2024 Rule as more compatible with the modern economy than the NPRM. For example, GFI asserted that because “independent contracting—both in legitimate forms and via misclassification—occurs through a wide variety of working arrangements,” the Department should retain a “flexible, comprehensive” analysis instead of one that “focus[es] on core factors that may not capture all relevant features of the relationship.”
See also
Coalition of State Officials (asserting that “the gig economy, changes in technology, and their impacts on workplace dynamics . . . highlight[] the need for a flexible test, like the one set forth in the 2024 rule”). Coalition of State Officials additionally commented that, unlike the NPRM's proposed analysis, the 2024 Rule included language identifying “whether the potential employer uses technological means to supervise the performance of the work (such as by means of a device or electronically)” as a relevant consideration within the control factor,
[
159
]
asserting that the NPRM's silence on such control contradicts the stated rationales for this rulemaking.
See also
Allegheny County et al. (asserting that the NPRM “ignores that modern employers commonly use technology and algorithms to automatically and invisibly track, supervise, and control the conditions of work for supposed independent contractors”); NELP (asserting that the NPRM “misses the sophisticated yet nuanced ways that corporations set or control the material terms of the work . . . including [with] productivity trackers, webcam monitoring, wearable devices, and algorithms and apps used for wage-setting”).
Having reviewed these comments, the Department remains persuaded, as it made clear in 2021, that the diversity of work arrangements in the modern economy underscores the need for an analysis that provides more predictable outcomes than the 2024 Rule. In particular, the 2024 Rule's failure to provide guidance on the relative importance of the different economic reality factors was a missed opportunity to promote more consistent classification outcomes—even in similar factual circumstances.
[
160
]
While some degree of flexibility in the economic reality test is necessary and required by Supreme Court precedent,
[
161
]
an analysis which is too flexible can result in arbitrary and unpredictable outcomes. “People are entitled to know the legal rules before they act, and only the most compelling reason should [justify] an approach under which no one can know where he stands until litigation has been completed.”
[
162
]
Moreover, an analysis which affords equal weight to every economic reality factor fails to account for the fact that some characteristics no longer correlate as strongly as they once did with a particular classification outcome—and is at odds with how courts have considered and applied these factors in practice. To be specific, commenter feedback (described above) suggests that more independent contractors today lack “specialized skills,” perform work which is “integral” to their clients, and have lengthy, recurring relationships with their clients. Accordingly, a rule prioritizing the economic reality factors that remain most relevant and indicative of the difference between employees and independent contractors—control and opportunity—would be a better fit for the modern economy than the 2024 Rule.
Finally, as explained later in section IV.F.1. of this final rule, the Department's omission of regulatory text from the 2024 Rule noting that workers may be supervised through “technological means” is not tantamount to “[e]ncouraging courts to
(
printed page 75664)
ignore these practices,” as asserted by Coalition of State Officials. As under the 2021 Rule, where the NPRM's proposed regulatory text identified considerations which should be excluded from the analysis, the text does so explicitly—including in the control factor.
[
163
]
As explained in greater detail in section IV.F.1, the Department believes that all relevant facts should be considered, including ways in which new technologies can both empower individuals to be in business for themselves and can serve to control employees as supervisors or managers have historically done. To the extent that the 2024 Rule's regulatory text implied that any technological influence in a work arrangement is evidence of employment, the Department agrees with the advocacy group TechNet that such a perception “would undermine both innovation and the Department's broader goals of preparing the workforce for an AI-driven economy” in a manner neither required by law nor advisable as policy.
D. Concerns Over Negative Effects if the 2024 Rule Were Left in Place
As a downstream consequence of the 2024 Rule's analytical flaws, the Department is concerned that leaving the 2024 Rule in effect could have led to undesirable policy outcomes. Specifically, a classification analysis which is ambiguous or is perceived as overly restrictive of independent contracting may induce businesses to unnecessarily classify economically independent workers as employees or deter businesses from engaging with such individuals at all—outcomes with harmful consequences for the broader economy.
As the Department acknowledged in the 2024 Rule, “independent contractors and small businesses play an important role in our economy.”
[
164
]
Independent contracting offers individuals the ability to control when, where, and how they work, and it provides businesses—particularly small enterprises and new ventures—with access to specialized skills and scalable workforces.
[
165
]
While independent contractors are not entitled to FLSA protections, they often prize the autonomy and flexibility their work affords; indeed, many pursue contracting arrangements as a preferred mode of work.
[
166
]
A rule that operates to complicate or discourage these arrangements may inadvertently limit work opportunities for individuals seeking flexibility due to caregiving responsibilities, education, retirement, geographic constraints, or other personal circumstances. For businesses, unclear or one-sided regulations can deter growth and investment. To the extent that the 2024 Rule curtailed or discouraged legitimate independent contracting, investment, and innovation, it may have led to negative effects on consumers, who may have faced higher prices and a reduced number of alternatives to meet their needs. These potential effects are discussed in greater detail in the regulatory impact analysis for this rule in section VI. Ultimately, this rule helps workers and businesses properly classify employees and independent contractors under the law at the outset of their work arrangements. It neither favors nor disfavors employees or independent contractors—and it neither facilitates nor complicates classification in any one direction over the other.

While most commenters tended to criticize one effect or the other, the Department rejects the premise that it must choose between the lesser of these two evils. As explained more fully in section IV of this notice, the economic reality test adopted in this rulemaking is consistent with longstanding judicial precedent, notwithstanding refinements that will make the test more predictable and easier to apply. (

[
176

the Act was not intended to disrupt legitimate independent contracting.

177

The Department notes that none of the federal wage and hour statutes at issue in this rulemaking preempt state law, so states and localities remain free to enforce or enact tests that are more restrictive of independent contracting if they so choose.

178

Correctly classifying workers, whether as employees or independent contractors, remains vitally important to the proper application and enforcement of the FLSA. One of the most effective ways to prevent misclassification is to clarify how workers and businesses may properly and reliably apply the appropriate analysis across a wide array of industries, companies, and individual working arrangements. The Department's role is not to incentivize or disincentivize companies from classifying workers as employees or independent contractors, either by placing a regulatory finger on one side of the scale or the other or by allowing legal ambiguity to discourage the correct classification of individuals. In this rulemaking, the Department is adopting a rule that is more consistent with Supreme Court precedent, provides a cogent synthesis of the over 80 years of case law since the FLSA's enactment that has helped to interpret the relevant statutory terms, and also seeks to minimize potential negative effects on independent contractors and their business partners while still effectively addressing misclassification and abuse.
E. The Need for Uniformity and Consistency in the Analysis of Employee or Independent Contractor Status Under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA, Which Share the Same Statutory Definitions of Employment
As noted earlier, the FMLA and MSPA both incorporate the FLSA's broad definition of “employ,” including “to suffer or permit to work.”
See
29 U.S.C. 2611(3)
(FMLA);
29 U.S.C. 1802(5)
(MSPA). Thus, it has been the Department's longstanding position that the analysis for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor should be the same under all three statutes—
i.e.,
the analysis which applies under the FLSA.
However, as noted in the NPRM, the Department's regulations have not reflected a single standard for the three statutes.
[
179
]
For example, the MSPA regulation noted that MSPA and the FLSA share the same employment definitions and advised that a determination of employee or independent contractor status “may include consideration of whether” there is an employee or independent contractor relationship under the FLSA.
[
180
]
However, the regulation also advised that determining whether agricultural workers or farm labor contractors are independent contractors “should be resolved in accordance with the factors set out” therein, “based upon an evaluation of all of the circumstances.”
[
181
]
Those factors are not exactly the same as the factors that the Department is adopting in this rule, and of particular relevance, the MSPA regulation did not—like this rule's FLSA analysis—advise how to weigh the factors. There are also differences between the economic reality factors in the MSPA regulation and some of the factors described in the 2024 Rule and the analysis from FAB 2025-1 that the Department applied under the FLSA beginning in May 2025. Thus, retaining the MSPA regulation's instruction to assess employee or independent contractor status “in accordance with” that regulation's enumerated factors could create uncertainty over whether any FLSA guidance issued by the Department on this topic—including the analysis adopted in this rulemaking—also applies in MSPA cases.
Failing to make conforming edits to the MSPA regulation risks confusing agricultural employers, agricultural associations, and farm labor contractors which might be subject to both the FLSA and MSPA, as well as the agricultural workers that such entities engage. Revising the MSPA regulation (
29 CFR 500.20(h)(4)
) to conform it to the Department's FLSA regulatory guidance resolves these concerns and provides uniformity between MSPA and the FLSA on this issue.
The FMLA regulation's guidance for assessing employee or independent contractor status could be similarly unclear if conforming edits are not made. The regulation defined “Employee” as having the same meaning as that term has under the FLSA and noted that the “definition of employ for purposes of FMLA is taken from the [FLSA].”
[
182
]
However, the FMLA regulation did not mention the economic reality factors used to distinguish between employees and independent contractors under the FLSA or advise how the factors should be weighed. Instead, the regulation explained generally that “courts have said that there is no definition that solves all problems as to the limitations of the employer-employee relationship.”
[
183
]
It further advised that “an employee, as distinguished from an independent contractor who is engaged in a business of his/her own, is one who `follows the usual path of an employee' and is dependent on the business which [he or she] serves.”
Id.
This language, although accurate in describing the overall analysis, could be misinterpreted as suggesting that—unlike the FLSA (and MSPA)—there is no set of factors for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors in FMLA cases. The Department did not intend to create or imply any discrepancy between the FMLA and FLSA when it added the language in
29 CFR 825.105(a)
in 1995.
[
184
]
The Department believes that adding cross-references to part 795 in
29 CFR 825.102
(definition of “Employee”) and 825.105(a) addresses this concern and provides useful guidance when making the determination under the FMLA.
The risk that employee or independent contractor status under the FMLA could be assessed without
(
printed page 75668)
applying FLSA principles is not merely theoretical. In
Alexander
v.
Avera St. Luke's Hospital,
768 F.3d 756, 763-64 (8th Cir. 2014)—the only federal circuit-court-level case to decide such a dispute arising under the FMLA—the Eighth Circuit expressly declined to apply an FLSA economic reality test to determine whether the plaintiff was an employee or independent contractor. While acknowledging that the FMLA incorporates the FLSA's “suffer or permit” language, the Eighth Circuit concluded that “simply applying” an FLSA economic reality test in that FMLA case would “not [be] appropriate,” noting that the plaintiff's “work in a `professional capacity' was totally exempt from the FLSA's minimum standards.”
Id.
at 763 (citing
29 U.S.C. 213(a)(1)
). The Department believes that the Eighth Circuit's approach in
Alexander,
even if limited to cases where the worker would be exempt from the FLSA if an employee, is inconsistent with the FMLA's statutory text and the Department's regulations and guidance, as well as the approach taken by most federal district courts, which do apply an FLSA economic reality test to adjudicate employee or independent contractor disputes under the FMLA.
See, e.g., Hay
v.
ALH Admin. Servs.,
283 F. Supp. 3d 1273, 1276 (M.D. Fla. 2017);
Nichols
v.
All Points Transp. Corp. of Mich., Inc.,
364 F. Supp. 2d 621, 630 (E.D. Mich. 2005);
Edwards
v.
Cmty. Enters., Inc.,
251 F. Supp. 2d 1089, 1103 (D. Conn. 2003).
Although the Department is not aware of any court that has declined to apply an economic reality test under MSPA, several courts have cited to the Department's MSPA regulation and applied its formulation of the economic reality test at
29 CFR 500.20(h)(4)
to determine whether an individual is an independent contractor or employee under MSPA.
See, e.g., Fanette
v.
Steven Davis Farms, LLC,
28 F. Supp. 3d 1243, 1255-56 (N.D. Fla. 2014);
Arredondo
v.
Delano Farms Co.,
922 F. Supp. 2d 1071, 1075-82 (E.D. Cal. 2013);
Luna
v.
Del Monte Fresh Produce (Se.), Inc.,
No. 1:06-CV-2000-JEC, 2008 WL 754452, at *7-9 (N.D. Ga. Mar. 19, 2008). Of course, it is entirely appropriate for courts to apply the Department's MSPA regulation to adjudicate employee or independent contractor disputes under MSPA, as the Department's MSPA regulation is a legislative rule issued pursuant to an express delegation of rulemaking authority that is binding on regulated entities.
[
185
]
However, to the extent the MSPA regulation's specific articulation of the economic reality test differed in meaningful ways from the Department's FLSA guidance (including the analysis proposed in this rulemaking), the Department does not believe it is appropriate to have separate economic reality tests for employee or independent contractor status under laws which share the same statutory definitions for employment.
The Department declined to revise the MSPA regulations in the 2021 and 2024 Rules as it did not see a compelling need to do so at those times,
[
186
]
emphasizing in the 2021 Rule, for example, the Department's preference to “proceed incrementally.”
[
187
]
However, the Department recognizes that many stakeholders desire greater uniformity in the analysis for determining employee or independent contractor status across federal laws that explicitly share common statutory terms. As a result, the Department now agrees that it should make clear that the analysis is consistent under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA because these statutes share the same scope of employment.
Many commenters agreed with the NPRM's assessment that the analysis for independent contractor status should be the same across the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA. Noting that the three laws share the same definition of “employ,” the Washington Legal Foundation commented that “harmonizing the relevant FLSA regulatory definition with the FMLA's and MSPA's is just good housekeeping.” Numerous commenters asserted that adopting a uniform classification analysis across all three laws would reduce confusion and compliance costs.
See, e.g.,
Association for Competitive Technology; FSI; National Watermelon Association; NFIB. The Wisconsin Institute of Liberty commented that “[w]orkers, employers, and small businesses should not be required to navigate multiple classification standards across statutes administered by the same agency.”
Though several commenters made policy or legal criticisms of the NPRM's proposed analysis which were unique to the FMLA and MSPA,
[
188
]
few commenters opposed to the NPRM disagreed that analysis for assessing independent contractor status should be the same under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA.
See
IBT (commenting that IBT would “strongly support” a uniform test if the test at issue were “accurate, comprehensive, and faithful to law”); Justice for Migrant Women (asserting that NPRM's proposed analysis would be contrary to the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA because all three statutes share the same understanding of the term “employ”). However, the Department received a small number of comments suggesting that a uniform approach among all three statutes is not required.
See
Coalition of State Officials (asserting that a “one-size-fits-all-statutes” rule is unnecessary); Farmworker Justice (“Because the FLSA and the [MSPA] use the same definitions of `employ,' the case law under each statute can be applicable, but [MSPA] decisions are not always applicable to FLSA cases.”) (citing
Layton
v.
DHL Exp. (USA), Inc.,
686 F.3d 1172, 1177 (11th Cir. 2012)). Coalition of State Officials asserted that “unique structures and provisions” of the FMLA and MSPA require “reasoned consideration” before proceeding with a uniform approach. With respect to the FMLA, the Coalition asserted that the Department must consider the requirements set forth at
29 U.S.C. 2611(2)(A)-(B)
for an employee to be eligible for FMLA-protected leave as well as the Department's joint employment regulation at
29 CFR 825.106
. With respect to MSPA, the Coalition contended that the applicability of the FLSA's definition of “employ” to MSPA is “only for the purposes of implementing the FLSA” and subject to “limits that the proposed rule fails to address.”
Relatedly, some commenters asserted that the Department did not adequately explain its reasons for amending the FMLA and MSPA regulations now when it declined to do so in 2024 and 2021.
See
Coalition of State Officials; National Women's Law Center; NWJP. Some of these commenters relied on the Department's prior conclusion that it did not see a “compelling need” to revise the MSPA regulations,
see
86 FR 1177
, to suggest that the Department must have a “compelling need” now.
See
Coalition of State Officials; NWJP.
Having considered commenter feedback, the Department disagrees that its regulations can or should continue to feature different independent contractor
(
printed page 75669)
analyses under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA, as Congress plainly intended for the FMLA and MSPA to follow the FLSA in determining whether there is an employment relationship.
See
29 U.S.C. 2611(3)
(providing that “employ” and “employee” have the “same meanings given such terms” in the FLSA);
29 U.S.C. 1802(5)
(providing that “employ” has “the meaning given such term” under the FLSA);
see also Antenor
v.
D & S Farms,
88 F.3d 925, 929 (11th Cir. 1996) (“Both [FLSA and MSPA] utilize the same definition of `employ,' so if the growers employed the farmworkers under one statute, they necessarily employed them under the other.”);
Layton,
686 F.3d at 1177 (in FLSA joint-employer case, declining to apply MSPA case law because, while MSPA defines the employment relationship by reference to the FLSA, the reverse does not necessarily hold true—the FLSA employment relationship is not “invariably defined” by reference to MSPA). Commenters' suggestions that uniformity is not required only confirm that there is ambiguity over what analysis should apply to the FMLA and MSPA. The Department resolves that ambiguity now.
Regarding the “unique structures and provisions” of the FMLA and MSPA, Coalition of State Officials did not explain what bearing they should have on the question of what analysis to apply when determining employee or independent contractor status. The Department recognizes that an individual's eligibility for the rights and protections of the FMLA depends upon not only whether the individual is employed by a business but also whether the business employs a threshold number of employees near the individual's worksite, among other considerations.
See
29 U.S.C. 2611(2)(A)-(B)
. The FMLA is clear that the FLSA's definitions of “employ” and “employee” apply for purposes of determining both whether the individual is employed by the business and whether the business has the requisite number of employees,
see
29 U.S.C. 2611(3)
, and the Department's FMLA regulations have consistently reflected that fact,
see
60 FR 2185-86
;
29 CFR 825.102
(“Employee”). The applicability of the FLSA's definition of employ to MSPA is somewhat more limited because some of MSPA's requirements apply regardless of whether there is an employment relationship.
See, e.g.,
29 U.S.C. 1823(a)
(imposing requirements for the safety and health of housing on “each person who owns or controls a facility or real property which is used as housing for migrant agricultural workers”). Nothing in this rulemaking alters the application of such requirements.
The Department acknowledges that it must have “good reasons” for amending its prior regulations.
See Food & Drug Admin.
v.
Wages & White Lion Investments, L.L.C.,
604 U.S. 542, 570 (2025) (quoting
F.C.C.
v.
Fox Television Stations, Inc.,
556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009)). But the Department need not “provide a more detailed justification than what would suffice for a new policy created on a blank slate.”
Id.
Therefore, the fact that the Department stated in 2021 that it did not find a “compelling need” to revise the MSPA regulations,
see
86 FR 1177
, does not mean that it must articulate a “compelling need” now. In light of clear congressional intent to have the same scope of employment apply to the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA, and for all the reasons the Department has explained for amending the FLSA regulations, the Department finds good reasons to amend the FMLA and MSPA regulations.
In sum, this rulemaking is motivated partially by the fact that the analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors should be the same under the FMLA and MSPA as it is under the FLSA. Workers and businesses alike will benefit from the simplicity and certainty of having a single uniform standard for assessing employee or independent contractor status under all three laws.
IV. Final Regulatory Provisions
For all the reasons discussed above, the Department is rescinding the 2024 Rule's regulatory guidance on employee or independent contractor status and, separately, readopting at
29 CFR part 795
the 2021 Rule's regulatory guidance, with modifications and enhancements that are explained in the sections below. In the Department's view, this rule's rescission of the 2024 Rule is independent and severable from the regulations adopted in its place, which includes:
an introductory provision in § 795.100 explaining the purpose of part 795 (with a minor modification to the version of this provision that was adopted in the 2021 Rule);
a provision in § 795.105(a) explaining that independent contractors are not employees under the FLSA;
a provision in § 795.105(b) discussing the “economic reality” test for distinguishing FLSA employees from independent contractors, including that the ultimate inquiry of economic dependence turns on whether an individual is in business for him- or herself (independent contractor) or is economically dependent on an employer for work (employee), with additional context on the meaning of economic dependence that was not in the 2021 Rule;
provisions in § 795.105(c) and (d) describing factors examined as part of the economic reality test, including two “core” or primary factors—the nature and degree of the individual's control over the work and the individual's opportunity for profit or loss—which, as has been the case in many judicial decisions, here too typically carry greater weight in the analysis,
[
189
]
as well as three other factors that may serve as additional guideposts in the analysis;
[
190
]
a provision in § 795.110 advising that the parties' actual practice is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible;
a provision with 14 fact-specific examples in § 795.115, including updates to three of the six examples that originally appeared in the 2021 Rule and eight new examples;
[
191
]
and
a severability provision in § 795.120.
Additionally, this rule revises the regulations addressing employee or independent contractor status under MSPA and the FMLA so that the analysis in part 795 applies when determining employee or independent contractor status under those statutes too. In particular, this rule revises
29 CFR 500.20(h)(4)
in the MSPA regulations to replace the analysis there with a cross-reference to the analysis in
29 CFR part 795
, and revises the definition of “Employee” in
29 CFR 825.102
and the language in
29 CFR 825.105(a)
to incorporate into the FMLA regulations the analysis for determining employee or independent contractor classification in
29 CFR part 795
.
This rule does not amend the existing versions of
29 CFR 780.330(b)
and
788.16(a)
, which the 2024 Rule updated to include cross-references to the guidance at
29 CFR part 795
.
[
192
]
As noted above and for the reasons provided herein, the Department believes that the analysis adopted in this rule represents the best
(
printed page 75670)
construction of the FLSA—and by extension the FMLA and MSPA—with respect to whether an individual is an independent contractor or an employee. The Department's response to commenter feedback on the specific features of this rule is provided below.
A. Introductory Statement (§ 795.100)
The Department proposed an introductory statement, § 795.100, at the beginning of the FLSA regulatory provisions. The proposed introductory statement advised that: part 795 contains the Department's “general interpretations of the text governing individuals' classification as employees or independent contractors under the [FLSA]”; the WHD Administrator will use the interpretations “to guide the performance of his or her duties under the [FLSA]” and intends them “to be used by employers, employees, and courts to understand employers' obligations and employees' rights under the [FLSA]”; “prior administrative rulings, interpretations, practices, or enforcement policies relating to classification as an employee or independent contractor under the [FLSA]” are rescinded to the extent that they “are inconsistent or in conflict with” part 795; and employers may rely on the interpretations to satisfy the good faith reliance defense in the Portal-to-Portal Act (
29 U.S.C. 259
), notwithstanding that after any such act or omission in the course of such reliance, any such interpretation is modified or rescinded or is determined by judicial authority to be invalid or of no legal effect.
[
193
]
The Department explained that the proposed introductory statement would provide clarity as to how WHD intends to use part 795 and how employers, businesses, workers, and courts should use part 795. The proposed introductory statement would also address how part 795 relates to prior interpretations and explain how employers can rely on part 795 for purposes of the good faith reliance defense in the Portal-to-Portal Act. The Department further explained that the proposed introductory statement would clearly and concisely summarize the purposes of part 795.
[
194
]
The Department received very few comments addressing the introductory statement or related issues. Center for Workplace Compliance supported proposed § 795.100 and its explanation of the purpose and scope of part 795 and how “the Department's interpretations may be relied upon consistent with the Portal-to-Portal Act.” Trevar D. Kolodny, who identified himself as a Visiting Fellow at the Heritage Foundation commenting in his individual capacity, stated that the proposed introductory statement was a “considerable improvement” compared to the introductory statement in the 2024 Rule, and he particularly disputed the basis for citing
Skidmore
in the 2024 Rule's introductory statement (the proposed introductory statement in this rulemaking did not cite to
Skidmore

Relatedly, Flex Association urged the Department to confirm in this final rule “that prior subregulatory guidance inconsistent with the rule is no longer operative”—particularly AI 2015-1 and “pre-2008 versions of Fact Sheet #13.” The Department agrees that, by the plain language of § 795.100, AI 2015-1 and the pre-2008 versions of Fact Sheet #13 are rescinded by this final rule (to the extent that they had not already been rescinded) as they are inconsistent or in conflict with part 795 as adopted herein. B. Determining Employee and Independent Contractor Classification Under the FLSA (§ 795.105)
As explained in the following sections, the Department is readopting—with some modifications and augmentation—the analysis for determining employee or independent contractor classification under the FLSA that it published as § 795.105 of the 2021 Rule.
C. Independent Contractors Are Not Employees Under the Act (§ 795.105(a))
The Department proposed to readopt the regulatory text of § 795.105(a) from the 2021 Rule, which recognized a foundational legal truism—that independent contractors are not employees under the Act. This provision explains that an individual who renders services to a person (a putative or potential employer) as an independent contractor is not an employee of that person under the FLSA, which means that the minimum wage, overtime pay, and recordkeeping obligations for employers under sections 6, 7, and 11 of the FLSA do not apply with respect to services received from the independent contractor.
[
195
]
The 2024 Rule contained a similar provision.
[
196
]
Having received no substantive comments on this section, the Department is now finalizing as proposed this provision that it has included consistently across rulemakings.
D. Economic Dependence as the Ultimate Inquiry (§ 795.105(b))
The Department proposed to readopt, with a few modifications, the regulatory text of § 795.105(b) from the 2021 Rule. The proposed section explained, as the Supreme Court and courts of appeals have long held, that economic dependence is the ultimate inquiry—to which the underlying factors are directed—when determining an individual worker's status under the FLSA. The section referenced the relevant statutory provisions, explaining that an “employee” under the FLSA is an individual whom an employer suffers, permits, or otherwise employs to work.
See
29 U.S.C. 203(e)(1)
, (g). It further explained that an employer suffers or permits an individual to work as an employee if, as a matter of economic reality, the individual is economically dependent on that employer for work, as distinguished from an independent contractor, who is in business for him- or herself.
[
197
]
(
printed page 75671)
In the NPRM, the Department noted that in the 2021 Rule, the Department explained that the “touchstone” of the economic reality test is “economic dependence.”
86 FR 1178
. As the 2021 Rule further explained: “ `Economic dependence is
not
conditioned reliance on an alleged employer for one's primary source of income, for the necessities of life.' ”
Id.
(quoting
Brock
v.
Mr. W Fireworks, Inc.,
814 F.2d 1042, 1054 (5th Cir. 1987)). Rather, courts have framed the question as “ `whether, as a matter of economic reality, the workers depend upon someone else's business for the opportunity to render service or are in business for themselves.' ”
Id.
(quoting
Saleem,
854 F.3d at 139). Moreover, as explained in the NPRM, the Department observed in the 2021 Rule that some courts have relied on a worker's entrepreneurship with respect to one type of work to conclude that the worker was also in business for him- or herself in a second, unrelated type of work, but this “approach is inconsistent with the Supreme Court's instruction that the economic reality analysis be limited to `the claimed independent operation.' ”
Id.
(quoting
Silk,
331 U.S. at 716). Thus, “the relevant question in this context is whether the worker providing certain service to a potential employer is an entrepreneur `in that line of business.' ”
Id.
(quoting
Mr. W Fireworks,
814 F.2d at 1054). Otherwise, businesses would be required to make FLSA classification decisions based on facts outside of the working relationship at issue.
Id.
The 2024 Rule contained a similar provision, explaining that economic dependence is the ultimate inquiry for determining whether a worker is an independent contractor or an employee and clarifying that economic dependence does not focus on the amount the worker earns or whether the worker has other sources of income.
[
198
]
The Department therefore proposed explanatory guidance that it has consistently provided across rulemakings that economic dependence for work rather than economic dependence for income is the proper inquiry. As the Third Circuit has explained, economic dependence “does not concern whether the workers at issue depend on the money they earn for obtaining the necessities of life . . . . Rather, it examines whether the workers are dependent on a particular business or organization for their continued employment.”
Donovan
v.
DialAmerica Mktg., Inc.,
757 F.2d 1376, 1385 (3d Cir. 1985). As noted in the 2021 Rule, economic dependence does not mean that a worker who works for other employers, earns a very limited income from a particular employer, or is independently wealthy cannot nevertheless be economically dependent on any particular employer for purposes of the FLSA.
See
86 FR 1173
;
see also McLaughlin
v.
Seafood, Inc.,
861 F.2d 450, 452 (5th Cir. 1988),
modified on reh'g,
867 F.2d 875 (5th Cir. 1989) (reasoning that “[l]aborers who work for two different employers on alternate days are no less economically dependent than laborers who work for a single employer”);
Halferty
v.
Pulse Drug Co.,
821 F.2d 261, 267-68 (5th Cir. 1987) (rejecting the employer's argument that the worker's wages were too little to constitute dependence). As the Fifth Circuit has explained, “it is not dependence in the sense that one could not survive without the income from the job that we examine, but dependence for continued employment.”
Id.
at 268.
Consistent with the explanations above, and to provide further context on the meaning of economic dependence, the Department proposed to make two modifications to the regulatory text of § 795.105(b) as compared to the 2021 Rule. The purpose of the first modification was to clarify the nature and character of the economic dependence that an employee typically has on an employer for work, as distinct from the relationship that a business owner has to another business with which it works. The purpose of the second modification was to reinforce the Department's consistent guidance that economic dependence for work rather than economic dependence for income is the proper inquiry. Specifically, the Department proposed adding the following sentences to the end of the 2021 Rule's version of § 795.105(b): “Though both employees and independent contractors are dependent on others in some sense, economic dependence in this context means the dependence that a typical employee has on an employer for work, as opposed to an individual who has more of the nature and character of a business owner who has a separate business. Economic dependence does not focus on the amount of income the worker earns, or whether the worker has other sources of income.”
[
199
]
Commenters in favor of and opposed to the proposal overall generally agreed with the additional explanatory language that the Department proposed.
See, e.g.,
Flex Association (“Flex endorses the Proposed Rule's focus on an individual's dependence for
work
rather than for
income”
); IBT (agreeing that “a proposed rule should correctly distinguish dependence-for-work from dependence-for-income,” elaborating that the focus should be “on whether the workers are dependent on a particular business or organization for their continued employment”); Littler WPI (commenting that the new language “captures the core of the economic-reality test”); Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) (expressing support for the modified definition, which “aligns with SHRM's position that [the] analysis must focus on the specific worker-business relationship rather than individual financial circumstances”); Uber (“The Rule correctly points out that economic dependence is not synonymous with income. Economic dependence does not turn on whether a worker gets most or all of her revenue from a single source. Instead, it turns on whether the worker relies on a single source for continued work.”). U.S. Chamber of Commerce supported the first proposed clarifying sentence but opined that “the presence of multiple income sources does matter” because “one of the most desired and characteristic aspects of independent contracting is the availability of multiple sources of income.” U.S. Chamber of Commerce thus requested that the Department amend the second sentence or clarify that “the opportunity to work for other businesses, and to seek other revenue streams, still weigh in favor of independent contractor status.”
FSI supported the Department's proposal but commented that the Department should ensure that its broader articulation of economic dependence “does not inadvertently reintroduce the 2024 Rule's flawed premise that entrepreneurial drive and business acumen are indispensable characteristics of independent contractors.” International Franchise Association (IFA) supported the inclusion of the sentence explaining that “economic dependence in this context means the dependence that a typical employee has on an employer for work, as opposed to an individual who has more of the nature and character of a business owner who has a separate business,” but it did not agree that “economic dependence” is the ultimate inquiry according to Supreme Court precedent but rather the “economic realities” and whether the workers are in business for themselves. IFA also asked the Department to state that “the economic reality of the typical franchisor and franchisee relationship reflects an independent contractor relationship where the franchisee is not economically dependent upon the
(
printed page 75672)
franchisor for purposes of the FLSA.” Similarly, Instacart supported the statement that “economic dependence does not turn on income level” but requested that the Department add a sentence stating that “[a]n individual's engagement in work on a part-time, intermittent, or supplemental basis, including in combination with other employment or income sources, does not, by itself, indicate economic dependence on a potential employer.”
In response to U.S. Chamber of Commerce's comment about the need to clarify that the opportunity to work for other businesses and seek income from multiple sources still weighs in favor of independent contractor status, the Department confirms that the control factor in § 795.105(d)(1)(i) addresses this in regulatory text by stating that “the ability to work for others, which might include the potential employer's competitors, weighs towards the individual being an independent contractor.” With regard to the concern raised by FSI, the Department does not agree that it is reiterating any language from the 2024 Rule that the commenter found objectionable. Regarding IBT's concern that the proposed language in this section might replace the analysis of the worker's relationship with a particular business, the Department emphasizes that the language in this section describes overarching concepts and is not a substitute for applying the economic reality factors to the working relationship at issue. With respect to IFA's concerns, the Department believes that IFA may have misconstrued the term “economic dependence” in § 795.105(b) in this section, as it is part of the consideration of whether “as a matter of economic reality, the individual is economically dependent on that employer for work,” and is therefore an employee, or whether “the individual is, as a matter of economic reality, in business for him- or herself,” and is therefore an independent contractor.
Id.
Further, the Department declines to make any absolute or categorical statement about the economic reality of any work relationship such as the statement IFA asked the Department to make about franchisees; as IFA accurately states in its comment, the “economic realities” always need to be considered. Finally, the Department does not agree with Instacart that it would be helpful to add the clarifying language that Instacart proposed stating that a combination of intermittent work with various income sources “does not, by itself, indicate economic dependence on a potential employer.” As the Department makes clear throughout this rule, no one factor or fact alone is determinative of economic dependence or employment classification.
The Department is finalizing this section as proposed.
E. Determining Economic Dependence and Identifying Core Factors (§ 795.105(c))
In the Department's proposal, the readoption of § 795.105(c) represented the most critical change from the 2024 Rule's multifactor analysis in which no factor carries any particular weight to the 2021 Rule's multifactor test that highlights two primary, or core, factors: control and opportunity for profit or loss. Specifically, the Department proposed to readopt the regulatory text of § 795.105(c) from the 2021 Rule, which explains that the control and opportunity for profit or loss factors are more probative in determining whether an individual is an employee or independent contractor under the FLSA.
[
200
]
As in the 2021 Rule, the Department proposed that these two primary factors typically carry greater weight in the analysis than any other factor. Thus, these two factors should be considered first, and if both point toward the same classification (either employee or independent contractor), there is a substantial likelihood that is the accurate classification for the individual. The Department also proposed that the three additional factors described in § 795.105(d)(2)—skill, permanence, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production—provide additional direction for the analysis, but are less probative (and, in some cases, may not be probative at all). As a result, these factors would be very unlikely, either individually or collectively, to outweigh the combined probative value of the two core or primary factors when together they point toward the same classification. As in the 2021 Rule, the Department proposed that this provision also explains that all these “economic reality” factors are not exhaustive, and that no single factor is dispositive.
As the Department explained in the NPRM, this provision was proposed to improve the certainty and predictability of the multifactor economic reality test by focusing it, much in the way that many courts have effectively done, on two principal elements, which the Department refers to as the “core” factors. Absent clear, generally applicable guidance about how to balance the broad and overlapping factors and facts encompassed in the multifactor economic reality test, there is an excessive amount of uncertainty as to “which aspects of `economic reality' matter, and why.”
Lauritzen,
835 F.2d at 1539 (Easterbrook, J., concurring). As the Department explained in its proposal and when proposing the 2021 Rule, although the Department and courts historically analyzed “the totality of the circumstances making up the economic reality of the relationship to determine a worker's classification” without “identifying which types of facts or factors are the most important,” the significance of facts may sometimes be unclear or factors may point in opposite directions under this approach, exacerbating uncertainty in application of the analysis.
[
201
]
However, even within the multifactor, totality of the circumstances test, courts have tended to focus on the two principal factors as the primary, central indicators of whether an individual is an employee or independent contractor. The Department, taking its cue from the courts, sought in the 2021 Rule to provide greater clarity and focus by identifying the two factors it believed were most salient in determining relevant economic dependence, explaining that the two primary factors “drive at the heart of what is meant by being in business for oneself: Such a person typically controls the work performed in his or her business and enjoys a meaningful opportunity for profit or risk of loss through personal initiative or investment.”
[
202
]
Even though no one test can perfectly harmonize the variations of factors, language, and emphasis among the tests of the Supreme Court and circuit courts of appeals, the Department has attempted to distill the central commonality in these approaches to a single framework that workers and employers alike may accurately apply and on which they may confidently rely.
As explained in the NPRM and the 2021 Rule, highlighting the combined probative value of the two primary factors in the manner set forth in the regulatory text proposed in § 795.105(c) is supported by case law. The Supreme Court has never required a factor-by-factor analysis. And in the seminal Supreme Court cases applying the economic reality test under the FLSA, the Court listed multiple relevant considerations but ultimately resolved the classification question by focusing on whether the worker exercised control and had a genuine opportunity for profit or loss based on initiative or
(
printed page 75673)
investment—factors that go to the heart of whether an individual is truly in business for him- or herself.
[
203
]
The NPRM further explained that, as part of the 2021 rulemaking, the Department reviewed the results of federal appellate decisions since 1975 applying the economic reality test under the FLSA, noting “a remarkably consistent trend” where “the classification favored by the control factor aligned with the worker's ultimate classification in all except a handful where the opportunity factor pointed in the opposite direction. And the classification favored by the opportunity factor aligned with the ultimate classification in every case.”
[
204
]
These two findings imply that whenever the control and opportunity factors both pointed to the same classification—whether employee or independent contractor—that was the court's conclusion regarding the worker's ultimate classification. In other words, “courts of appeals have effectively been affording the control and opportunity factors greater weight, even if they did not always explicitly acknowledge doing so.”
[
205
]
The Department acknowledged in the NPRM that proposing to return to the 2021 Rule's core factor analysis represented a change with respect to the interpretation of the economic reality analysis as compared to the 2024 Rule.
[
206
]
However, the Department believed such a change was warranted for significant and valid legal and policy reasons—primarily that providing a more focused analysis distilled from judicial precedent would offer greater certainty for employers, employees, and those who wish to engage with or as independent contractors. Additionally, the Department reviewed the concerns identified in the 2024 Rule about the 2021 Rule's approach and considers them misplaced,
[
207
]
as discussed further below.
The Department sought comments from the public regarding their experiences using the economic reality analyses provided in the 2021 and 2024 Rules, and why one might be preferable to another. The Department also welcomed comments about any other effective and reliable circuit court analyses, or other appropriate analyses for determining employee or independent contractor status. Additionally, the Department solicited input on whether further streamlining of the two-core-factor analysis would provide even greater clarity and focus on the question whether an individual is an employee or an independent contractor under the FLSA. To that end, the NPRM presented for commenters' consideration an alternative analysis to the two-core-factor approach, in which the control factor would be considered first and, if it points to employee status, the analysis would end there and the worker would be an employee. Under this analysis, the opportunity for profit or loss and other factors would be considered only if the control factor is inconclusive or points to independent contractor status.
[
208
]
The comments received, and the Department's responses, are discussed below.
1. Comments and Responses Regarding the Alternative “Control First” Streamlined Analysis
A wide range of commenters opposed the proposed alternative of a further streamlined “control first” analysis. Commenters representing businesses and workers alike stated that it is inconsistent with longstanding case law providing that no single factor is dispositive under the economic reality test.
See, e.g.,
Coalition to Promote Independent Entrepreneurs; Coalition of State Officials; National Retail Federation; National Partnership for Women & Families et al.; UBC; U.S. Chamber. Many commenters stated that the proposed alternative resembles a common law control test and is therefore inconsistent with the economic reality test applied under the FLSA and with the Department's rejection of the common law test.
See, e.g.,
Coalition of State Officials; CWI; Flex Association; Nichols Kaster; SHRM. Commenters from the business community characterized it as imbalanced and stated that it would tilt the scales in favor of employee status.
See, e.g.,
American Bakers Association; Coalition to Promote Independent Entrepreneurs; Flex Association; Littler WPI; National Retail Federation; U.S. Chamber.
Three commenters expressed support for this proposed alternative. CHRO Association and ShiftKey applauded what they viewed as the enhanced predictability and efficiency of this alternative. Landmark Legal Foundation argued that this alternative is grounded in Supreme Court precedent establishing that the FLSA's employment definitions were intended to capture workers beyond the common law control test. By “leading with control,” this alternative “would ensure that workers who are unambiguously subject to an employer's direction are covered without requiring further inquiry,” while consideration of opportunity for profit or loss and other factors would preserve the “broader reach of the `suffer or permit' standard for cases where control alone is inconclusive.”
Upon consideration of these helpful comments, the Department declines to adopt this proposed alternative analysis. Although the control-first analysis proposed in the NPRM would differ from the common law control test, the Department recognizes that the proposed alternative engendered significant confusion on this point. As the Department has explained throughout this rulemaking and in prior years, it does not intend to adopt a common law control test and believes it is legally constrained from doing so. Consistent with this position, the Department declines to adopt an analysis that considers control as the potentially only factor. Having considered these comments and as discussed below, the Department believes that approach of two principal, central factors strikes the right balance in providing a clear and predictable framework while still considering the other economic reality factors and the circumstances of the whole activity.

Allegheny County et al. (“Because the proposed rule conflicts with the text of the FLSA as well as with Supreme Court and circuit court authority interpreting the statute, it constitutes an improper exercise of the Department's rulemaking authority.”); AFSCME (“The Department . . . lacks authority to recast the economic-realities inquiry by elevating two factors above the totality of the circumstances.”). After considering the comments received, the Department is finalizing § 795.105(c) as proposed. The Department agrees that it is important and useful to adopt a practical economic realities analysis distilled from federal case law that both workers and businesses may readily, accurately, properly, and reliably apply to classify employees and independent contractors. Rather than set forth a myriad of factors and considerations without direction regarding their application, the Department considers the standard it finalizes best suited to facilitate accurate classification at the outset of relationships, not after years of costly litigation. This provides more certainty and predictability for employers, employees, and independent contractors. The standard is consistent
(
printed page 75676)
with the way courts have decided employee or independent contractor cases under the FLSA for decades. As a result, all persons can gain efficiencies in their interactions, and there will likely be a reduced need for litigation in cases where the rule is properly applied, reducing the number of instances in which a court must ultimately reach a conclusion years later about the proper classification of one or more individuals. And though the Department understands why commenters such as the Pacific Legal Foundation seek even more certainty through a rebuttable presumption if the two primary factors point in the same direction, the Department believes a rebuttable presumption improperly injects burdens of proof into an analysis where all factors are properly considered, even though some factors are generally considered to be more probative than others.
The Department disagrees with commenters contending that the Department's proposal is contrary to case law stating that no single factor in the economic reality test is determinative and that the totality of the circumstances must be considered in a holistic rather than mechanical fashion. The core factor analysis finalized by the Department centers on two primary factors—that is, first to be considered and first in importance in most cases—and does not run afoul of this precedent. Specifically, this final rule in § 795.105(c) states—
consistent
with judicial precedent—that no one factor is determinative, nor are the enumerated factors exhaustive. To be clear, by identifying two factors that encompass the considerations that are generally most relevant to determining economic dependence, the Department is certainly not implying that either one of these two core factors alone would be determinative. To the contrary, as the Department has repeatedly explained, these two factors in combination and pointing to the same classification (employee or independent contractor) are rarely going to be outweighed by the probative value of the other economic reality factors. This is not because the Department declares it so, but rather because decades of federal courts applying the tests from which the Department derived this rule demonstrate that such is the practical reality. Indeed, the Department continues to be unaware of any federal appellate case in which the court's ultimate conclusion as to an individual's classification under the FLSA—whether employee or independent contractor—was not in alignment with the court's analysis that the control and opportunity for profit or loss factors both favored that classification. Moreover, the Department has not found any commenter that has identified such a case.
[
211
]
Submissions by commenters appear to confirm the point. For example, an analysis submitted by FSI supports the Department's decision to highlight control and opportunity for profit or loss as core factors, as its independent review of almost 50 appellate cases also concluded that “in no case did both factors point the other way” from the court's ultimate decision.
The more important point remains. For decades, the outcomes of federal appellate court decisions have overwhelmingly (if not unanimously) aligned with the Department's approach, indicating the saliency of examining the two central factors first. Put another way, according to the courts, the Department's test—properly applied—will produce accurate results. And this further bolsters the reasoning underlying the Department's proposal and negates the view that such a focus is inconsistent with the relevant FLSA case law. The point of disagreement between these commenters and the Department is at bottom a difference between two accurate observations of the governing FLSA case law. The Department's approach recognizes that, notwithstanding courts' general articulations of the test, the two primary factors—when pointing in the same direction—are in effect, synonymous with the classification outcome. On the other side, the commenters in opposition correctly observe that courts have not specifically and explicitly elevated any factors over the others, as the Department's approach does in this rule.
[
212
]
Within this space, it is appropriate for the Department to set forth an analysis distilled from the case law in the effort to promote a more practical and efficient way to determine employee or independent contractor status.
The two principal factors are also more probative because the rule relocates to them the most probative aspects of certain other factors. To reduce overlap and confusion, exclusivity, which has traditionally been considered under both permanence and control, is more appropriately analyzed under control, as explained in greater detail in section IV.F.1. of this preamble. Similarly, initiative, which is often considered under skill, is more appropriately analyzed under opportunity for profit or loss.
[
213
]
This reorganization necessarily increases the probative value of the two core factors because they now incorporate considerations that other formulations distribute among the permanence and skill factors. Correspondingly, the remaining aspects of permanence and skill are generally less probative once exclusivity and initiative are considered elsewhere. The rule therefore does not omit or diminish relevant evidence. It does the opposite by placing the most probative considerations within the factors to which they most directly relate while avoiding duplicative consideration of the same facts.
Further, the two principal factor analysis provided in § 795.105(c) does not run afoul of judicial admonitions to avoid a mechanical application of the economic reality test because the regulatory text recognizes that these two factors “typically” (but not necessarily) carry more weight. The regulatory text also makes clear that alignment of the primary factors creates a “substantial likelihood,” not a conclusive
(
printed page 75677)
presumption, of the indicated classification. Decades of federal appellate decisions support the Department's construction, confirming that courts of appeals have not reached a classification contrary to that indicated when control and opportunity for profit or loss both clearly pointed in the same direction. Although a contrary result remains possible—and the rule requires consideration of the remaining factors—the consistency of appellate outcomes over decades is itself probative and warrants bringing to the attention of regulated parties. Recognizing that consistent decision pattern does not make the analysis mechanical.
Moreover, the core factors will not always align or point clearly toward either classification. As the Department explained in the NPRM and the 2021 Rule, there may be situations in which “a core factor does not weigh very strongly toward a particular classification because considerations within that factor point in different directions,” or where a “core factor may even be at equipoise, in which case it would not weigh at all in favor of a particular classification.”
[
214
]
For example, in
Carrell
v.
Sunland Constr., Inc.,
the two central factors did not clearly point toward the same classification because the court found some of the facts germane to control and opportunity for profit or loss indicated employee status and some indicated independent contractor status.
[
215
]
In that case, the court relied more heavily on other factors to conclude that the welders at issue were “as a matter of economic reality, in business for themselves.”
[
216
]
The court noted that many of the welders spent little time working for Sunland and they “worked from job to job and from company to company”; the welders were also highly skilled and had invested significantly in the equipment that they supplied to perform their work.
[
217
]
Thus, analyzing the non-core factors including skill and permanence provided a more complete picture that allowed the court to reach its conclusion regarding the welders' classification. As this case illustrates, identifying two factors as core factors does not mean that the analysis is or should be applied mechanically or simplistically, but rather makes clear that it must be administered just as carefully, as there are often a variety of relevant facts and concepts to consider within each individual factor before determining whether the factor points toward a particular classification.
As the Department explained in the 2021 Rule and reiterates here, the “other economic reality factors—skill, permanence, and integration—are also relevant as to whether an individual is in business for him- or herself,”
[
218
]
and “each factor should be analyzed.”
[
219
]
In cases where the two core factors clearly weigh in favor of a particular classification, there would be less need to rely on the other factors, though they should still be considered to determine if they would either individually or collectively outweigh the combined probative value of the two core factors.
[
220
]
For example, in
McFeeley,
825 F.3d at 244, after determining that the control, opportunity for profit or loss, and investment factors favored employee status, the court stated that “[t]he final three factors are more peripheral to the dispute here and will be discussed only briefly: the degree of skill required for the work; the permanence of the working relationship; and the degree to which the services rendered are an integral part of the putative employer's business.”
In response to comments that warned about a confusing legal landscape were the Department to adopt the two-core-factor approach, which has never been formally or explicitly adopted by a federal court, the Department reiterates that the landscape is already confusing and fraught with uncertainty that was only exacerbated by the 2024 Rule. As a great number of commenters explained (as discussed above), simply describing the factors without providing any additional guidance as to how they should be weighed or which are more likely to be salient to a court and to align with the court's outcome—like the 2024 Rule did—leaves stakeholders uncertain as to how to proceed. Additionally, during the time period following the district court's decision ruling that the 2021 Rule had taken effect (between March 2022 and March 2024), there was no surge of litigation based on lack of clarity regarding that rule's analysis, contrary to the assertions made by some commenters (discussed earlier in section III.A). Therefore, the Department believes these concerns are overstated, speculative, and are not a basis for declining to adopt the two-core-factor analysis from the 2021 Rule.
In response to comments contending that elevating control as one of the two central factors brings the analysis closer to the common law control test that courts have rejected when interpreting employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA, the Department believes that a multifactor analysis that recognizes a different core factor (opportunity for profit or loss), requires the consideration of three other factors, and allows for the consideration of additional factors (provided that such factors are germane to economic dependence) is readily distinguishable from a control test. As discussed further below, the opportunity for profit or loss factor that the Department is again proposing to adopt in § 795.105(d)(1)(ii) encompasses an individual's opportunity to earn profits, or incur losses, based on his or her initiative or management of investments, and as such, includes a number of critical considerations in evaluating economic dependence that go beyond the nature and degree of control over work. As a result, the Department believes that giving greater probative value to both the control and opportunity for profit or loss factors (especially given the considerations that comprise that factor) is not akin to adopting the common law control test, which specifically designates control as the overarching consideration. And importantly, the “ultimate inquiry” of the analysis proposed by the Department would remain the individual's economic dependence (§ 795.105(b)), which is different from the common law's inquiry into control.

In response to comments that raised concerns about increased misclassification of employees as independent contractors due to the proposal's “narrowing” of the facts that should be considered when determining employee or independent contractor status, the Department believes that focusing on core factors that are typically more probative does not eliminate or narrow the relevant considerations. Notably, the analysis does not stop at the two primary factors, but rather identifies three other economic reality factors and also provides for the possible consideration
(
printed page 75678)
of additional factors in § 795.105(c) and (d) that may be relevant in certain cases. Although the other factors are generally likely to be less probative, and in some cases, may not be probative at all, the analysis still requires the remaining factors to be considered when determining economic dependence. Again, as the Department has stated previously, the “other economic reality factors—skill, permanence, and integration—are also relevant as to whether an individual is in business for him- or herself,”
86 FR 1196
