id.
at 1201. Thus, “[a]ssigning one factor less weight than another does not restrict the circumstances being considered because the very act of determining relative weight requires considering both factors.”
Id.
The Department thus believes that all relevant facts can and will be considered, as detailed below in the discussions of each factor.
Under the Act, actual practice trumps written descriptions when they conflict. Far from being uniquely susceptible to manipulation because employers could “rely on contractual disclaimers of control, even where control is exercised in practice” and “manufacture illusory `entrepreneurial opportunity' through theoretical or employer-created mechanisms,” the “primacy of actual practice” provision in § 795.110 (discussed in more detail below) makes unutilized contractual disclaimers of control, hypothetical potentialities, and theoretical opportunities less relevant than actual practices and events. Despite some comments, nothing in the rule, which is devoted to ascertaining the economic
reality
of a relationship, provides for the theoretical to govern the actual. In other words, just because control and opportunity for profit or loss are designated as core factors, that does not mean that an employer has the ability to manufacture facts that would favor independent contractor status for these factors. Nor would contrived, “illusory,” or vague assertions of “entrepreneurial opportunity” prevail over contrary actual practice under the rule.
Commenters' concern on this point is curious; notably, the 2024 Rule did not include regulatory text emphasizing the primacy of actual practice.
[
222
]
In this respect, the analysis adopted in this rule could be more effective in curbing the kind of abuse described by AFL-CIO. For example, in the scenario AFL-CIO posited where a delivery company could classify its drivers as independent contractors by contractually disclaiming control, while simultaneously dictating routes through an application, setting non-negotiable prices, imposing performance metrics, and retaining the right to deactivate workers who do not meet those standards, the Department would (and any court, worker, or business applying the rule should likewise) look at the control that the company was actually exercising. Similarly, if the company pointed to opportunities that are illusory or otherwise effectively meaningless, the Department would rely on what actually happens. The rule does not countenance determinations regarding any factor in the analysis that are based on illusory options. As a result, the Department does not agree that the two-core-factor approach is inherently more susceptible to manipulation that would achieve a result that does not reflect the economic reality of the working relationship. To further illustrate some of these points, and as discussed further below, the Department is adding an illustrative example pertaining to platform work in § 795.115(b)(2) and (b)(3).
The Department appreciates commenter concerns that purportedly diminishing certain factors could particularly prejudice farmworkers, but believes they are misplaced because case law shows that the control and opportunity factors almost always indicate that farmworkers are employees.

1. The Nature and Degree of Control Over the Work (§ 795.105(d)(1)(i))
The Department proposed to readopt the regulatory text of § 795.105(d)(1)(i) from the 2021 Rule, which discussed the first economic reality core factor—the nature and degree of control over work.
[

This provision explains that the control factor weighs toward the individual being an independent contractor where the individual, rather than the potential employer, exercises substantial control over key aspects of the performance of the work such as scheduling, selection of projects, and the ability to work for others (which may include the potential employer's competitors). By contrast, the control factor would weigh in favor of the individual being an employee where the potential employer, rather than the individual, exercises substantial control over key aspects of the performance of the work, such as by controlling the individual's schedule or workload, or by directly or indirectly requiring the individual to work exclusively for the potential employer.
Additionally, the Department proposed to readopt guidance from the 2021 Rule advising that when a potential employer places certain compliance requirements on an individual, it “does not constitute control that makes the individual more or less likely to be an employee under the Act.”

For example, as illustrated in the example in § 795.115(b)(1) (which the Department is finalizing as proposed, as explained below), where a logistics company contracts with an individual owner-operator of a tractor-trailer to provide transportation services and the logistics company requires the owner-operator to comply with federally-mandated transportation safety rules requiring drug and alcohol testing, and requires the owner-operator to meet certain contractually agreed-upon delivery deadlines, this does not constitute control that would make it more or less likely that the owner-operator is an employee under the FLSA. Another example would be requiring all workers to complete anti-harassment training. Such training is intended to make the workplace safer, benefits everyone in the workplace, and is not control that makes an individual worker more or less likely to be an employee under the FLSA.

Preliminarily, the Department notes that many of the items for which these commenters requested additional examples and clarification already fall within the provision stating that requiring an individual to comply with legal obligations or to meet contractual deadlines, quality-control standards, or other similar terms typical of contractual relationships between businesses does not constitute control or—even assuming some deem these elements control—the type or nature of control that makes the individual more or less likely to be an employee. As discussed in more detail in the section addressing comments received regarding that provision, the Department declines to add numerous additional examples. The Department's overall intent in this rulemaking is to provide an analysis that takes a balanced approach and does not favor either employee or independent contractor outcomes. Therefore, the Department declines to make these many changes requested to the control factor that would imbalance the factor in favor of independent contractor status by detailing the many ways in which workers control work but businesses do not, including delving into increasingly detailed examples of requirements that extend beyond the rule's balanced requirements. The Department certainly agrees that businesses should maintain robust compliance oversight in general and ensure they and their contractors are abiding by the law, and that such general requirements are not indicative of employer-employee controls. However, it also recognizes that at some point extensive and detailed prescriptions and restrictions may indicate such control, as discussed further in section IV.F.1.d.
CWI and U.S. Chamber of Commerce further requested the Department to clarify that a lack of supervision is probative of independent contractor status under the control factor, in contrast to the 2024 Rule, which stated that “[a] lack of supervision is not alone indicative of independent contractor status, such as when the employer's business or the nature of the work make direct supervision unnecessary.” Additionally, Flex Association urged the Department to clarify that “routine supervision or monitoring of the status of work is not control indicative of employee status,” commenting that monitoring is common in the commercial market and that obtaining information about the status of work is distinct from controlling the work. The Department declines to provide in this rule that both a lack of supervision and routine supervision favor independent contractor status. Not only is this not borne out by logic, it is inconsistent with case law. Several federal appellate cases have held that a lack of supervision does not negate employee status, and that routine supervision may indicate employee status.
[
227

That being said, the Department recognizes, as did these commenters, that there are situations in which a lack of supervision does indicate independent contractor status,

228

and that routine monitoring is often done for operational purposes and is targeted toward the particular goods or services at issue rather than the manner and means by which a worker performs work. An employment relationship would not be indicated in such circumstances. The regulatory text does not speak to supervision, and so does not prohibit either factual scenario or classification outcome. In this space, this rule's analysis is best constructed to allow for proper consideration of these elements given the diversity of the work arrangements in which they apply.

Scopelitis also requested that the Department remove the word “indirectly” from the provision that states “this factor weighs in favor of the individual being an employee under the Act to the extent the potential employer . . . exercises substantial control over key aspects of the performance of the work, such as by . . . directly or indirectly requiring the individual to work exclusively for the potential employer” because federal motor carrier leasing regulations make it difficult to work for others and the commenter was concerned that this might be construed as “indirectly” prohibiting a lessee from working for others. In the Department's view, the proposed regulatory text in the NPRM and that is being finalized appropriately addresses these issues. With respect to exclusivity, the regulatory text states that the ability to work for others weighs toward the individual being an independent contractor—this is not conditioned on whether the worker chooses not to do so, provided that the worker is not, as a practical matter, prevented from exercising that choice. This is because it is the ability to
choose,
not
how
the choice is exercised, that indicates an independent contractor. An individual who exercises that independence to work a packed schedule with a wide variety of other entities is no more or less an independent contractor than another who carefully selects fewer contracts for
(

Additionally, the regulatory text states that “directly or indirectly requiring the individual to work exclusively for the potential employer” weighs in favor of employee status, which is what commenters suggested. Where there are particular legal rules such as the federal motor carrier regulations, an action taken to ensure compliance with those rules would not be viewed as control that makes the worker more or less likely to be an employee under § 795.105(d)(1)(i). Therefore, the Department does not believe that it is necessary to provide the further clarification on these points requested by commenters.

See, e.g.,
Anonymous 0059 (“Practices such as acceptance-rate tiers, hidden pay until after acceptance, and algorithmic penalties for declining orders undermine genuine independence.”); Delivery Platform Driver 1 (“[A]lgorithmic management tools, such as `Acceptance Rates,' constitute a significant degree of employer control . . . . The Department appreciates the breadth of input provided on this issue, particularly because SI and similar technology has evolved—and continues to evolve—rapidly and extensively since the Department began general rulemaking on employee or independent contractor classification under the Act in 2020, and technology certainly has continually changed since the FLSA was enacted in 1938. The Department has considered the comments received and agrees with Flex Association and Uber that there have always been forms of technology through which work is mediated, and the key questions are not whether or which form of technology is used with which workers but what the effect or result is. For example, whether a supervisor historically used a phone to call an employee to monitor the status of the work but now would use an SI tool to monitor the status of the work does not change the fact that the inquiry is always about the economic reality of a work relationship. As Uber commented, “[t]echnology isn't what makes these actions control; it is the actions themselves, which limit the employee's autonomy and make the employee dependent for continued work.”
The Department thus responds to commenters like The Scaffold Initiative that criticized the Department's proposal for not providing guidance on how to distinguish between a worker who uses SI in their work to exercise independence and a worker who is subject to algorithmic control by explaining that the same concepts that have guided the analysis since the 1940s continue to apply today: what is the economic reality of the situation, and is the worker economically dependent on the potential employer for work? That overarching inquiry does not change when the technological tools change. While it is certainly always helpful to have an understanding of the technology being used in any particular case to better understand the economic realities, the Department does not believe that the technologies themselves change how specific factors in the economic reality test are applied, contrary to the views of many commenters.
As this discussion illustrates, the Department reiterates that all facts relevant to control should be considered. Where technological tools are performing the kinds of activities that human supervisors historically handled in terms of, for example, setting schedules, assigning work, reviewing work, and providing rewards for good work and discipline or termination for bad work, those activities are just as relevant to the analysis as they would be if a human supervisor carried them out.
(
printed page 75684)
Nevertheless, to be responsive to commenter feedback requesting that the Department provide more guidance regarding technology and control, the Department has added a pair of examples in the final rule (§ 795.115(b)(2) & (b)(3)) to provide additional clarity on the kinds of technological practices that are indicative of employer-like control or indicative of independent contractor status. In these examples, an individual earns money by making food deliveries to customers from restaurants and grocery stores through an application operated by a digital platform company. In one example (adopted in § 795.115(b)(2)), the company pressures drivers to accept job offers by giving them seconds to accept delivery opportunities with limited information about the pay, size, or timeframe for the delivery, penalizes drivers who fail to accept a certain percentage of delivery orders by demoting their status in a tiered “rewards” program such that they lose access to preferred delivery orders, and makes it practically impossible to “multi-app” and still complete the minimum number of deliveries or avoid negative consequences for declining work. In this example, the control factor weighs toward employee status because the company is exercising substantial control over key aspects of the performance of the work, including the individual's ability to select her own projects, manage the workload, and work for others.
See Scantland,
721 F.3d at 1313, 1316-17 (finding control indicative of employee status where the workers at issue “could not bid for jobs or negotiate the prices for jobs” and “could not reject a route or a work order . . . without threat of termination or being refused work in the following days”).
By contrast, in the second example (adopted in § 795.115(b)(3)), the digital platform company allows drivers to decline delivery opportunities without consequence and “multi-app” with competing businesses, although the company will terminate a driver's account if they cancel too many accepted deliveries. The company's application dynamically adjusts its pricing, shares pay information with drivers before they accept work, and remotely monitors driver locations while the application is engaged to efficiently match drivers to delivery opportunities. In this example, the control factor weighs toward independent contractor status because the individual is exercising substantial control over key aspects of the work.
See Gray
v.
Killick Grp., LLC,
113 F.4th 543, 550 (5th Cir. 2024) (finding independent contractor status in part because the worker “possessed the freedom to accept or reject projects without retaliation”). That the company monitors the location of drivers while the application is engaged, dynamically adjusts prices in response to supply and demand, and terminates the account of drivers with excessive cancellation rates are not indicative of an employment relationship under these facts. Using technology to facilitate business operations does not indicate control over the driver; in fact in this example it also serves as an aid for the driver to make informed decisions about delivery opportunities. Further, termination of a driver's account due to excessive cancellation of accepted deliveries is a quality control measure to ensure food safety and edibility, and timeliness requirements are typical of contractual relationships between businesses, so such termination does not constitute control that makes the individual more or less likely to be an employee. Both examples demonstrate how the use of technology such as a digital platform and application may be relevant in determining whether the control factor weighs in favor of employee or independent contractor status.
The Department declines to provide any additional regulatory text, including commenter requests for the Department to state that various business practices commonly used by digital platform companies are not indicative of control, and that business use of SI would not indicate control but that a worker's ability to use SI would indicate a worker's control over the work. The Department does not believe this would be consistent with the balanced approach in this rule that does not favor either employee or independent contractor outcomes, as all these requests appear to lean in favor of an independent contractor outcome. Finally, with respect to the commenter requests about the use of technology to comply with legal obligations, such practices would appear to fall within the provision stating that requiring an individual to comply with legal obligations does not constitute control that makes the worker more or less likely to be an employee, as discussed below.

i.e.,

Therefore, the Department would view rules requiring satisfaction of such standards with an eye toward whether they actually pertain to health and safety, as opposed to being pretext for the type of control exercised over workers to meet the business' own needs.
The breadth of comments and views on this aspect of the control factor has prompted the Department to provide additional clarification on how it should be understood and applied. Merely labeling requirements “health and safety,” for example, does not automatically mean they could not possibly indicate employer-type controls regardless of their nature, content, or extent. The inquiry turns on the substance and practical operation of the requirement, not the characterization of its purpose. A measure that genuinely establishes a health or safety standard typical of a business-to-business relationship would not indicate employee status. But detailed instructions governing how, when, or where the worker must perform the work may constitute employer-like control even if described as promoting health or safety. Otherwise, a potential employer could evade the control analysis simply by attaching a safety rationale to directives that, in practice, substantially govern the performance of the work. The Department has decided to add explanatory text to this provision in the control factor in order to strike the proper balance and sufficiently describe when such compliance measures will not make a worker more or less likely to be an employee. The newly-added explanatory text is the following: “The nature of a particular requirement turns on its substance and practical operation, not the characterization of its purpose. For example, detailed instructions governing how, when, or where the worker must perform the work may indicate control typical of an employment relationship even if described as promoting health or safety or maintaining quality control standards.”
Other than the additional text described above (as well as a minor non-substantive edit changing “and/or” to “or”), the Department is finalizing the control factor as proposed.

a. Comments Regarding Considering Investment Within the Opportunity for Profit or Loss Factor
Numerous commenters opposed the NPRM's consideration of investment within the opportunity for profit or loss factor. For example, Coalition of State Officials asserted that the NPRM did “not justify its decision to diverge from . . . case law, or address the confusion that would result from that divergence, except to offer, without support, that its approach would provide `greater explanation and clarity' ” (quoting NPRM). See also, e.g.,

Numerous other commenters supported the NPRM's consideration of investment within the opportunity for profit or loss factor. For example, FSI commented that “[i]nvestment is properly considered as part of the `opportunity for profit or loss' ” factor and that this would “eliminate redundancy and double counting.” American Association of Advertising Agencies asserted that, “[b]y integrating investment into the broader profit-and-loss inquiry, the Department properly recognizes that [representative expenditures by a freelancer] are entrepreneurial tools used by creative professionals to increase their marketability, enhance their project efficiency, and ultimately drive their own business profits.” Flex Association “support[ed] eliminating `investment' as a stand-alone factor,” saying that “[i]nvestment is an entrepreneurial activity: perhaps the most fundamental choice an entrepreneur makes is where to allocate and invest her capital. Whether she is buying equipment, taking out ads, or taking skills training to enhance her human capital, she is engaged in the core business activity of allocating [scarce] resources. Investments are therefore properly considered under the `opportunity' factor.”
See also, e.g.,
National Retail Federation (describing the 2024 Rule as “misguided in attempting to make investment its own factor” because “[a]ny investments naturally impact a contractor's ability for profit or loss,” and “investments are so interrelated with profits and losses that analyzing them separately would be duplicative”); Littler WPI (stating that including investment in the opportunity factor “is a welcome change that will bring clarity and reduce overlap,” and adding that “[w]ise decisions about investments are perhaps the clearest path to increasing profits or suffering losses”).
Having considered the comments on this issue, the Department adopts its proposal to consider investment as part of the opportunity for profit or loss factor. As an initial matter, whether opportunity and investment are articulated as separate factors, the worker's investment is a longstanding consideration, is particularly probative of a worker's status, and should be considered in all cases, and the Department's inclusion of investment within the opportunity factor reflects this important reality. However, mechanically articulating the worker's investment as a separate factor in the analysis because that is how a majority of courts
recite

16 F. App'x at 106-07 (finding that the worker's capital investments in tools, equipment, and a truck indicated independent contractor status under both the opportunity and investment factors). Considering investment within the opportunity factor rather than in isolation also prevents an investment by the worker that is unrelated to, and outside of, the business from becoming part of the analysis.
See, e.g.,
Parrish,
917 F.3d at 384 (giving weight to consultant's investment in, and losses relating to, a goat farm that was unrelated to his consulting work for an oil drilling
(
printed page 75689)
company that was the issue in the case). As explained above, the economic reality factors are limited to the individual's “claimed independent operation,” and anchoring investment in opportunity helps to ensure that the analysis does not drift away from that focus.
[
274
]
In sum, the Department finds the Second Circuit's approach to opportunity for profit or loss and investment to be particularly persuasive and best aligned with the Department's goal in this rulemaking of sharpening the employee/independent contractor analysis, including by avoiding duplication among the factors.
b. Comments Regarding Considering the Individual Worker's Investments Only Instead of Relative Investments
Some commenters opposed the NPRM's consideration of the individual worker's investments only instead of comparing the worker's investments to the potential employer's investments. For example, Nichols Kaster asserted that the NPRM, “to the clear detriment of workers, assigns no relevance to how the workers' investment compares to the size of the putative employer's investments,” adding that “[t]his focus solely on workers' investment, without an analysis of how it compares to the putative employer's investment, is contrary to established law” and “unfounded” and “will make it easier for businesses to deny workers the protection of the FLSA.” Farmworker Justice commented that the NPRM fails to “consider that a worker's relatively small investment is unlikely to sway an operation to a point of profitability” and that “[i]t is impossible to understand whether a worker's investment was relevant to profit or loss without understanding its overall impact, which requires an analysis of the potential employer's contribution.” NWJP argued that this aspect of the NPRM “contradicts existing case law,” “does not offer any guidance for how one should evaluate investment related facts in absence of [comparing the worker's investments to that of the potential employer],” and “only confuses.” This commenter added that the 2024 Rule “adequately addresses the Department's named concern that when comparing amount of money invested the business will frequently have more money on the table by instructing one to compare the types of investment as well.” SEIU stated that “[t]his is a notable departure from the [2024 Rule], which . . . compares the employer's investments to the worker's.”
Numerous other commenters supported the NPRM's consideration of the individual worker's investments only instead of comparing the worker's investments to those of the potential employer. For example, Independent Bakers Association asserted that “[t]he relevant question is whether the
worker
has a significant investment in his or her business,” “[t]he other party's investment amount is beside the point,” “[a]nd comparing investments could result in a contractor's status changing simply based on the size of the party with which they contract, surely an illogical outcome.” Landmark Legal Foundation commented that the Supreme Court in
Silk
“focused exclusively on the worker's own investments” and that the “2024 Rule departed from that approach” by adopting a “comparative framework [that] has no support in Supreme Court precedent.” This commenter added that the 2024 Rule's comparative framework “produces a structurally biased result” because “[i]n most cases an independent contractor's investments will be smaller than a corporate client's total business investment,” and “the comparison will systematically show employee status regardless of whether the worker is genuinely in business for herself.” CWI agreed, saying that the 2024 Rule's comparative investment approach “was inherently skewed against finding an opportunity for profit or loss” because a “sole proprietor's investment will almost always appear small in comparison with a corporate client's total capitalization,” adding that the NPRM's approach “is consistent with the Supreme Court's ruling in
Silk,
where the Court found that the truck drivers held independent contractor status despite the coal companies' far greater total capitalization.” Uber stated that a worker's investments “should be considered on their own terms—not in comparison to investments by some other party,” adding that “[w]hen the worker invests in things that will support her own business, it is irrelevant whether someone else also invests a larger sum;” otherwise, “no small business could contract with a larger one.” Littler WPI argued that comparing investments “provides no useful insight as to whether that worker is in fact in business for him- or herself” and has little relevance to the economic reality test. Other supportive commenters included American Association of Advertising Agencies, American Council of Life Insurers, Associated Builders and Contractors, Coalition to Promote Independent Entrepreneurs, FSI, Private Care Association, Scopelitis, ShiftKey, Transportation Intermediaries Association, and WAFLA.
Having considered the comments on this issue, the Department adopts its proposal to consider the worker's investments only instead of comparing the worker's investments to the potential employer's investments. Throughout this rule, the Department is seeking to articulate the factors in a way that connects them to the ultimate inquiry of economic dependence and actually delineates clearly between employee and independent contractor status (if a factor points always or usually in one direction, it has little to offer). Everyone agrees that the nature and scope of the worker's investments (or the lack thereof) is probative of the worker's economic dependence. And as it did in the 2021 Rule,
[
275
]
the Department believes that comparing the worker's investments to the investments of the potential employer saps the probative value from the consideration of investments. Instead of shedding light on the worker's economic situation and capacity to operate as an independent business, comparing the worker's investments to those of the potential employer merely compares their respective sizes and resources. In almost all cases, the potential employer is larger than and has greater resources than the individual worker (which would constantly indicate one status over the other). Yet, if that individual worker has made a meaningful investment in, or capital expenditure on, helpers or equipment or material to further his or her work, then that consideration indicates a degree of economic independence that should not be overridden by the size of the potential employer. For this reason, the approach of the 2024 Rule, to the extent it was perceived to compare solely the size of the worker's investments to the size of the potential employer's investments, could have created absurd results. For example, this factor might indicate employee status for a worker who has made such meaningful investments if engaging with a massive corporation and independent contractor status if engaging with a small business. This is because the comparative value of
(
printed page 75690)
investment is far less probative of economic independence than the nature and extent of the worker's investment in his or her business. Considering the worker's investments without comparing them to those of the potential employer thus ensures that this consideration remains tied to the ultimate inquiry of the economic dependence and can indicate employee or independent contractor status as appropriate depending on the facts.
The Department's position is consistent with the Supreme Court's articulation of the economic reality test, which has never compared a worker's investments to those of the potential employer. In
Silk,
for example, the Court recognized that the truck drivers' ownership of their vehicles supported independent contractor status even though the coal company that engaged them undoubtedly had far greater overall capital investments.
[
276
]
And the Court recognized that the unloaders' lack of meaningful investment (they “provided only picks and shovels”) supported employee status without regard to the coal company's investment.
[
277
]
In other words, the Court found the realities of the respective workers' investments to be probative—not the coal company's investments.
Of course, the Supreme Court's analysis takes precedence over decisions of the circuit courts. Nonetheless, some circuits do consider the worker's investments without comparing them to the potential employer's investments in its business. For example, the Seventh Circuit found that the investments factor indicated that a truck driver was an employee without considering the trucking company's investments in its business.
[
278
]
The Second Circuit found that the fact that the workers “invested heavily in their driving businesses” indicated that they were independent contractors without comparing their investments to those of the potential employer, adding that, under the economic reality test, whether the worker has “`large capital expenditures'—as opposed to `negligible items, or labor itself'—are highly relevant to determining whether an individual is an employee or an independent contractor.”
[
279
]
The Eleventh Circuit has likewise focused on the nature of the worker's investments without comparing them to the potential employer's investments.
[
280
]
The Department recognizes that a number of circuits compare the worker's investments to those of the potential employer.
[
281
]
The Department notes, however, that, among these circuits, how the Fifth and Eighth Circuits have applied the comparative investments approach to the facts of cases reveals that the approach has little probative value. In
Cornerstone Am.,
for example, the Fifth Circuit stated that it was of course “clear that [the insurance company's] investment—including maintaining corporate offices, printing brochures and contracts, providing accounting services, and developing and underwriting insurance products—outweighs the personal investment of any one Sales Leader.”
[
282
]
The court, however, never explained how this fact was probative of the Sales Leaders' economic dependence, and when summing up the entirety of the facts and analyzing whether the workers were economically dependent on the insurance company as a matter of economic reality, the court did not even mention the insurance company's larger investment.
[
283
]
And in
Parrish,
the Fifth Circuit compared the relative investments, but noted that “[o]bviously, [the oil drilling company] invested more money at a drill site compared to each plaintiff's investments” and accorded the factor little weight in light of the other evidence.
[
284
]
In
Karlson,
the Eighth Circuit found that comparing the worker's investment with the potential employer's total operating expenses had little relevance because “[l]arge corporations can hire independent contractors, and small businesses can hire employees.”
[
285
]
Additionally, the Department notes that this final rule preserves a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry, which is particularly important when analyzing opportunity for profit and loss. The enumerated factors focus the analysis on the facts within that totality that ordinarily matter and why. But additional facts or considerations may nevertheless be relevant (and, therefore, should be considered) if they indicate whether the worker is in business for himself or herself or is economically dependent on the potential employer for work. A comparison of the parties' relative investments is one such unenumerated consideration and may be examined when it meaningfully illuminates that inquiry in a particular case. For the reasons explained above, however, the Department believes that such a comparison will ordinarily have little or no value because it measures the parties' relative scale rather than the worker's economic independence. Incorporating that comparison as an enumerated component of the investment consideration would therefore dilute, rather than enhance, the opportunity factor's probative force. This rule accordingly does not foreclose comparison of relative investments in uncommon circumstances in which it may be genuinely informative, but it declines to make that generally unhelpful comparison part of the enumerated investment analysis.
The 2024 Rule considered the worker's and the potential employer's relative investments but acknowledged that strict comparisons of the investments were not helpful.
[
286
]
The 2024 Rule thus took an approach that did not simply compare “the dollar values of investments or the sizes of the worker and the potential employer” and instead focused “on comparing the investments to determine whether the worker is making similar types of investments as the potential employer (even if on a smaller scale) to suggest that the worker is operating independently, which would indicate independent contractor status.”
[
287
]
This approach, however, still injects the potential employer's investments into the analysis without any basis for why the potential employer's investments are probative of the economic dependence
(
printed page 75691)
or independence of the individual worker at issue. In sum, comparing the relative investments in any manner does not illuminate the worker's economic dependence or independence. By contrast, as explained herein, analyzing the extent to which the individual worker has an opportunity for profit or loss because of his or her investment in, or capital expenditure on, helpers or equipment or material to further his or her work is probative of the worker's economic dependence or independence.
Relatedly, several commenters raised issues regarding how the opportunity factor would apply to workers with small investments. For example, Farmworker Justice stated that “a worker's relatively small investment is unlikely to sway an operation to a point of profitability,” and “[f]armworkers make de minimis, if any, `capital contributions' to their employers' businesses.” Although other facts would have to be considered too, the Department agrees that such farmworkers do not seem to have an investment indicating that they have an opportunity for profit or loss. Philadelphia Legal Assistance similarly commented that “[s]mall spending on transportation or tools does not reflect business independence and is unlikely to meaningfully affect whether the business makes money.” The Department does not disagree and reiterates that, although other facts would need to be considered too, small spending on transportation or tools does not seem to be an investment indicating an opportunity for profit or loss. Indeed, as explained in the 2021 Rule,
[
288
]
the investment must be capital in nature and consistent with the worker being in business for him or herself for the investment to indicate an opportunity for profit or loss. UBC took issue with the example in proposed § 795.115(b)(2), saying that “[t]his example will be interpreted as supporting independent contractor status for construction workers dispatched to a job site through an app if they have tools—and all building trades workers will have tools.” This example, however, does not mention tools and explains that the facts presented indicate independent contractor status under the opportunity for profit or loss factor because the worker “is able to meaningfully increase his earnings by exercising initiative and business acumen and by investing in his own equipment,” notwithstanding that the potential employer has made a substantially larger investment in its own business operations.
[
289
]
American Society of Travel Advisors suggested that “the regulations expressly recognize that workers in many service industries may make only a minimal investment in equipment or materials and in such situations this consideration, by itself, should not be taken to weigh in favor of employee status.” The Department declines to do so. A minimal investment in equipment or tools, by itself, does typically indicate employee status. Adopting this suggestion would be contrary to the Department's general approach to articulating the factors in this final rule, unlike how the 2024 Rule articulated certain factors, in a way that is neutral toward employee or independent contractor status. More generally, a worker who makes a minimal investment in equipment or tools may have an opportunity for profit or loss indicating independent contractor status if the worker may earn profits or incur losses based on his or her exercise of initiative (such as managerial skill or business acumen or judgment).
[
290

And as the Department explained in the 2021 Rule,
[

the absence of a substantial capital investment may be less probative in more knowledge-based occupations and industries, and for example, freelance journalists, graphic designers, or consultants may be entrepreneurs with little more than a personal computer and smartphone. As Judge Easterbrook has explained, “possess[ing] little or no physical capital . . . is true of many workers we would call independent contractors. Think of lawyers, many of whom do not even own books. The bar sells human capital rather than physical capital, but this does not imply that lawyers are `employees' of their clients under the FLSA.”

Finally, National Association of Home Builders expressed concern that “the proposed description of th[e opportunity] factor may unnecessarily limit consideration of entrepreneurial investments that are not capital in nature” and suggested that the Department “consider alternative or additional regulatory text that allows for the consideration of entrepreneurial investments that are not capital in nature.” The regulatory text in § 795.105(d)(1)(ii) identifies the worker's “investment in
or

Although the Department believes that capital expenditures and entrepreneurial investments are similar, the regulatory text does not limit consideration to capital expenditures, and entrepreneurial investments that affect a worker's opportunity to earn profits or incur losses are considered too.
c. Other Comments Regarding the Opportunity for Profit or Loss Factor
The Department received numerous additional comments regarding the opportunity for profit or loss factor.
For example, several commenters stated that the Department drafted the proposed opportunity factor to favor findings of independent contractor status. AFSCME commented that this factor “favors independent contractor status on the whole when either opportunity or investment favor independent contractor status, while both aspects must point to employee status in order for it to favor employee status as a whole,” thus it “is structured to give the advantage to independent contractor status rather than consideration of all the relevant facts for each of these two aspects of the test.” Nichols Kaster stated that the proposed opportunity factor “indicates independent contractor status if there are facts that support
either
worker initiative or investment (even if either a
(
printed page 75692)
lack of initiative or lack of investment suggests that the worker is an employee).” OOIDA commented that, “[i]f the Department intends to say there doesn't need to be skill exercised when making an investment for this factor to weigh toward independent contractor, then we believe it may indicate independent contractor status where it isn't warranted.” On the other hand, National Retail Federation asserted that “initiative alone—without any corresponding investment—can be sufficient to satisfy this factor,” especially considering that, “in today's economy, there is less of a barrier to entry to starting and operating a business thanks to technology and other developments that streamline business operations and lower overhead costs.”
As an initial matter, both the individual worker's exercise of initiative and management of investment should be considered in all cases under the opportunity for profit or loss factor even if the factor may indicate independent contractor classification based on only one. The worker's exercise of initiative and management of investment are longstanding considerations and particularly probative of a worker's status. The Department's inclusion of them within the opportunity factor reflects that. However, the ultimate focus of this factor is the worker's opportunity for profit or loss, which the Department believes is a core or primary indicator of a worker's status as explained above. While exercising initiative
and
managing investments would certainly be stronger evidence that a worker has the opportunity for profit and loss, providing that the worker
must
both exercise initiative and manage investments for this factor to indicate independent contractor status would detract from this factor's ultimate focus on the worker's opportunity and would impose an unwarranted mechanical element or checklist on how this factor is applied. Thus, although initiative and investment are both paths to arrive there, a worker must have, as a matter of economic reality, an opportunity for profit or loss to indicate independent contractor status.
Ultimately, the focus of this factor is whether the worker has a meaningful opportunity for profit or loss characteristic of an independent business. Such an opportunity may arise from the worker's exercise of initiative, management of investment, or both; the worker need not demonstrate it through both considerations. Initiative and investment should each be considered where relevant, but they are neither applied mechanically nor tallied against each other. Evidence relating to either consideration does not automatically determine the factor's direction without regard to contrary evidence regarding the other. Rather, evidence concerning initiative and investment must be evaluated together to determine whether the worker possesses a genuine entrepreneurial opportunity to affect profits or losses. Thus, one consideration may be sufficient for the factor to indicate independent contractor status when it meaningfully establishes such an opportunity, but weak evidence under one consideration may be outweighed by stronger contrary evidence under the other. Weak evidence under one consideration favoring independent contractor status, for example, could be outweighed by strong evidence under the other consideration favoring employee status, and vice versa. Undoubtedly the particular facts of each case will produce rules along the scale between independent contractor and employee status. This certainly includes cases in which the evidence, considered as a whole, points equally in opposite directions or does not point meaningfully in either direction. In these and other indeterminate circumstances, the factor may be neutral. To make clear that initiative and investment should be considered as a whole under this factor and to avoid any confusion when applying this factor, the Department has added: (1) “or both” to the end of the first sentence in the regulatory text; and (2) a sentence in the regulatory text explaining that evidence under one consideration pointing to either independent contractor or employee status could be outweighed by more persuasive evidence under the other consideration pointing in a different direction.
AFL-CIO asserted that the proposed factor “conflates true entrepreneurial independence with ordinary variations in wages or output that exist in many employment relationships,” and added that “[w]orkers who can increase earnings by working longer hours, accepting more assignments, or marginally adjusting how they perform tasks are not thereby operating independent businesses.” Similarly, IBT stated that merely working more or faster is more like piecework than an enterprise requiring entrepreneurial judgment. The Department does not disagree and believes that such concerns are already addressed by the regulatory text for this factor, which states that this factor indicates employee status if the worker “is unable to affect his or her earnings or is only able to do so by working more hours or faster.” Indeed, Farmworker Justice, although it opposed the proposed analysis generally, acknowledged that the NPRM did “appropriately explain that, for those workers with a fixed hourly rate, where the employer determines the tasks to perform, the worker does not have a meaningful opportunity for profit or loss.”
Among commenters that generally supported the proposed analysis, Americans for Prosperity Foundation suggested that the factor's final sentence (explaining that it indicates employee status if the worker “is unable to affect his or her earnings or is only able to do so by working more hours or faster”) be removed, saying that it “is overbroad and could be construed to extend to circumstances where individuals use their initiative, skills, and judgment to perform more efficiently and thus earn greater profit or invest in their own . . . tools to allow them to achieve this result.” On the other hand, Center for Workplace Compliance asserted that distinguishing “between entrepreneurial opportunity driven by managerial skill, initiative, and business decisions” and “changes in earnings that depend primarily on working more hours or working faster . . . aligns directly with the economic dependence inquiry and helps distinguish workers who are in business for themselves from those who depend on another entity for work.” Similarly, CWI endorsed the proposal's articulation of this point as compared to the 2024 Rule but requested clarification that accepting additional engagements “through one's own independent business operations reflects the exercise of entrepreneurial
initiative
relevant to the opportunity-for-profit-or-loss Core Factor.”
The Department declines to remove the final sentence of this factor's regulatory text. To the extent that a worker who is paid a fixed hourly rate or a fixed rate per piece is only able to affect his or her earnings “by working more hours or faster,” the Department believes that this fact indicates that the worker is an employee. This is well-settled in the case law.
[
293
]
And the
(
printed page 75693)
Department agrees that this sentence is consistent with its discussion of economic dependence in this final rule (§ 795.105(b)) as a worker who can affect his or her earnings only by working more or faster is dependent on the employer for those more hours or pieces (
i.e.,
the work) rather than having the nature and character of a business owner who has a separate business.
[
294
]
The Department acknowledges though that working more hours or completing more pieces for an employer is different than accepting additional engagements from an employer through the worker's own independent business operations, in which case the opportunity factor could indicate independent contractor status provided there is exercise of initiative or management of investment.
Relatedly, Texas RioGrande Legal Aid commented that, “[u]nder the proposed regulation, factors as unremarkable as a worker's opportunity for earning tips based on their customer service skill or bonuses based on their managerial or sales skill somehow weigh in favor of independent contractor status.” As an initial matter, the NPRM did not mention tips or bonuses, and certainly did not state that receiving such compensation, standing alone, indicates independent contractor status. The relevant inquiry is whether the worker's ability to earn tips and bonuses reflects an opportunity for profit or loss arising from the worker's own initiative, managerial judgment, or investment, rather than an earning opportunity created and controlled by the potential employer.
For example, a musical performer who decides when and where to perform, obtains engagements at different venues, manages those different performance opportunities, maintains her own equipment, and earns tips based on the success of each performance may have an opportunity for profit or loss reflecting operation of an independent business. The relevant evidence would not be the receipt of tips, but the performer's ability to obtain and manage engagements and affect earnings through independent initiative and investments. By contrast, a musician who, as a matter of actual practice, is required to perform exclusively for one venue, works according to opportunities and conditions determined by that venue, uses equipment provided by that venue, and can increase earnings only through tips received while performing the assigned work would more likely be an employee. The mere possibility of earning tips would not convert that employment relationship into an independent business.
The same principle applies to bonuses. Bonuses may arise in either employment or independent contractor relationships, and the existence of a bonus is not itself significant. What matters is whether the worker can affect profits or losses through independent business decisions or instead receives additional compensation under terms and opportunities controlled by the potential employer.
Texas RioGrande Legal Aid further commented that the proposed opportunity factor “chang[es] the focus from whether the
business

worker

Indeed, the 2024 Rule's opportunity factor “considers whether the worker has opportunities for profit or loss based on managerial skill (including initiative or business acumen or judgment) that affect the worker's economic success or failure in performing the work.”
[
295

In fact, the 2024 Rule's opportunity factor references the worker 10 times and does not mention the potential employer's business once.

Although actions by the potential employer may be relevant, the proposed opportunity factor properly focuses on the worker's opportunities.

In any event,

Several commenters addressed workers who use for their work materials and equipment that they already own for personal use. Thus, whether an employee who is required to bear certain costs has an opportunity for profit or loss involves an inquiry into the nature of the possible investment and his or her ability to manage it. For example, a company that hires independent contractors to haul freight may obviously require that drivers bring their own vehicles.

Having considered these comments, the Department believes that the ultimate outcome of independent entrepreneurship (profit or loss) is separate from the actions indicative of entrepreneurship (initiative, investment, or both) that largely determine that outcome, and this factor makes clear that independent contractors typically “exercise . . . initiative,” “manage[ ] . . . investment,” or both. Thus, as explained in the 2021 Rule, a lack of profit or loss viewed in hindsight says little about a worker's economic independence; instead, the focus is the degree to which the worker actually exercised initiative or actually managed investments.

The provision in § 795.110 that “the actual practice of the parties involved is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible” applies to all of the factors and applies regardless whether it suggests employee or independent contractor status. As further explained in the 2021 Rule, a worker's theoretical ability to, for example, exercise initiative is weaker evidence than the worker's actual practices.

]
On the other hand, a worker's conscious decision to not make a particular investment (especially when choosing among a range of investments) or to not take a particular action (especially when choosing among a range of options) may constitute an affirmative exercise of initiative to consider among others when evaluating opportunity for profit or loss. In sum, in the context of the opportunity factor, the focus is the individual worker's opportunity for profit or loss, as shown by meaningful investments or the exercise of personal initiative; actual profits or losses are less relevant.
Finally, some commenters who supported the proposal suggested numerous additional considerations or examples for inclusion in the Department's discussion of the opportunity for profit or loss factor in this final rule. For example, U.S. Chamber of Commerce suggested twelve “examples of a worker's initiative or investment that may impact a worker's profit or loss” and three “examples of fact situations which are neutral in the analysis of whether the worker controls their profits and losses.” For this (and each other factor), the Department's goal, however, is to provide a clear and generally-applicable standard that can point to independent contractor or employee status depending on the facts presented. The Department is of course addressing many of the specific considerations and examples raised by commenters to provide as fulsome guidance as possible, but identifying every possible consideration would undermine the Department's overall goal of providing a clear, workable, and generally-applicable standard.
For all these reasons, the Department is finalizing the regulatory text in § 795.105(d)(1)(ii) describing the opportunity for profit or loss factor with two additions as set forth above.
d. New Examples Regarding Drivers Who Lease Trucks From Motor Carriers
A number of commenters addressing the trucking industry requested more examples and guidance in applying the factors to truck drivers. The commenters generally recognized that truck drivers may be properly classified as employees or independent contractors depending on their circumstances and discussed drivers who are owner-operators and who lease trucks. For example, Real Women in Trucking expressed concern that “any leasing arrangement between a driver and the company for which they drive would likely suggest independent contractor status.” OOIDA, although it generally supported the proposed analysis, requested clarification that a lease-purchase agreement is not the type of investment that indicates independent contractor status. SBA Office of Advocacy reported that its roundtable participants from the trucking industry requested that the Department address fraud or abuse in lease-purchase programs. National Association of Small Trucking Companies discussed various business models for one-driver, one-truck operators and how they can grow into small motor carriers themselves. And Truckers Integral to Our Economy discussed the role that company-drivers and independent owner-operators play in the economy and requested clear guidance so that owner-operators can structure relationships to preserve their economic independence.
Having considered these comments, the Department generally believes that the fact that a driver owns a truck and exercises initiative in how to operate it seems to plainly indicate independent contractor status under the opportunity for profit or loss factor. How that factor applies to drivers who lease trucks seems more nuanced, and accordingly, the Department is adding to the final regulatory text (in § 795.115(b)(8) and (9)) two new examples illustrating how the factor can indicate employee or independent contractor status.
The first example (in § 795.115(b)(8)) involves a driver who leases a truck from and hauls freight for a motor carrier company. The company determines the rates that it pays the worker for each shipment, does not negotiate those rates, and assigns shipments to the worker without informing him of the rates before he must commit to the shipment. The worker's monthly lease payments to the company may theoretically allow him or her to purchase the vehicle one day, but the reality of the economic terms of the lease agreement most likely prevents the worker from ever reaching that point. Those facts would indicate employee status under the opportunity for profit or loss factor.
The second example (in § 795.115(b)(9)) likewise involves a driver who leases a truck from and hauls freight for a motor carrier company. Unlike the circumstances of the worker in the above example, the company offers the worker shipments at proposed rates, and the worker is able to negotiate those rates before committing to shipments. When possible, the worker seeks to negotiate a separate shipment for the return leg (
i.e.,
a “backhaul”) to avoid driving an empty vehicle. The economic terms of the lease agreement actually provide an opportunity for the worker to own the vehicle in the future. Those facts would indicate independent contractor status under the opportunity for profit or loss factor.
The Department believes that these two new examples will provide sufficient clarification in response to a multitude of comments on this topic.

G. Economic Reality Factors—Other Factors (§ 795.105(d)(2))
This section discusses the comments addressing the three other factors proposed by the Department in addition to the two core factors. As discussed in § 795.105(c) above, these other factors are less probative than the core factors, and in some cases, they may not be probative at all. Nevertheless, they are still considered in every case for whatever value they bring to analyzing the character of an individual's economic dependence for work—namely, whether it is more in the nature and character of a business owner or a typical employee.

Having considered the comments, the Department does not share commenters' concerns that the skill factor will incorrectly indicate either employee or independent contractor status when properly applied as part of this rule. These comments overlook that “no single factor is dispositive” (§ 795.105(c)), “skill required” is just one factor, and it is not a primary factor. Accordingly, contrary to the suggestions in some comments, the fact that the work requires specialized training or skill will not automatically result in a finding of independent contractor status, and the fact that the work does not require specialized training or skill will not automatically result in a finding of employee status. Although courts have traditionally considered “skill” as evidence of economic independence, skilled workers can be employees, and unskilled workers can be independent contractors. Put simply, skills are not the monopoly of independent contractors or employees. Indeed, to the extent that commenter feedback suggests that such outcomes are more common in the modern economy than in decades past,
[
320

such a trend supports the Department's decision to afford skill less weight as a non-core factor in the analysis. In any event, adopting commenter suggestions to revise the application of this factor to favor one status or the other would be inconsistent with the balance in this rule that avoids framing the analysis and factors in ways that favor either employee or independent contractor outcomes. More importantly, the Department believes that its description of this factor is consistent with the ultimate inquiry whether the worker is economically dependent on the potential employer for work or is in business for him- or herself. To the extent that the work requires specialized training or skill that the potential employer does not provide, the fact that the worker brings specialized training or skills to the work indicates a degree of independence. And to the extent that the work requires no specialized training or skill or the worker depends on the potential employer to provide any necessary skills or training, those facts indicate a lack of independence.
Thus, comments about the example in proposed § 795.115(b)(5) by UBC (it “makes every skilled construction craft journeyperson an independent contractor”) and NWJP (it “implies that an experienced roofer may be an independent contractor on that ground alone”) plainly misapprehend and misapply both the example and the overarching analysis. The example in proposed § 795.115(b)(5) involving a roofer simply illustrates a fact pattern under which the skill factor would indicate independent contractor status. No single factor is dispositive (§ 795.105(c)), and whether that roofer (or any construction worker) is an employee or independent contractor would be determined by applying all the factors, particularly the core factors.

Experience is not the same as skill, and, even if the worker is skilled through experience, this factor will indicate employee status if the work at issue requires no specialized training or skill or the individual is dependent upon the potential employer to equip him or her with any skills or training necessary to perform the job. In response to the comment by American Association of Advertising Agencies, skill can come from work experience, independent study, or simply practice and repetition. The absence of a formal license or certification is not dispositive of whether a worker has specialized skills. Of course, skill can also come from educational or training programs which award degrees, credentials, and licenses.
[
321
]
Indeed, as the name of the “skill required for the work” factor indicates, the fact that a worker possesses skills does not necessarily indicate independent contractor status; the factor specifically examines whether the work at issue requires specialized training or skill and whether the potential employer provides the specialized training or skill (if it is required). In other words, this rule is not a box-checking exercise, or an inventory list, but rather sets forth an analysis designed to resolve whether the economic reality of a particular worker is that of an independent contractor or employee.
