Regarding delivery services more generally, however, the possible circumstances are too varied (compared to a CDL) for the Department to agree or disagree with these commenters' requests regarding delivery work not involving a CDL; it depends on the facts, including whether the delivery work requires specialized training or skill and, if so, whether the potential employer provides it.
For all these reasons, the Department finalizes the “skill required” factor in § 795.105(d)(2)(i) as proposed, with the exception of a minor non-substantive edit (changing “and/or” to “or”).
2. The Degree of Permanence of the Working Relationship Between the Individual and the Potential Employer (§ 795.105(d)(2)(ii))
The Department proposed to adopt the regulatory text from the 2021 Rule, § 795.105(d)(2)(ii), which describes the degree of permanence of the working relationship between the individual and the potential employer, as the second other economic reality factor. The Department proposed that this factor would weigh in favor of the individual being an independent contractor to the extent the work relationship is by design definite in duration or sporadic, which may include regularly occurring fixed periods of work, although the seasonal nature of work by itself would not necessarily indicate independent contractor classification. The proposal also provided that this factor would weigh in favor of the individual being an employee to the extent the work relationship is instead by design indefinite in duration or continuous. The Department further proposed in the NPRM to not include the concept of exclusivity in the permanence factor, as exclusivity is more directly related to the control factor.
[
323
]
Many commenters supported the framing of the permanence factor as proposed in the NPRM.
See, e.g.,
FSI; Flex Association; Independent Work Coalition; National Retail Federation; U.S. Chamber. They generally felt that this factor was appropriately categorized as a secondary, less-probative factor,
see, e.g.,
FSI; U.S. Chamber, though some commenters thought that this factor should be eliminated altogether,
see
American Trucking Association; CWI; FedEx. Additionally, several commenters supported the proposal to not consider the exclusivity of the relationship as an aspect of the permanence factor,
see
CWI; National Association of Home Builders; U.S. Chamber, whereas others felt that exclusivity was critical, urging the Department to “clarify in the final rule that the duration of a working relationship is only probative of employee status under this factor when the potential employer has actually imposed requirements or restrictions that prevent the worker from being in business for themselves—such as exclusivity requirements or prohibitions on working for others,” National Retail Federation;
see also
American Society
(
printed page 75701)
of Travel Advisors; American Trucking Association.
Business commenters frequently emphasized their concern that focusing on the length of a work relationship was not appropriate because it would encompass many situations in which contractors and businesses choose to have or negotiate continual, repeat, or long-term engagements with one another that do not indicate economic dependence.
See, e.g.,
Bowling Proprietors Association of America; CWI; Flex Association; Independent Work Coalition; Littler WPI; U.S. Chamber. For example, U.S. Chamber of Commerce urged the Department to revise this factor to focus on the “indefiniteness of the relationship, not the length of the relationship,” explaining that “[i]ndependent workers and businesses enter into long-term contracts and contracts that are renewed regularly due to superior service, competitive costs, or the lack of alternative service providers, and these relationships are not evidence of the permanence of the relationship or employee status.” CWI similarly believed that this factor “penalizes long-term contractor relationships that both parties voluntarily renew because the relationship works well” and encouraged the Department to revise the language to focus instead on the parties' contractual terms and “whether the relationship is contractually indefinite by design, not merely long-running in practice.” Some of these commenters specifically noted the nature of work engagements in particular industries, contending that the application-based, trucking, and construction industries often use discrete task-based or project-based engagements, and that each of these must be considered independently rather than as a continuous relationship.
See
Flex Association; Independent Work Coalition; Instacart; Littler WPI; Scopelitis.
On the other hand, some worker organizations noted that in certain industries where work has fixed end points, such as construction and agriculture, the fact that there is a fixed term should not favor independent contractor status as it does not indicate economic independence.
See
IBT; NWJP; SMART and SMACNA. For example, NWJP argued that the Department should retain the language from the 2024 Rule that provided guidance that permanence should be considered in the context of the type of business or industry, such as how the agricultural industry relies heavily on seasonal labor, which it noted is well-established in case law. Similarly, SMART and SMACNA highlighted the importance of the “proper application” of the permanence factor in the project-based construction industry and urged the Department to recognize that this factor is “generally less likely to be probative of worker status in industries characterized by seasonal, temporary, sporadic, or project-based work relationships but permanent and exclusive employment for the duration of a project weighs in favor of employee status.” And IBT requested additional guidance explaining that “a worker's lack of permanent or indefinite employment status is in many cases not due to the worker's own business initiatives but rather to the employer's unilateral structuring of the relationship.”
Another frequent request raised by business commenters was for the Department to address “continuity driven by employer requirements” as compared to choices that workers make to accept future work or to continue working for a particular entity. TechNet;
see also
Flex Association; Instacart; National Retail Federation. For example, Instacart requested revisions to the regulatory text to provide that “[c]ontinuity that originates with the worker's own choices is fundamentally different from continuity that originates with the employer's expectations and requirements.”
Several commenters emphasized the importance of permanence in the analysis. For example, SHRM conducted a survey of its members to determine which of the economic reality factors organizations found most useful when determining employment status under the FLSA, and commented that survey respondents consistently ranked permanence as the second most useful indicator (following control, which they ranked as the most useful indicator). And IBT commented that “[u]nder decades of jurisprudence, permanence strongly indicates economic dependence. Workers who rely on a firm for steady, ongoing work, even when paid per task, are employees.”
After considering the comments received on this factor, the Department believes it is appropriate to retain permanence as one of the less-probative factors in the economic reality analysis and declines to eliminate this factor. As noted in the NPRM, courts and the Department routinely consider this factor when applying the economic reality analysis under the FLSA to determine employee or independent contractor status.
[
324
]
Indeed, the Department is not aware of a circuit that does not identify permanence as a standalone factor. As the SHRM survey showed, this factor is viewed as a useful indicator among human resources professionals as well.
Moreover, the Department believes that its regulatory text ameliorates many of the concerns raised by commenters. First, regarding the concern that this factor fails to recognize that business entities often have repeat work engagements without their relationship being one of employer-employee, the regulatory text explicitly states that “this factor weighs in favor of an individual being an independent contractor to the extent the work relationship is by design definite in duration . . . which
may include regularly occurring fixed periods of work”
(emphasis added). As American Association of Advertising Agencies observed in supporting this language, this may encompass situations in which, for example, advertising agencies “frequently re-engage specialized independent contractors . . . for successive defined-duration client campaigns” that are “dictated by the specific needs of [the campaign] rather than an indefinite employment relationship.”
Additionally, commenters that were concerned that their long-standing business relationships with particular service providers or specialized contractors alone would somehow override the two primary factors and establish an employment relationship seem to misunderstand the analysis.
See, e.g.,
Bowling Proprietors Association of America, WAFLA. The Department has clearly stated—both in the preamble and regulatory text—that the two core factors are the first properly considered and most important in making the proper classification—and that the other factors such as permanence are “less probative and, in some cases, may not be probative at all, and thus are highly unlikely, either individually or collectively, to outweigh the combined probative value of the two core factors.” § 795.105(c). Thus, it should be clear that a long-standing relationship alone would not disqualify an individual from recognition as an independent contractor under the economic reality test.
The Department does not believe it is necessary to provide any additional guidance on this issue or to establish a more rigid approach that prioritizes the definite or indefinite nature of the work
(
printed page 75702)
(including discrete “engagements”) over the duration of the working relationship between the parties, as requested by some commenters. In response to similar comments received during the rulemaking for the 2021 Rule, the Department similarly declined to change the regulatory text. At the time, the Department noted that because the focus of the economic realities test is not on technical formalities, it may be that a long relationship could be evidence of permanence despite a contract with a definite end, and an employer may have a permanent relationship with an employee despite requiring the employee to enter into annual employment contracts or a potential employer may have a long-term relationship reflected in several short-term contracts.
[
325
]
Although the Department viewed indefiniteness as a strong indicator of permanence, it still viewed the length of a working relationship as relevant to this factor. The Department continues to believe this is the appropriate view and proper approach.
Second, the Department agrees with the commenters that emphasized that case law supports recognizing that the seasonal nature of work is not necessarily associated with independent contractor status. Indeed, the regulatory text for this factor explicitly states that “the seasonal nature of work by itself would not necessarily indicate independent contractor classification.” § 795.105(d)(2)(ii). The Department explained in the NPRM that the seasonal nature of work would not indicate independent contractor status where the worker's position is permanent for the duration of the relevant season and where the worker has done the same work for multiple seasons.
[
326
]
Additionally, as the Department explained in the 2021 Rule and the NPRM, “in certain industries where employees are often employed for short periods, a short term of employment would not indicate independent contractor status.”
[
327
]
Regarding the issue of worker choice versus continuity requirements imposed by an employer, the Department does not believe that further explanation in the regulatory text for the permanence factor is necessary. The Department agrees with the commenters who posited that whether a work relationship is exclusive is best considered under the control factor, and it sees these types of employer-imposed continuity requirements as akin to requirements that workers work for that employer rather than for others. Rather than blurring these concepts by considering them under both the control and permanence factors, the Department elects to maintain consideration of these concepts under control. Further, as explained when responding to similar comments in the 2021 Rule, “explicitly stating that a relationship is not permanent whenever the worker chooses for it to be long-term is not accurate. After all, every employee to some extent chooses whether to continue working for their employer, and . . . [a] long-term relationship is always the result of choices by both the potential employer and the worker.”
[
328
]
Finally, as this rule is intended to be generally applicable to all industries, the Department declines to provide additional industry-specific regulatory text or examples on how the permanence factor would be applied in particular industries, as several commenters requested.
See, e.g.,
American Association of Advertising Agencies; IFA; National Restaurant Association; WAFLA. The Department believes that the regulation discussing permanence is generally understandable and applicable in all industries. Accordingly, the Department finalizes § 795.105(d)(2)(ii) as proposed.
3. Whether the Work Is Part of an Integrated Unit of Production (§ 795.105(d)(2)(iii))
In § 795.105(d)(2)(iii), the Department proposed to return to considering “whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.” This factor weighs in favor of an individual being an independent contractor “to the extent his or her work is segregable from the potential employer's production process” and weighs in favor of an individual being an employee “to the extent his or her work is a component of the potential employer's integrated production process for a good or service.” This factor is “different from the concept of the importance or centrality of the individual's work to the potential employer's business.”
As the NPRM explained, the Department believes the “integrated unit” framework is more probative of whether a worker is economically dependent on the potential employer for work than the 2024 Rule's consideration of whether the work is “an integral part of the employer's business.” The NPRM further explained that the 2024 Rule's inquiry into whether the work is “critical, necessary, or central to the potential employer's principal business” lacks sufficient precision for the modern economy.
[
329
]
Most business-side commenters expressed support for the “integrated unit” factor as compared to the “integral part” framework.
See, e.g.,
American Association of Advertising Agencies; American Society of Travel Advisors; CWI; FSI; Independent Bakers Association; Instacart; Littler WPI; Private Care Association; ShiftKey. For example, SHRM stated that this framework “more accurately captures the distinction between independent contractors and employees and provides a clearer, more administrable standard for worker classification.” Coalition to Promote Independent Entrepreneurs observed that “whether a specific service is a component of a client's integrated production process for a good or service is readily apparent to an independent contractor and the client at the outset,” while the “integral part” analysis “interjects profound uncertainty into worker-status determinations” by requiring two highly factual determinations—defining the potential employer's “principal business” and assessing whether the worker's services are “critical, necessary, or central” to that principal business.
See also
IFA (“[B]usinesses do not pay employees or independent contractors to engage in work that is not in some sense critical or necessary to their operations.”); Flex Association (“Businesses that pay for non-critical, non-essential, unnecessary work tend not to stay in business very long. So the work's importance says very little about a worker's classification.”).
Some commenters expressed uncertainty regarding the meaning of “integrated unit of production” as applied in the modern service-oriented, technology-based economy.
See, e.g.,
Littler WPI (stating that “a `production line' analogy is of limited usefulness in an economy becoming more and more service-oriented and technology-based”); Richard Reibstein (asking the Department to clarify this factor using “words that include businesses that provide services”). A small number of commenters suggested that this factor should be eliminated altogether due to the difficulty of defining a potential employer's “production process” in the modern economy.
See
National Home
(
printed page 75703)
Delivery Association (“Despite a step in the right direction, NHDA believes this factor has little probative value in today's service-based economy and should be eliminated altogether.”); Institute for the American Worker (“If the Department determines, after considering comments, that the integrated-unit factor remains difficult to apply consistently even in its corrected form, we would alternatively urge the Department to eliminate this factor from the analysis altogether.”).
Several worker-side commenters criticized the departure from the “integral part” framework and its consideration of the centrality of the work, which they described as more consistent with Supreme Court and circuit court precedent.
See, e.g.,
AFL-CIO; AFSCME; Coalition of State Officials; NWJP. These commenters criticized the relative narrowness of the “integrated unit” approach and the relegation of this factor to non-core status.
See, e.g.,
AFL-CIO (asserting that this rule would permit employers to “label essential functions such as delivery, driving, warehousing, and customer service as peripheral or externally provided, even where those functions define the business itself”); Farmworker Justice (emphasizing the centrality of farmworkers' role in farming operations).
Having considered these comments, the Department adopts the “integrated unit” factor as proposed. As the NPRM explained, the Department believes that the Supreme Court's articulation of this factor in
Rutherford Food
—which considered whether the work is “part of the [potential employer's] integrated unit of production,” 331 U.S. at 729—better reflects how it considered this factor in both
Rutherford Food
and
Silk.
The “integral part” language in
Silk
was not included among the enumerated factors that the Court identified as “important for decision.” 331 U.S. at 716. To the extent it can be read as such a factor, it was not very probative because both groups of workers at issue in that case were “integral,” but one group of workers were employees and the other independent contractors.
Id.
at 717-19. Elsewhere in
Silk,
the Court used “integrated” in relation to the scope of a potential employer's business: “[f]ew businesses are so completely integrated that they can themselves produce the raw material, manufacture and distribute the finished product to the ultimate consumer without assistance from independent contractors.”
Id.
at 714. Thus, it is integration rather than integrality that determines the scope of a potential employer's business and whether it encompasses a specific worker's services.
As it did in the NPRM and in the 2021 Rule, the Department acknowledges that its approach diverges from that taken by most circuit courts. The Department nonetheless finds the divergence appropriate based on how those courts have considered integrality. There are many cases in which integrality bears little weight in the final analysis, demonstrating its lesser probative value.
See Express Sixty-Minutes,
161 F.3d at 305 (finding independent contractor status despite arguments that “the work performed by the drivers is an integral and indispensable part of Express' business”);
Paragon,
884 F.3d at 1237-38 (integrality supported independent contractor status but was outweighed by factors supporting employee status);
Flint Eng'g,
137 F.3d at 1443-44 (finding that rig welders' work was “important” but not reiterating that fact when summarizing the ultimate conclusion that they were employees);
see also Mednick,
508 F.2d at 300-01 (finding “no clear cut conclusion” from the fact that plaintiff's work was “not an integrated part” of the defendant's business but “may have been very useful or even necessary”). There are also some cases in which the integrality of the work is functionally synonymous with its integration into the potential employer's business, such that focusing on integration will have the same result.
See, e.g., Castillo,
704 F.2d at 191 (describing cotton chopping interchangeably as “part of an `integrated economic unit'” and “an integral phase” of the defendant's cotton growing operation);
Antenor,
88 F.3d at 937 (in joint employer context, describing snap bean pickers' work as “a routine line-job integral to the growers' business” and “one part of an `integrated economic unit' operated by the growers”). The critical difference between the two approaches rests in this rule's curtailment of considerations of “importance” or “necessity,” which extend beyond the original meaning of this factor in
Rutherford Food
and fail to provide meaningful guidance.
See Zheng
v.
Liberty Apparel Co.,
355 F.3d 61, 73 (2d Cir. 2003) (“Interpreted broadly, this factor could be said to be implicated in
every
subcontracting relationship [in the joint employer context], because all subcontractors perform a function that a general contractor deems `integral' to a product or a service.”);
Lauritzen,
835 F.2d at 1541 (Easterbrook, J., concurring) (“
Everything
the employer does is `integral' to its business—why else do it? ”).
The divergence recognized above should not be mistaken for divergence regarding the overarching legal framework because consideration of “integrality” is not itself integral to the economic reality test. The Fifth Circuit, for example, typically does not include integrality among its enumerated factors, yet that variation has never been understood to create a circuit split. This rule—like the legal precedent from which it is distilled—is not mechanical, and courts may organize and articulate factors differently while applying the same ultimate inquiry into economic independence. Nor is consideration of whether a worker's services are “integral” to the potential employer's business prohibited by this rule. The economic reality inquiry remains a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis, and § 795.105(d)(2)(iv) permits consideration of facts and factors beyond those enumerated to the extent they indicate whether the worker is operating an independent business or is economically dependent on the potential employer for work. Integrality may be considered when the circumstances make it relevant. For the reasons explained above, however, the Department believes that integrality—understood as the importance, centrality, or necessity of the work—will ordinarily have little or no probative value. Nearly every business obtains work because it regards that work as useful or necessary, including work performed by independent contractors. Treating importance as evidence of employee status tends to produce the same answer regardless of the worker's actual economic independence. This rule does not prohibit consideration of integrality where appropriate but declines to include that generally uninformative consideration among the enumerated factors and instead includes, consistent with Supreme Court precedent, consideration of integration into the potential employer's business.
Regarding the criticisms from the business community, the Department does not believe that applying the “integrated unit” factor poses any special difficulties in the modern economy. As the regulatory text explains, this factor is intended to apply to production processes “for a good or service” and is, therefore, not limited to businesses with production lines and is not incompatible with a service-based economy. The Department recognizes that there may be cases where the scope of a particular business's integrated operation, and whether it encompasses a particular individual's work, may be
(
printed page 75704)
difficult to ascertain. However, the Department does not believe the task is so difficult that it is necessary to exclude a factor that was important to the decision in
Rutherford Food
and that has some bearing on the ultimate inquiry, particularly in cases where the two core factors do not both point toward the same classification.
Beyond expressing general support for or criticisms of the “integrated unit” factor, many business commenters requested specific language to delineate, elevate, or diminish the relevance of certain considerations.
See, e.g.,
Flex Association (requesting four specific criteria to find that a worker is integrated into a potential employer's business); Richard Reibstein (requesting clarification that providing “services that no one else at the company provides” weighs in favor of independent contractor status); Uber (requesting language stating that a potential employer's production process “terminates with a usable product or service” and “does not extend to independent uses of the product”). The Department does not attempt to identify every potentially relevant consideration under this factor, nor will it demarcate any specific consideration as relevant in every case. What is relevant in one case may not be relevant in another. Steering this factor toward specific considerations that may not always be relevant, or perhaps even intelligible as applied to a specific business or service, will only complicate the analysis, diminishing the utility and value of the rule, especially to the Department, to the detriment of the Department's goal of fostering predictable outcomes.
Institute for the American Worker requested the Department to state that this factor “does not weigh against independent contractor status merely because the worker performs the same type of service that the hiring entity provides to its customers.” Whether a worker performing the same type of service as a business is integrated into the business's production process depends on the facts of the case. For example, a waiter who takes orders from, and delivers food to, customers dining in a restaurant performs the same type of service as the restaurant itself,
i.e.,
serving food to the restaurant's customers. The waiter in this scenario is part of the restaurant's integrated production process for food services. On the other hand, a law firm may hire an outside lawyer to represent it in a matter unrelated to the legal services that it provides to its own clients. Despite performing the same type of service as the law firm, the lawyer is not a part of the law firm's integrated production process for legal services. As these examples illustrate, the fact that a worker performs the same type of service as the potential employer may be highly relevant in some cases but not so relevant in others.
U.S. Chamber of Commerce requested that this factor be revised to state that a worker who “performs the majority of services off the premises of the business, including at consumer locations, in transit, or via remote means, is generally not part of an integrated unit of production.” As the Department explained in the 2021 Rule, whether work is performed on the business's physical premises is not always relevant to this factor.
[
330
]
And more generally, as explained in the discussion of possible additional factors below (§ 795.105(d)(2)(iv)), the Department is confident that where the work is performed is not material to the determination of employee or independent contractor status. In any event, there are many instances where an employee may be part of an integrated unit despite performing work at a different location than other employees, including at consumer locations and in transit, and vice versa.
See, e.g., Whitaker House,
366 U.S. at 32 (holding that workers who produced copies of a sample product at home were employees);
Thomas
v.
Brock,
617 F. Supp. 526, 535 (W.D.N.C. 1985),
aff'd in part, modified in part on other grounds,
810 F.2d 448 (4th Cir. 1987) (door-to-door seller of cookies and candy was “completely integrated” in the distributor's business). There are also instances where a worker may perform work on a business's physical premises that is discrete, segregable, and unrelated to any integrated process.
See, e.g.,
Richard Reibstein (suggesting that “a landscaper that mows the lawn on a company's suburban headquarters” is a “classic misapplication of this factor”). Thus, although the location of the work may inform whether particular work is part of the integrated unit of production, it is not always the case that it will be probative.
Some commenters requested the Department to clarify that a worker's use of systems or technologies provided by a business does not mean the worker is part of the business's integrated unit of production. Securities Industry Financial Markets Association (financial advisors' use of a broker-dealer's platform to effect securities transactions); U.S. Chamber (workers' use of SI tools or protocols provided by a business). The relevance—whether to the “integrated unit” factor or to any other factor considered under this rule—of a worker's use of technologies provided by a business will depend on all the circumstances of each case. Particularly for technologies that are constantly evolving, it is not possible to draw any firm conclusions about their use in this generally applicable rule.
Some commenters requested clarification that this factor does not depend on whether a worker's output is “commercially significant” or “valuable” to a business.
See
CWI; Instacart. Relatedly, U.S. Chamber of Commerce requested that the Department revise the example in proposed § 795.115(b)(8) to illustrate that a worker may produce work that is important to a business for commercial reasons, such as increasing revenue, without being a component of the business's integrated unit of production. It is true that the commercial value of work does not necessarily make it integrated. For example, a successful advertising campaign can have significant value for a business without necessarily rendering the individual who came up with the campaign a component of the business's integrated operation. The Department believes the regulatory text properly addresses this distinction by differentiating integrated work from work that is merely “important.”
Finally, many commenters requested that the Department clarify, through explanations or examples, how this factor would apply in specific industries, including trucking, construction, financial advising, insurance, food services, and delivery services, or to specific contractual arrangements, such as franchising.
See
American Council of Life Insurers; American Securities Association; Associated Builders and Contractors; IFA; National Restaurant Association; National Retail Federation; OOIDA. Many commenters requested examples involving multi-sided platforms, particularly an example involving a worker who provides services to end-market consumers through a digital platform, modeled after the virtual marketplace company described in WHD Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2 (though the opinion letter used the “integral part” formulation, not the “integrated unit” formulation).
See, e.g.,
Flex Association; Independent Work Coalition; Littler WPI; U.S. Chamber; U.S. Hispanic Business Council. The facts that inform the “integrated unit” factor are too circumstance-specific to apply blanket statements to entire industries or broad types of contractual arrangements. Any particular task that is common in a particular industry may be
(
printed page 75705)
performed in one instance by a worker who is part of an integrated unit of production and in another instance by a segregable unit. In other words, this factor may point in a different direction for workers who perform similar duties in the same industry but who are more or less integrated into the potential employer's processes based on the potential employer's business model. That said, the Department appreciates that examples are helpful to understanding how each factor operates, which is why the Department is readopting the related examples in proposed § 795.115(b)(7) and (8), now reordered to § 795.115(c)(4) and (5), which involve an editor and a journalist respectively.
The Department received some requests to revise or eliminate these examples, including from self-identified freelance writers and editors. One freelance writer, Brittany VanDerBill, requested that the Department eliminate proposed § 795.115(b)(7), which she compared to “prong B of the disastrous ABC test,” referring to the test used in some states which requires work to be outside the usual course of the potential employer's business in order for the worker to be an independent contractor. Another freelance writer, Karen Anderson criticized proposed § 795.115(b)(8) for “suggest[ing] that a freelance journalist shouldn't be submitting anything more than once every two to three weeks, and that the submission must be subjected to being either accepted or rejected by the publisher[.]” U.S. Chamber of Commerce requested that the Department abandon or revise proposed § 795.115(b)(7), specifically objecting to the phrase “entire production process” as a “looser formulation” that risks encompassing nonemployees such as management consultants or lawyers who may have “some kind of `involvement' with a business's `entire production process.'” Three freelance writers and editors submitted a joint comment that was generally supportive of these examples but suggested several modifications.
See
Kim Kavin et al. Among other suggestions, they advised changing the potential employer in both examples from a newspaper to a “media brand” to reflect the types of entities that are more common in the modern technological environment. Regarding proposed § 795.115(b)(7), they asserted that laying out articles should not indicate employee status because modern publishing software allows freelancers to deliver content where layout choices are made simultaneously with the writing. Regarding proposed § 795.115(b)(8), they objected that a frequency of one article submission every 2 to 3 weeks is “as antiquated as the idea of print-only newspapers.” They also criticized proposed § 795.115(b)(8) for suggesting that a freelancer's communications with the potential employer should be limited to a single employee, noting that a freelancer may have many reasons to communicate with several different employees regarding, for example, handling rights to artwork accompanying the freelancer's work or the freelancer's invoice for payment.
Upon consideration of these comments, the Department will retain these examples with modifications. The Department believes the commenters that have requested elimination of these examples have misunderstood them. To be clear, neither of these examples conclude that the worker is an employee or independent contractor. Like all the examples in § 795.115, these examples focus on a single factor. Under this rule, the ultimate determination requires consideration of all the factors, with control and opportunity for profit or loss being the most probative. The fact that one worker's work is part of an integrated unit while another worker's is segregable does not automatically mean that one is an employee and the other is an independent contractor. Therefore, these examples neither resemble an ABC test nor require freelancers to conform their conduct to specific parameters to continue being independent contractors. Finally, the phrase “entire production process” in proposed § 795.115(b)(7) (now § 795.115(c)(4)) is not meant to indicate that the editor is involved in the production process in a generalized or tangential sense but rather the opposite. The editor not only writes articles but also assigns them, reviews and revises them, and publishes them in coordination with other editors. Therefore, the editor is involved in the entire production process and not segregable from it.
Although the Department is retaining these examples, it takes the point made by several freelancers that the proposed regulatory text does not accurately reflect journalistic practices in the digital age. Accordingly, it has made revisions to modernize these examples. First, the Department has changed the context from a newspaper to a digital news outlet to reflect the increasing prominence of online-only media sources. For simplicity and ease of understanding, the Department maintains the focus on a publisher of a single type of content that is generally familiar to the public (news articles). Second, instead of layout decisions, these examples use decisions regarding the timing of publication to illustrate the extent of each worker's integration into the publication's production process, with the editor being responsible for determining when articles will be published and setting deadlines accordingly, while the journalist is responsible only for the specific articles he writes. The purpose of this revision is to reflect digital editorial practices in which individual contributors may make layout decisions without involvement in the overall production process. Third, the Department has deleted the reference to a specific frequency of article submissions in § 795.115(c)(5)(i). The Department did not intend to imply that a specific threshold of productive output would determine whether an individual is part of an integrated production process and therefore omits this reference to avoid confusion. Finally, the Department has revised the sentence in § 795.115(c)(5)(i) describing the journalist's interactions with the potential employer's employees to distill the salient point that the journalist does not work in concert with the employees.
See
86 FR 1196
(noting that employee status is indicated where a worker “performs identical or closely interrelated tasks” as employees);
see also Rutherford Food,
331 U.S. at 726, 729 (finding that workers “work[ing] alongside admitted employees of the plant operator” were part of an integrated economic unit). This sentence as proposed indicated that the journalist communicated with only one of the potential employer's employees, but a journalist may need to communicate with many different persons employed by a single entity on matters relating to his otherwise segregable work. Whether a worker's interactions with employees demonstrate integration will depend more on the content of the communications than the fact of them. As revised, this sentence now shows how the journalist's work is distinct from the employees' rather than how many employees interact with the journalist.
For all the reasons explained above, the Department finalizes § 795.105(d)(2)(iii) as proposed and finalizes the related examples in § 795.115(c)(4) and (5) with modifications.
4. Additional Factors (§ 795.105(d)(2)(iv))
The Department proposed regulatory text in § 795.105(d)(2)(iv) providing that: “Additional factors may be
(
printed page 75706)
relevant in determining whether an individual is an employee or independent contractor for purposes of the FLSA, but only if the factors in some way indicate whether the individual is in business for him- or herself, as opposed to being economically dependent on the potential employer for work.”
[

Advising that certain additional considerations cannot indicate employee status but can indicate independent contractor status would be contrary to the Department's overall goal in this final rule.

However, § 795.105(d)(1)(i) may not apply because the provision of (or contributions to) benefits or portable benefits may not involve the potential employer requiring the individual worker to do anything. And in any event, many of the commenters focused on the voluntary provision of benefits. Indeed, some states have enacted laws so that the provision of (or contributions to) portable benefits to workers does not make them employees, or is not relevant to determining employee status, under those states' laws. For example, earlier in 2026, Georgia and West Virginia joined states like Tennessee, Alabama, and Utah in enacting such laws. The comment from the Senate HELP Committee (Chair and three Majority members) described efforts in states to pass such laws as well as an analogous bill that was introduced in the Senate.
Commenters offered policy arguments in support of this request. For example, the Senate HELP Committee (Chair and three Majority members) asserted that “entities that work with independent workers fear they are restricted from offering portable benefits,” but “labor and employment laws were never intended to prevent workers from accessing benefits,” and “[t]his is backwards-looking and unfairly disadvantages independent workers, as most companies decline opportunities to provide non-employees benefits altogether over fears of expensive litigation.” Littler WPI stated that “businesses fear to provide such benefits to independent contractors as doing so can bring with it obligations of employment status that are often incompatible with the independent contracting relationships freely entered into by individuals and businesses,” and suggested that the Department not “discourage changes in state or other laws that require or permit businesses to provide protections and benefits to their independent contractor partners.” CHRO Association commented that “[s]uch clarification would meaningfully encourage the extension of
(
printed page 75708)
benefits and protections to contingent workers, would further the Department's statutory mission of protecting workers, and would in no way impede the Department's ability to address intentional misclassification where it occurs.”
Having considered the comments, the Department believes that it should counter any perceived disincentive and encourage businesses to provide (or contribute to) benefits for non-employee workers consistent with the growing interest in making portable benefits available, which would benefit workers and society. Accordingly, in the Department's view, whether the potential employer provides (or contributes to) benefits or portable benefits is not relevant in determining whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor. Contrary to Flex Association (which asserted that “a company's decision to participate in a portable benefits program established by a state is not indicative of employment under the FLSA, and, in fact, highly suggests that the worker is an independent contractor”), the Department believes that both the provision and non-provision of benefits should be irrelevant when determining employee or independent contractor status. This is a more balanced approach that does not favor either outcome, consistent with the Department's overall intent in this rulemaking, as explained above, to provide an analysis that does not favor employee or independent contractor outcomes. Thus, the provision of benefits to a worker would not be indicative of employee status, and the non-provision of benefits to a worker or the participation in a portable benefits program geared to non-employee workers would not be indicative of independent contractor status.
[
345
]
Additionally, consistent with the discussion of economic dependence in this rule, the provision or non-provision of benefits to workers is not relevant to whether the worker is economically dependent on the potential employer
for work
(the ultimate inquiry). Whether the worker is provided benefits is often a function of how the potential employer classifies the worker and thus is not necessarily indicative of the economic reality of the worker's working relationship with the potential employer. And providing portable benefits to non-employee workers is a laudable effort to make benefits available to workers for whom benefits were previously not available because of their non-employee status and thus does not reflect the underlying economic reality of those workers' working relationships with potential employers.
[
346
]
For all these reasons, the Department is finalizing § 795.105(d)(2)(iv) as proposed.
H. Primacy of Actual Practice (§ 795.110)
Proposed § 795.110 stated that the actual practice of the parties—of both the individual and the potential employer—is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible. Proposed § 795.110 further stated that an individual's theoretical abilities to negotiate prices or work for competing businesses are less meaningful if, as a practical matter, the individual is prevented from exercising such rights and, likewise, a business's contractual authority to supervise or discipline an individual may be of little relevance if in practice the business never exercises such authority.
As it did in the 2021 Rule, the Department explained that this principle is grounded in the Supreme Court's holding that “ `economic reality' rather than `technical concepts' is to be the test of employment” under the FLSA.
[
347
]
The NPRM further explained that the emphasis on actual practice does not mean that unexercised contractual powers, rights, and freedoms are never relevant but merely less relevant than powers, rights, and freedoms that are actually exercised.
Several worker advocacy organizations criticized this provision for minimizing the significance of a potential employer's unexercised contractual right of control to the question of economic dependence.
See, e.g.,
National Partnership for Women and Families et al.; NWJP. Some commenters emphasized the “implicit threat” that a potential employer may hold over workers where it reserves contractual rights to discipline and terminate them.
See
NWJP (“A right to terminate workers' employment becomes an implicit threat that, of course, makes them more dependent on the business that has that right, regardless of whether a worker ever is terminated.”);
see also
Farmworker Justice (“We encourage the DOL to not discount the ultimate control that a business holds when it has the ability to fire or discipline a worker.”). Some commenters focused on “indirect approaches [to control] like algorithmic management or productivity tracking.” Philadelphia Legal Assistance;
see also
Coalition of State Officials (stating that the Department “ignores the importance of employers' reserved control using modern technology for intense surveillance and algorithmic control of workers”). Coalition of State Officials asserted that the focus on control actually exercised by a potential employer is “read generously, equivalent to the common law standard” and counter to the FLSA's broad standard of employment, citing
New York
v.
Scalia,
490 F. Supp. 3d 748, 786-87 (S.D.N.Y. 2020).
Business commenters generally expressed support for this provision, but several of them requested revisions to address circumstances where a party voluntarily chooses not to exercise contractual rights.
See, e.g.,
CWI; Flex Association. U.S. Chamber of Commerce requested the Department to state that a worker's voluntary choice not to exercise a contractual right either indicates independence or is not determinative of his or her employment status, whereas a business's choice not to exercise a contractual right of control should weigh in favor of independent contractor status. SHRM requested that the Department state that a worker's unexercised contractual rights “affirmatively weigh in favor of independent contractor status,” but that a business's unexercised contractual rights are “materially less probative than actual practice.” Some commenters requested a revision stating that a worker must identify conduct by the potential employer “that, as a matter of fact, prevented the worker from exercising” contractual rights such as the ability to negotiate prices or work for competing businesses. National Home Delivery Association; Scopelitis;
see also
American Bakers Association (requesting that “employee status is suggested only when a potential employer prevented the individual, as a
(
printed page 75709)
matter of contract or fact, from exercising [certain] rights”).
Several labor unions, without specifically addressing § 795.110, supported the importance of looking beyond contractual provisions. IBT stated that “actual practice, not contract labels or unilateral paper designations by employers, controls the classification inquiry.” AFSCME and SEIU invoked Judge Easterbrook's observation that the FLSA is “designed to defeat rather than implement contractual arrangements.”
Lauritzen,
835 F.2d at 1545 (Easterbrook, J., concurring). AFL-CIO criticized the Department for “elevating factors that can be readily shaped through contract design and business structuring,” but did not acknowledge that § 795.110 is designed to ensure that the FLSA is “applied in a way that looks beyond `technical concepts' and contractual labels,” AFL-CIO (quoting
Whitaker House,
366 U.S. at 33).
Having considered the views expressed by commenters, the Department is finalizing § 795.110 as proposed. The Department believes that the primacy of actual practice is a neutral interpretive principle, intended to encompass both workers' and businesses' actual practices, consistent with the way courts and the Department have long applied the FLSA's economic reality test.
See, e.g., Usery,
527 F.2d at 1312 (“It is not significant how one `could have' acted under the contract terms. The controlling economic realities are reflected by the way one actually acts.”). The Department declines commenter suggestions that would disrupt that neutrality by assigning greater weight to one party's unexercised contractual rights but not the other's—both from worker-side commenters placing the emphasis on a business's reserved rights of control and from business-side commenters requesting unequal treatment of individuals' and businesses' decisions not to exercise contractual rights. As the NPRM explained, this provision does not categorically disregard unexercised contractual rights.
[
348
]
Parties may proffer evidence regarding unexercised contractual provisions, and such evidence may well be relevant, even if it is not as relevant as evidence of actual practice.
See, e.g., Saleem,
854 F.3d at 141 (workers' ability to terminate contracts at any time “constituted a significant restriction on the ability of [the potential employers] to exercise control”);
Brant,
43 F.4th at 665-67 (finding that potential employer's “right to gather remotely and to monitor huge quantities of data,” coupled with “constant threat of termination,” favored employee status).
The Department disagrees with Coalition of State Officials' contention that prioritizing control that is actually exercised is equivalent to the common law control test instead of the broader scope of employment that the FLSA requires. In many cases, the actual practices of the parties will establish the existence of an employment relationship despite what a “skillfully devised” contract might suggest.
Silk,
331 U.S. at 715;
see, e.g., Scantland,
721 F.3d at 1313-14 (dismissing the probative value of plaintiffs' contractual right to decline work assignments where they testified that doing so led to threats of termination or being refused future work assignments);
Usery,
527 F.2d at 1312 (contractual right to set hours does not show worker control where the hours are controlled by the potential employer in reality). Furthermore, while the economic reality test is broad in the sense that it covers more workers as a general matter, a reserved right of control that might establish employee status under common-law analysis does not necessarily do so under the economic-reality test. In
Bartels,
the court of appeals concluded that musicians were employees of the dance halls under the common-law test because the contracts gave the halls a right to control their services.
Birmingham
v.
Bartels,
157 F.2d 295, 304 (8th Cir. 1946),
rev'd,
332 U.S. 126 (1947). The Supreme Court reversed, applying the economic reality test to hold that musicians were not employees of the dance halls notwithstanding a contractual stipulation that the halls “shall at all times have complete control of the services which the [musicians] will render.”
Bartels,
332 U.S. at 128 n.1, 132. The Court looked beyond that contractual allocation of control to the circumstances of the parties' relationship as a whole to reach that conclusion.
Id.
at 130-32.
[
349
]
The Department also disagrees with the interpretation suggested by various business commenters that only affirmative conduct by a potential employer to prevent a worker from exercising contractual rights should diminish the relevance of such rights. The extent to which such a right is probative depends on whether it represents a genuine and practicable opportunity, rather than merely appearing in a written agreement. Courts have therefore discounted rights that were hypothetical or could not realistically be exercised.
See, e.g., Hobbs,
946 F.3d at 833 (discounting the proposition that welders “could hypothetically negotiate their rate of pay” where the evidence did not show negotiation in practice);
Keller,
781 F.3d at 808 (finding a genuine dispute of fact concerning whether a technician could work for other companies where his schedule was dictated by circumstances outside his control, including customer locations and availability);
Mitchell
v.
John R. Cowley & Bro., Inc.,
292 F.2d 105, 109 (5th Cir. 1961) (discounting a watchman's contractual right to furnish services to others based on practical constraints affecting his ability to do so). Affirmative interference by the potential employer may be strong evidence that the right lacks practical significance, but such interference is not required. At the same time, a particular worker's voluntary decision not to exercise an otherwise available contractual right does not, standing alone, make that right merely theoretical. Evidence that similarly situated workers exercise the same contractual right may demonstrate that the opportunity is real and practically available even though the particular worker whose status is at issue elects not to pursue it. The relevant inquiry is whether the worker has a genuine ability to exercise the right under the actual circumstances.
Finally, the Department received some requests for minor clarifications or revisions. Some business commenters requested the Department to clarify that “nothing in the proposed rule changes the burden of proof in a challenge to a worker's classification under the FLSA.” National Home Delivery Association; Scopelitis. The Department confirms that nothing in this rule is intended to alter the burden of proof in FLSA misclassification cases. That said, the Department considers it unnecessary to revise proposed § 795.110, which does not address the burden of proof but rather the weight of the evidence. Some business commenters requested the Department to clarify that contractual terms that accurately reflect the actual practices of the parties may be relevant. Flex Association; Instacart; TechNet;
see also
IFA (arguing that contracts are relevant as “one part of the economic reality” and should not be “completely disregarded”). As discussed, this rule does not categorically disregard the relevance of contractual terms. Where the evidence regarding the parties'
(
printed page 75710)
actual practices is consistent with terms of the applicable contractual agreement, such terms may have substantial probative value.
[
350
]
The probative value of such terms follows from their consistency with actual practice. Accordingly, § 795.110 properly confirms the primacy of actual practice.

The Department proposed to revise the regulations addressing employee or independent contractor status under the FMLA and MSPA to clarify that the analysis in part 795 applies when determining employee or independent contractor status under those statutes too. For the FMLA regulations, the Department proposed to revise the definition of “Employee” in
29 CFR 825.102
by adding a statement that “the criteria set forth in §§ 795.105 through 795.110 of this chapter apply to any determination of whether an individual is an employee or independent contractor.” The Department also proposed to revise
29 CFR 825.105(a)
by adding the following sentence: “The criteria set forth in §§ 795.105 through 795.110 of this chapter apply to any determination of whether an individual is an employee or independent contractor.” Additionally, the Department proposed to delete the following sentence in
29 CFR 825.105(a)
: “Mere knowledge by an employer of work done for the employer by another is sufficient to create the employment relationship.” For the MSPA regulations, the Department proposed to revise
29 CFR 500.20(h)(4)
to remove the six economic reality factors (as well as reference to the factors and several case citations) and replace them with a cross-reference providing that questions of employee or independent contractor status under MSPA “should be resolved in accordance with the criteria set forth in §§ 795.105 through 795.110 of this chapter.”
The NPRM explained that both the FMLA and MSPA statutorily incorporate the FLSA's definitions regarding the scope of employment and the Department's FMLA and MSPA regulations recognize that the scope of employment under those statutes is determined by the FLSA.

A. Need for Rulemaking
As explained more fully in section III of this rule, the Department is concerned that the 2024 Rule failed to provide an analysis for distinguishing between independent contractors and employees under the FLSA that was sufficiently clear and led to predictable outcomes. The Department is separately concerned that the 2024 Rule's description of several economic reality factors could have been viewed as setting a higher bar to find independent contractor status than required under the law. Among other harms, an analysis which is ambiguous or perceived as too restrictive of independent contracting can deter
(
printed page 75715)
businesses from engaging with bona fide independent contractors or cause them to unnecessarily classify such individuals as employees—concerns emphasized by many self-identified independent contractors who have participated in the Department's recent rulemakings on this topic.
Accordingly, in this rulemaking, the Department is rescinding the 2024 Rule and largely readopting the 2021 Rule (with some modifications and enhancements), which provided a sharpened economic reality analysis and did not impede successful enforcement actions by the Department to pursue and remedy misclassification of FLSA-covered employees as independent contractors.
[
369
]
Additionally, the Department is revising the regulations addressing employee or independent contractor status under MSPA and the FMLA so that the analysis in part 795 applies when determining employee or independent contractor status under those statutes too.
B. Overview of Estimated Effects
The Department believes that replacing the 2024 Rule with the 2021 Rule is likely to improve the welfare of both workers and businesses on the whole. With respect to businesses, the Department believes that the improved clarity provided by the rule would increase the efficiency of the labor market, allowing businesses to be more productive and decreasing their litigation burden. With respect to workers, broadly speaking, this rule would likely have three categories of potential effects.
First, this rule would make it easier for the millions of individuals who currently work as independent contractors and those who hire them to comply with the law. Compliance cost savings would be shared between the independent contractors and businesses for which they work.
Second, legal clarity may encourage firms to create independent contractor arrangements for roles that did not previously exist, which may attract workers who otherwise would not work in that field. Such job creation would benefit workers and firms alike.
[
370
]
Third, as a result of the improved clarity of the rule, businesses might convert some existing positions from employee status to independent contractor status. Although the Department maintains that the streamlined core factor analysis in this rule is neither more nor less permissive of independent contractor relationships as compared to the Department's prior analysis,
[
371
]
the Department expects that this rule could reduce to some degree the voluntary classification of independent contractors as employees—a practice several commenters called “overclassification.”
[
372
]
This refers to situations where businesses classify workers who are in business for themselves (and thus independent contractors) as employees to avoid legal risk (in the event that the business does not satisfy the FLSA's requirements).
[
373
]
This rule would provide the greatest legal certainty to employers classifying a worker as an independent contractor if the worker substantially controls the work and has a meaningful opportunity for profit or loss—a scenario that, to the Department's knowledge, no federal appellate court has ever found to be an FLSA employment relationship.
Businesses would only reclassify workers classified as employees into independent contractors if the clarity provided by this rule outweighs legal risk. Any benefit to businesses of modified classifications would need to outweigh the costs, including any autonomy they cede to workers in such arrangements and any costs associated with implementation or modifying the classification itself, and such a relationship would need to be compatible with their business models. Further, in many cases, workers would have a choice of whether to agree to the new independent contractor arrangement in the sense that the worker could decide to end his or her relationship with a business unless he or she remains classified as an employee. AFSCME submitted a comment countering the Department's position that workers would have the freedom to choose to enter into independent contractor arrangements, asserting that the most vulnerable and least informed of workers would either accept such reclassification willingly, are coerced to accept, or are unaware of how their employers should classify them. Conversely, the Chamber of Progress submitted a comment emphasizing that many workers prefer the option of an independent contractor arrangement because it affords them greater autonomy and schedule flexibility. The overall effect of job conversion on workers would be ambiguous and could vary from worker to worker, but the Department expects that any reclassification of workers classified as employees into independent contractors attributable to this rulemaking would be minimal, as the Department is not aware of significant reclassification that occurred when the 2021 Rule was in effect, nor did commenters note that any significant reclassification occurred.
The Department has attempted to place the magnitude of these potential impacts into context. Drawing on the best available evidence from the Contingent Worker Supplement (CWS), labor market studies of flexible work (Mas and Pallais, 2017; Chen et al., 2019),
[
374
]
and a recent evaluation of a 2019 California law that changed that state's standard for determining independent contractor classification in a manner that restricted independent contracting
[
375
]
(Palagashvili et al.,
(
printed page 75716)
2024),
[
376
]
the Department estimates that the number of independent contractors could increase by 1 to 3 percentage points following the implementation of this rule. On today's labor force of approximately 25 million workers who rely on independent contracting as their primary or secondary job,
[
377
]
this would represent between 0.25 million and 0.75 million additional independent contracting relationships, with a central estimate of 0.5 million.
[
378
]
The rationale for this estimate is explained in greater detail in section VI.E.3.
The Department assumes that this increase would occur almost entirely through new labor force entry rather than through the reclassification of existing employees. This assumption reflects Palagashvili et al.'s findings that, while AB 5 reduced independent contracting, there was no statistically significant evidence that it increased traditional employment, contrary to the impact that may have been anticipated as the law discouraged independent contractor classification.
[
379

This suggests few independent contractors were “switched” to traditional employees as a result of California's law. The Department believes the converse would be true here—that the reclassification of employees to independent contractors would remain small while new entry of independent contractors would be more significant (though lower, in terms of magnitude, than the converse impact under AB 5). Indeed, the final rule's effect on reclassification should be even smaller than under AB 5 because, unlike AB 5, it would not change the underlying classification standard (
i.e.,

As such, permissible reclassification would be limited to workers who already possess the characteristics of being in business for themselves but are classified as employees due to perceived legal uncertainty. Meanwhile, employers that are holding back from engaging independent contractors would have the clarity to expand opportunities, creating genuine new participation.
The Department acknowledges that these estimates are subject to significant uncertainty. The precise number of new entrants, the distribution of reclassified positions across industries and firm sizes, and the demographic characteristics of affected workers cannot be reliably projected.

C. Current Number of Independent Contractors
The Department estimated that there were 24.8 million independent contractors in the United States in 2023, the most recent year of data available.
[
381
]
As explained above, the Department believes the number of independent contractors for purposes of the FLSA, MSPA, and FMLA would increase as a result of this rule. There are a variety of estimates of the number of independent contractors, and these span a wide range based on methodologies and how the population is defined. In its comment, the American Association of Advertising Agencies cited a survey conducted by the Upwork Research Institute that claims 64 million Americans performed freelance work in 2023.
[
382
]
The Americans for Prosperity Foundation referenced a study by Matthew Zane in its comment that estimates that there are approximately 70.4 million freelance workers in the United States.
[
383
]
The Department believes that the Current Population Survey (CPS) Contingent Worker Supplement (CWS) is the most appropriate estimate of the number of independent contractors; however, there are potential biases in these data, as noted. Estimates from other sources are presented as well to demonstrate the potential range.
1. Department of Labor Estimate
The CPS is conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau and published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). The sample includes approximately 60,000 households and is nationally representative. Periodically since 1995, and most recently in 2023, the CPS has included a supplement to collect data on contingent and alternative employment arrangements. Based on the CWS, there were 11.9 million independent contractors in 2023, amounting to 7.4 percent of workers.
[
384
]
The CWS measures those who say that their independent contractor job is their primary job and that they worked at the independent contractor job in the survey's reference week. However, while the Department refers to the CWS measure of independent contractors throughout this analysis, due to the survey's design it should be uniformly recognized as representing a constrained subsection of the entire independent contractor pool. Due to its methodological constraints, the CWS measure should be differentiated from other, more comprehensive measures.
The BLS's estimate of independent contractors includes workers “who are identified as independent contractors, independent consultants, or freelance workers, regardless of whether they are identified as wage and salary workers or self-employed.” Workers reporting that they are self-employed are asked: “Are you self-employed as an independent contractor, independent consultant, freelance worker, or something else?” Those identified as wage and salary workers in the basic CPS are asked: “Last week, were you working as an independent contractor, an independent consultant, or a freelance worker?”
The Department believes that the CWS offers an appropriate lower bound for the number of independent contractors. However, there are several possible limitations in this data. It is important to note that independent contractors are identified in the CWS in the context of the respondent's main job (
i.e.,
the job with the most hours).
[
385
]
Therefore, the estimate of independent contractors does not include those who may be employees for their primary jobs but also work as independent contractors for a secondary or tertiary job. This is likely the largest limiting factor in the data when trying to estimate the population of workers doing any work as an independent contractor. For example, Lim et al. (2019) estimates that for 48 percent of independent contractors, such work is their primary source of income.
[
386
]
Applying this estimate to the 11.9 million independent contractors estimated from the CWS results in 24.8 million independent contractors.
[
387
]
The CWS's large sample size results in small sampling error. However, the questionnaire's design may result in some non-sampling errors. For example, one potential limitation of the data is that the CWS includes information to calculate estimates of the prevalence of independent contractors at a single point in time, that is, during a specified week (generally the week prior to the interview). These numbers will thus underestimate the prevalence of independent contracting over a longer timeframe, which may better capture the size of the population.
[
388
]
For example, Farrell and Greig (2016) used a randomized sample of 1 million Chase customers to estimate prevalence of the Online Platform Economy.
[
389
]
They
(
printed page 75718)
found that “[a]lthough 1 percent of adults earned income from the Online Platform Economy in a given month, more than 4 percent participated over the three-year period.” However, a factor of four is likely too large of an adjustment because a 3-year period does not represent the current workforce any more than does a 1-week period, and because there is likely more week-to-week volatility in participation in the Online Platform Economy than among independent contractors.
CWS also uses proxy responses, which may underestimate the number of independent contractors. The RAND American Life Panel (ALP) survey conducted a supplement in 2015 to mimic the CPS CWS questionnaire. The results of the survey were summarized by Katz and Krueger (2018).
[
390
]
This survey found that independent contractors comprise 7.2 percent of workers.
[
391
]
Katz and Krueger identified two primary factors to explain the 0.5 percentage point difference in magnitude between the 2017 CWS and the ALP: (1) cyclical conditions and (2) differences in survey methods (
e.g.,
the use of self-responses only in the ALP supplement). The first factor does not reflect a bias in either survey or estimate, whereas the second factor
may
reflect an underestimate in the CWS estimate. Therefore, the Department believes a reasonable upper-bound on the potential bias due to the use of proxy responses in the CWS is 0.5 percentage points (7.2 versus 6.7).
[
392
]
Another potential source of bias in the CWS data is that some respondents may not self-identify as independent contractors, and others who self-identify may be improperly classified. There are reasons to believe that some workers, who are legally considered independent contractors, would not self-identify as such. For example, individuals who do only informal work may not view themselves as independent contractors.
[
393
]
In the CWS, one person answers the survey questions about everyone living in the household. Thus, respondents provide data about themselves and others living with them. People who report about other household members may not be able to answer all questions about others' employment arrangements.
[
394
]
Conversely some workers misclassified as independent contractors may answer in the affirmative, despite not truly being independent contractors. The prevalence of misclassification is unknown, but it is generally understood to be common. NELP conducted a literature review of federal studies and state-level audits estimating misclassification of employees as independent workers and found that the share of employers misclassifying workers ranged from 10 percent to 30 percent.
[
395
]
Because reliable data on the potential magnitude of these biases are unavailable, the Department has not calculated any estimates of how these biases may impact the estimated number of independent contractors.
Because the CWS estimate represents only the number of workers who worked as independent contractors on their primary job during the survey reference week, the Department applied the research literature and adjusted this measure to include workers who are independent contractors in a secondary job or who were excluded from the CWS estimate due to other factors. As noted above, integrating the estimated proportions of workers who are independent contractors on secondary or otherwise excluded jobs produces an estimate of 24.8 million. Given the prevalence of independent contractors who work sporadically and earn minimal income, adjusting the estimate according to these sources captures some of this population. It is likely that this figure is still an underestimate of the true independent contractor pool.
