D. Potential Costs
The Department considered several costs in evaluating the rule. The Department quantified regulatory familiarization costs and estimated that they will total $495.7 million in Year 1. Other potential costs, including those raised by commenters, were not quantified, for reasons explained in the sections that follow.
1. Regulatory Familiarization Costs
Regulatory familiarization costs represent direct costs to businesses associated with reviewing a new regulation. To estimate the total regulatory familiarization costs imposed, the Department used (1) the number of establishments and government entities; (2) the wage rate for the employees reviewing the rule; and (3) the number of hours that it estimates employers would spend reviewing the rule. This section presents the calculation for establishments first and then the calculation for independent contractors.
Regulatory familiarization costs may be a function of the number of establishments or the number of firms.
[
402
]
Presumably, the headquarters of a firm would conduct the regulatory review for businesses with multiple locations and may also require some locations to familiarize themselves with the regulation at the establishment level. Other firms may either review a rule to consolidate key takeaways for their affiliates, or they may rely entirely on outside experts to evaluate a rule and relay the relevant information to their organization (
e.g.,
a chamber of commerce). The Department used the number of establishments to estimate the fundamental pool of regulated entities—which is larger than the number of firms. This assumes that regulatory familiarization occurs at both the headquarters and establishment levels.
There may be differences in familiarization cost by the size of establishments; however, the analysis does not assess different costs for establishments of different sizes. Furthermore, the analysis does not revise down for states where the laws may more stringently limit who may be an independent contractor (such as California) and thus this rule will have little to no effect on classifications in those states.
[
403
]
To estimate the number
(
printed page 75720)
of establishments incurring regulatory familiarization costs, the Department used the Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB).
[
404
]
In 2022, the most recent year available, there were 8.3 million establishments. These data were supplemented with the 2022 Census of Government that reports 90,888 local government entities, and 51 state and federal government entities for a total universe of 8,389,450 establishments and governments.
[
405
]
The applicable universe used by the Department for assessing familiarization costs of this final rule is all establishments that engage independent contractors, which is a subset of the universe of all establishments. In 2019, Lim et al. used extensive IRS data to model the independent contractor market and found that 34.7 percent of firms hire independent contractors.
[
406
]
These data are based on annual tax filings, so the dataset includes firms that may contract for only parts of a year. Multiplying the universe of establishments and governments by 35 percent results in 2.91 million entities.
[
407
]
The Department did not estimate familiarization costs for companies that may decide to work with independent contractors only after this rule is finalized, because they would need to familiarize themselves with the current legal framework even in the absence of this rule.
[
408
]
As stated above, even without this rule any firm that does not currently engage any independent contractors but chooses to do so in the future would have to familiarize itself in the baseline case, so this rule does not impact those firms. Essentially, it would be reasonable to assume that any firm without independent contractors that reviews this rule and ultimately decides to hire independent contractors is doing so because the firm believes the new relationship will be beneficial. Such a situation would result in net benefits to the employer that compensate for any familiarization costs.
The Department assumes that a Compensation, Benefits, and Job Analysis Specialist (SOC 13-1141) (or a staff member in a similar position) will review the rule.
[
409
]
According to the most recent Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) estimates, these workers had a mean wage of $40.54 per hour.
[
410
]
Given the clarification to the Department's interpretation of who is an employee and who is an independent contractor, the Department assumes that it will take on average about 1 hour to review the final rule. Based on prior rulemakings, the Department believes that an hour, on average, is appropriate. Assuming benefits are paid at a rate of 42 percent of the base wage, and overhead costs are 17 percent of the base wage, the reviewer's effective hourly rate is $64.46; thus, the average cost per establishment would be $64.46.
[
411
]
Therefore, the undiscounted regulatory familiarization costs for establishments in Year 1 are estimated to be $187.6 million ($64.46 × 2,911,139). Regulatory familiarization costs in future years are assumed to be de minimis. This amounts to a 10-year annualized cost of $20.1 million at a discount rate of 7 percent.
For regulatory familiarization costs for independent contractors, the Department uses its estimate of up to 24.8 million independent contractors and assumes each independent contractor will spend an average of 30 minutes to review the regulation. The average time spent by independent contractors is estimated to be shorter than for establishments and governments. This difference is in part because the Department believes independent contractors will likely rely on summaries of the key elements of the rule made available by the Department, worker advocacy groups, media outlets, and accountancy and consultancy firms, as has occurred with other rulemakings. This time is valued at $24.85, which is the median hourly wage rate for independent contractors in the CWS of $23.94 updated to 2025 dollars using the gross domestic product (GDP) deflator.
[
412 413
]
Therefore, the undiscounted regulatory familiarization costs to independent contractors in Year 1 are estimated to be $308.05 million ($24.85 × 0.5 hour × 24.8 million). The total one-time undiscounted regulatory familiarization costs for establishments, governments, and independent contractors are estimated to be $495.7 million. Regulatory familiarization costs in future years are assumed to be de minimis. Employers and independent contractors will continue to familiarize themselves with the applicable legal framework, so this rulemaking is not expected to impose costs after the first year. This amounts to a 10-year annualized cost of $51.1 million at a discount rate of 3 percent or $53.0 million at a discount rate of 7 percent.
2. Other Costs
Aside from the familiarization costs described above, it is possible that the rule will result in additional costs. In the NPRM, the Department invited public comment on other potential costs of this rule. Apart from concerns over potential changes that would qualify as transfer effects (addressed in section VI.F.), commenter feedback on the potential costs of this rule generally fell into four categories: impacts to tax revenues; impacts on competition; impacts on minorities and women; and impacts on employer provided benefits. The Department evaluated all of the potential costs that were identified and examined many of the citations provided. Upon review, the Department was unable to confirm or substantiate any of these alleged cost categories in its own research. Therefore, in this section of the analysis, the Department addresses the points raised and discusses the qualitative merits but does not quantify estimates for inclusion in its top line figures.

The Department notes that this rule will not change the underlying legal standard for who is an employee or independent contractor, and that any reclassification of existing employees as independent contractors will not be substantial (and will involve to some extent workers who were already in business for themselves,

b. Comments Relating to Fair Competition
Mechanical Contractors Association of America (MCAA), joined in substance by several individual commenters, asserted that the rule will “accelerate the race to the bottom” in the construction and mechanical contracting industry. MCAA stated that construction contractors relying on the independent contractor business model “derive an almost 50% cost advantage over MCAA members and other ethical contractors” that invest in a skilled workforce, and cited estimates that the widespread industry use of independent contractor classification “allows these companies to avoid approximately $2.98 billion per year in Social Security and Medicare taxes,” “causes an estimated $1.74 billion annual shortfall in state workers' compensation programs and results in annual state unemployment insurance shortfalls of over $700 million.” MCAA further estimated that construction workers classified as independent contractors lose between $12,440.84 and $19,526.77 in annual wages compared to similarly-situated employees, and commented that easing independent contractor classification would make it easier for firms to engage “undocumented workers because businesses are not required to verify the work authorization of independent contractors.”
NABTU raised substantially similar concerns, citing additional data on the labor cost differentials that make misclassification attractive to construction employers. NABTU cited studies finding that employers who misclassify workers save as much as 30 percent in labor costs, and a Michigan study finding a labor cost differential of 20 to 40 percent of payroll when contractors avoid unemployment insurance tax, workers' compensation premiums, the employer share of Social Security, and pension or medical insurance, with avoided workers' compensation premiums alone amounting to as much as 50 percent of wages in some trades. NABTU cited a range of state-level misclassification-rate studies, including findings of 73 percent among Michigan residential construction workers, one-third of construction workers in North Carolina and Texas, 16 percent in Minnesota, 18 percent in Iowa, and one in six construction workers in California. NABTU added that because materials and equipment costs are largely standardized in construction, labor cost savings from misclassification translate directly into a substantial competitive advantage in bidding, disadvantaging contractors who properly classify their workers.
This rule does not alter the underlying legal standard, the economic reality test, and is not intended to make independent contractor classification more permissive; rather, it clarifies how the existing test should be applied. The Department's cost-benefit analysis in this section addresses regulatory familiarization, increased clarity, and litigation cost savings; it does not attempt to quantify the estimates MCAA and NABTU cite regarding existing industry-wide misclassification, because those estimates describe the current baseline level of misclassification under existing law rather than a cost attributable to this rulemaking. The Department notes that the wide range of state-specific misclassification-rate estimates NABTU cites (16 percent to 73 percent depending on the state and study) itself reflects substantial measurement variability that advises caution in attributing any particular figure to this rule's effect. To the extent misclassification already occurs under the applicable legal standards, the Department notes that such conduct is wrong and that resulting violations of the FLSA can be remedied regardless of this rule, which addresses the classification standard rather than the availability of enforcement against violators.

E. Potential Benefits and Cost Savings
This rule is expected to result in various benefits and cost savings. For example, this rule will increase clarity concerning whether a worker is an employee or independent contractor under the FLSA, which in turn could lead to more consistent classification outcomes while reducing compliance and litigation costs for firms that engage independent contractors. Relatedly, workers may benefit from having more clarity about their rights related to their work status. Additional benefits may accrue due to increases in availability of services across various sectors, constituting a consumer surplus. Finally, due to increased clarity, there could be a reduction in FLSA litigation involving alleged misclassification.
1. Increased Clarity
The Department anticipates that this rule will increase clarity concerning whether a worker should be classified as an employee or as an independent contractor under the FLSA. This will reduce the burden faced by employers, potential employers, and workers in understanding the distinction and how the working relationship should be classified. It is unclear exactly how much time would be saved, but the Department provides some quantitative estimates to provide a sense of the magnitude. The importance of increased clarity is noted by an article authored by Caitlin Kapolas on behalf of Lift HCM which notes that misclassification due to lack of clarity can result in fines, back taxes, and potential lawsuits (not necessarily under the FLSA)—all consequences businesses can avoid with proper worker classification.
[
417
]
The Department expects that this rule will produce cost savings by clarifying the classification process. To quantify this cost-savings, the following variables need to be defined and estimated: (1) the number of new employer-worker relationships being assessed to determine the appropriate classification; (2) the amount of time saved per assessment; and (3) an average wage rate for the time spent. The Department estimates this will result in an undiscounted annual cost savings of $681.4 million. The Department began with its estimate of the number of independent contractors as the basis for estimating the number of new relationships. As discussed, according to the CWS, there were 11.9 million workers in 2023 who were independent contractors in their primary job. Adjusting this figure to account for independent contractors in their secondary job results in 24.8 million independent contractors. According to Lim et al. (2019), in 2016 the average number of 1099-MISC forms issued per independent contractor was 1.43.
[
418
]
Therefore, the Department assumes the average independent contractor has 1.43 jobs per year. This number does not account for the workers who do not file taxes, a recognized limitation in the cited study. Because it is unclear whether those who do not file taxes would have a higher or lower number of jobs per year, the Department does not believe that this limitation biases the estimate in either direction. Multiplying these two numbers (1.43 jobs per year × 24.8 million independent contractors) results in an estimated 35.5 million new independent contractor relationships. A subset of new independent contractor relationships will have time savings associated with the rule. Such a reduction is difficult to quantify because it is unclear how many establishments and independent contractors will realize benefits of increased clarity. It is also possible that the increased clarity of classifying workers will lead to compound effects that generate far greater cost-savings over time. Nonetheless, because it is possible that only a subset of new independent contractor relationships receive the cost savings associated with increased clarity, the Department has reduced the number in the estimate by 25 percent.
[
419
]
This results in 26.6 million new independent contractor relationships with cost savings to both the engaging firm and the independent contractor.
[
420
]
Following a similar methodology to the 2021 Rule, the Department has assumed that employers would save 20 minutes of time and independent contractors would save 10 minutes per each new independent contractor relationship.
[
421
]
These numbers are small because they represent the marginal time savings for each relationship, not the entire time necessary to identify whether an independent contractor relationship holds.
To estimate the cost savings due to the increased clarity that the rule provides, the Department applies the following estimates. For employers, this time is valued at a loaded hourly wage rate of $64.46. This is the mean hourly rate of Compensation, Benefits & Job Analysis Specialists (13-1141) from the OEWS multiplied by 1.63 to account for benefits and overhead. For independent contractors, this time is valued at $24.85 per hour (median wage rate for
(
printed page 75724)
independent contractors in the CWS of $23.94 adjusted to 2025 dollars using the GDP deflator). Using these numbers, the Department estimates that contracting firms would save $571.3 million annually and independent contractors would save $110.1 million annually due to increased clarity. In sum, this is estimated to be an undiscounted annualized cost savings of $681.4 million. The Department assumes the parameters used in this cost savings estimate would remain constant over time. This assumes no growth in independent contracting, no real wage growth, and no subsequent innovation in the employer-worker relationship. These assumptions facilitate simplicity of calculation.

The Department multiplied the number of cases avoided during the quarter by 4 to determine the number of cases avoided over the course of the year. This results in an estimate of 40 cases related to independent contractor disputes avoided annually. This estimate of reduction in the number of independent contractor lawsuits filed does not take into account any reduction in filings resolved before litigation or by alternative dispute resolution, neither of which are captured in PACER data.
b. Average Litigation Cost per Case
The Department applied an estimate of litigation costs of $331,014 per case.
[

To obtain this estimate, the Department conducted a search for FLSA cases in the aforementioned sub-sample of 40 cases that contained sufficient litigation cost information to estimate the average costs of litigation in the Westlaw Case Evaluator tool and on PACER to ascertain how much plaintiffs in these cases were paid for attorney fees, administrative fees, or other costs, apart from any monetary damages

After determining the plaintiff's total litigation costs for each case, the Department then doubled the figures to account for litigation costs that the defendant employers incurred. 3. Increased Labor Force Entry
The Department anticipates that most benefits of this rule will arise from new labor force entry. A recent assessment of a 2019 California law (AB 5) that changed the standard for determining independent contractor classification under that state's law in a manner that restricted independent contracting found that self-employment fell by 10.5 percent in affected occupations and overall employment fell by 4.4 percent in affected occupations.
[
428
]
The Department believes this rule will have an effect in the opposite direction because it will be viewed as less restrictive of independent contracting than the 2024 Rule. However, this labor force effect would be smaller in magnitude because the change to California's independent contractor analysis codified under AB 5 was more substantial than the change to the Department's guidance regarding the analysis under Federal wage and hour law that could occur as a consequence of this rule, which will not change the underlying classification standard (
i.e.,
the economic reality test) and would primarily add clarity. Additionally, this rule will not likely impact some individuals operating in states that have tests under those states' own laws that are more restrictive of independent contracting, though the exact offsetting impact of such state laws is difficult to determine because of significant variation in state laws' exemptions and applications.
[
429
]
Accordingly, the Department estimates that the number of independent contractors will increase by 1 to 3 percent.
As explained, the Department assumes this increase results from independent contractors entering the workforce. That assumption is based on Palagashvili et al.'s finding that there was no statistically significant evidence that AB 5 increased traditional employment—suggesting that few independent contractors switched to traditional employment—but that AB 5 resulted in a statistically significant decrease of independent contractors in the labor force.
[
430
]
The converse effect will be an increase in independent contractors in the labor force without significant reclassification of employees to independent contractors. The Department acknowledges that, due to data limitations and complexities involving the interpretation of different state labor laws, the Department might be overestimating or underestimating the potential impact of this rule on the number of independent contractors and the overall labor force. Also, Palagashvili et al., admit a lack of parallel trends for the pre-treatment period—which raises questions about the reliability of their difference-in-difference identification strategy.
Using the above estimate of 24.8 million independent contractors, the Department's assumption results in between 248,000 and 744,000 (1 and 3 percent of all independent contractors respectively) new workers entering the workforce as independent contractors, with half being full-time and half being part-time independent contractors.
[
431
]
Using the above hourly wage estimate of $24.85 for full-time independent contractors and assuming that each works full-time (40 hours per week for 52 weeks per year), the Department estimates that each new full-time worker will have the opportunity to earn $51,690 per year. Using the median wage estimate of $415.17 weekly for part-time independent contractors and assuming they work year-round,
[

the Department estimates that each new part-time independent contractor will have the opportunity to earn $21,589 per year. Earnings are an intermediate result toward the goal of estimating worker surplus, which is a net value amount that accounts for the opportunity cost of time and effort. Bartik (2015) estimates such net value to range from 10 to 19 percent of earnings.

Based on this finding, the Department assigns a midpoint value of 14.5 percent to total earnings to quantify the social benefit derived from increased earnings. Assuming that the number of independent contractors increases by the central estimate of 2 percent, this results in estimated additional undiscounted total earnings of approximately $131.7 billion. Applying the 14.5 percent estimate of societal value to this finding yields a societal benefit attributable to those additional undiscounted earnings of $26.3 billion (for 496,000 new entries evenly split between full-time and part-time workers) over 10 years or an annualized increase of $2.63 billion at a 7 percent discount rate. Moreover, a
(

Along the same lines, a substantial body of evidence demonstrates that workers derive significant benefit from flexible work arrangements. Using administrative data on Uber drivers, Chen et al. (2019) estimate that the ability to choose when to work yields more than twice the surplus that drivers would obtain in less flexible alternatives.

The Department, however, does not quantify the economic value of additional flexibility (except insofar as it is embedded in the worker surplus quantification above).
4. Consumer Surplus
The Department anticipates that this rule will produce benefits by reducing uncertainty and improving labor market conditions. Removing uncertainty improves labor market efficiency by reducing deadweight loss. As discussed in section III (“Need for Rulemaking”) of this rule, the Department believes emerging and innovative economic arrangements that benefit both workers and business require reasonable certainty regarding the worker's classification as an employee or independent contractor. Legal uncertainty may deter businesses from offering independent contractor arrangements or developing them in the first place.
[
437
]
If so, the result would be economic deadweight loss: legal uncertainty prevents mutually beneficial independent contractor arrangements. This rule may produce cost savings by reducing deadweight loss. Nonetheless, due to the abundance of variables at play, the Department has not attempted to quantify the precise amount of that reduction.
Qualitatively, expanded participation in independent contracting also increases service availability in sectors such as ridesharing, delivery, personal services, and creative/professional contracting. Evidence from ride-hailing markets indicates that greater supply reduces wait times and rationing, generating consumer surplus.
[
438
]
While the Department does not attempt to quantify these gains in the base case, such benefits are conceptually distinct from transfers and may be material.
5. Broader Labor Market Benefits
Additional benefits may arise from expanding labor force participation among groups that highly value flexibility (
e.g.,
caregivers, students, older workers); supporting continued labor market attachment during periods when traditional employment is infeasible; and enhancing efficiency by better aligning heterogeneous worker preferences with available work arrangements. These effects are difficult to quantify but represent genuine improvements in worker welfare and economic efficiency.
Some commenters agreed that expanding independent contracting can lead to employment gains. For example, Americans for Tax Reform cited the results of their 2020 survey that indicated that 72 percent of application-based ridesharing and delivery drivers in California supported California Proposition 22, which provided application-based transportation and delivery companies an exception to AB 5 by classifying their drivers as independent contractors, rather than employees, while providing certain benefits for the drivers.
[
439
]
According to Americans for Tax Reform, these exemptions serve to encourage increased labor market participation by affording workers with increased flexibility. Americans for Tax Reform also reported that “[n]ine in ten drivers said they started driving so that they could have the flexibility of when and where to work, and 68 percent said they would have to stop their work if the state tried to force them into fixed employment arrangements.”
Flex Association agreed with the Department's position and noted that 88% of workers with children stated that the flexibility of application-based work makes it easier to balance family and work responsibilities. According to its internal estimates, this flexibility is “estimated to be worth $11 billion to these workers each year,” with this work bringing them “an additional $5.1 billion a year in higher income compared to their next best alternative.” Flex Association added that independent contractors have benefitted from the flexibility and entrepreneurial opportunity afforded by platform-based work.
F. Potential Transfer Effects
The substantive effect of the final rule is not intended to favor independent contractor or employee classification relative to the status quo. However, the Department assumes in this RIA that the increased legal certainty associated with the added clarity of this final rule could lead to an increase in the number of independent contractor arrangements. The Department expects that most of this increase would be attributable to the creation of independent contractor opportunities involving workers who were not previously in the workforce (
i.e.,
increased labor force entry) rather than the reclassification of employees into independent contractors. For example, as explained above, Palagashvili, et al., did not find that AB 5 resulted in a significant increase in traditional employment, suggesting that few independent contractors switched to traditional employment as a result of California's law.
[
440
]
The implication is that reclassification due to this final rule would likewise remain small, especially since the Department is not changing the underlying legal standard (
i.e.,
economic reality and economic dependence) but is instead merely clarifying the analysis.
Nonetheless, the Department believes that some reclassification may occur involving workers who are functionally in business for themselves but are currently being (or would be) classified as employees due to legal uncertainty that this rule dispels. To the extent that job conversion costs and other factors such as employee bargaining power deter businesses from reclassifying existing employment relationships, businesses might be more likely to prospectively alter the classification of future work arrangements, suggesting that this “reclassification” effect might be blunted in the short term.
Assuming that this rule alters the classification of some individuals who would otherwise be classified as employees, potential transfers may result from differences in employer-provided benefits, tax liabilities, and earnings between employees and independent contractors. Although affected individuals could experience a decrease in employer-provided benefits and an increase in tax liabilities,
(
printed page 75727)
independent contractors also tend to receive higher gross earnings than employees to offset tax, benefits, and other expenses, thus making much of the transfer impact intrapersonal (in other words, an individual worker may receive remuneration in a different form).
[
441
]
Overall, the Department believes the net impact on total compensation should be small in either direction.
1. Employer Provided Benefits
To the extent that employers currently provide employees benefits such as health insurance, retirement contributions, and paid time off, these would likely decrease with an increase in the use of independent contractors because independent contractors generally do not receive these benefits directly (although independent contractors are able to purchase at least some of these benefits for themselves, and portable benefits are becoming more available). Employer-provided benefits are often a significant share of workers' compensation. According to the BLS's Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC), the value of employer benefits that directly benefit employees average 21 percent of total compensation.
[
442
]
The Department notes that this 21 percent figure is for employees at the 50th (median) wage percentile and may not be representative of the subset of employees whose classification may be impacted by this rule. Since the 21 percent figure includes paid leave (6.9 percentage points) and retirement benefits (3.8 percentage points), and workers may value these benefits at very different levels, applying these elements does not seem reasonable in the context of this analysis.
The Department used the CWS to compare prevalence of health insurance and retirement benefits across employees and independent contractors to produce a highly generalized picture. However, it should be noted that these two populations may differ in other ways than just their employment classification and the particular elements of their compensation packages discussed in the preceding paragraph which may impact benefit amounts. For instance, an employee shifting to independent contractor status who already receives health benefits through a partner's benefit plan would not be impacted by losing health benefit eligibility. Additionally, lower benefits may be offset by increased base pay to attract workers because workers consider the full package of pay and benefits when accepting a job.
According to the CWS's relatively narrow definition of independent contractor:
74.2 percent of independent contractors have health insurance.
84.3 percent of employees have health insurance. Most of these workers receive health insurance through their work (54.4 percent).
Multiple commenters stated that workers newly classified as independent contractors will lose eligibility for unemployment insurance and are less likely to receive employer-provided benefits such as health insurance and retirement benefits, as well as losing their job-protected leave under the FMLA. NELP cited government data indicating that “independent contractors are more likely than employees to be uninsured and to rely on Medicaid.”
NABTU separately asserted that classification as an independent contractor “strips [workers] of job protections and access to society's safety nets,” including not only FLSA wage protections but access to unemployment insurance, workers' compensation, and OSHA coverage, and that “these changes in coverage come at a huge cost” particularly in construction given the industry's “high rates of illnesses and injuries,” as well as “opioid deaths and suicides.” NABTU further stated that “making it easier for employers to treat part of their workforce as independent contractors can also have a negative impact on the remaining employees, since they stand to lose various workplace protections if their numbers fall below the coverage thresholds” under statutes such as Title VII, the ADA, and the FMLA.
As discussed in section VI.D.2., the Department believes that in a competitive labor market, reduced benefits are generally offset, at least in part (especially once post-intervention equilibrium has been reached), by higher gross earnings for independent contractors, though the Department acknowledges this offset may not be complete for all workers or in all sectors. Regarding NABTU's point about coverage thresholds, the Department notes that this is a function of the referenced statutes' own employee-count thresholds rather than of this rule, which does not alter those thresholds or who is an employee under those statutes; the Department nonetheless acknowledges the point as a potential indirect effect worth noting qualitatively.
As explained earlier, the Department estimates a 1 to 3 percent increase in the total number of independent contractors as a result of this rule. The Department assumes that this 1 to 3 percent increase will come almost entirely from people who were otherwise not engaging in paid work and are entering the workforce as independent contractors, as this rule provides an analysis for assessing employee or independent contractor status which is clearer but not more permissive than the analysis applied under longstanding judicial precedent and the Department's pre-2021 guidance. This implies that: (1) most employees who receive the benefits listed above would remain employees and continue to receive those benefits; and (2) most of the workers who are newly independent contractors would not be receiving employer provided benefits in the absence of this rule.
2. Tax Liability
As self-employed workers, independent contractors are legally obligated to pay both the employee and employer shares of the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) taxes.
[
443
]
For example, the social security component of payroll taxes are split evenly between employers and employees at a rate of 6.2 percent
(
printed page 75728)
each.
[
444
]
Similarly, Medicare tax is paid at a rate of 1.45 percent each for employees and employers.
[
445
]
Independent contractors are classified as self-employed workers, and are legally obligated to pay both the employee and employer share of these taxes, an additional 7.65 percent of their earnings. Thus, if workers' classifications change from employees to independent contractors, there may be a transfer in federal tax liabilities from employers to workers.
Some commenters were concerned that workers newly classified as independent contractors would assume the full financial cost of Social Security and Medicare contributions rather than sharing that cost burden with their employers. For example, National Urban League stated that “the unnecessary economic burden on workers, who are often responsible for costs such as individual health insurance and the full cost of Social Security and Medicare contributions rather than sharing them with an employer, creates broader economic harm.” AFL-CIO expressed concern that widespread worker misclassification under this rule could result in the full burden of social insurance contributions being shifted onto workers while overall system contributions decline, externalizing costs onto workers and the public. As explained elsewhere, the Department disagrees that this rule will result in any wide-scale misclassification or reclassification of workers, and that instances of worker reclassification which do occur would involve individuals who are economically independent. Additionally, the Department expects that any tax-related transfers from employers to workers would likely be offset by higher wages employers pay independent contractors. Employers will not pay payroll taxes for work transferred to workers classified as independent contractors and market forces could compel them to pass the full wage (wage + payroll tax) to the independent contractors.
Companies also cover unemployment insurance and workers' compensation taxes for their employees. Independent contractors may choose to pay for comparable insurance protection offered in the private market, but are not obligated to. The resulting regulatory effect (experienced as savings, either by companies or employees, depending on who ultimately bears the cost of the tax) combines societal cost savings (the lessened administrative cost of incrementally lower participation in unemployment insurance and workers' compensation programs) and transfers (from individuals whose unemployment insurance or workers' compensation payments decline, to entities paying less in taxes). Independent contractors may recoup some or all of the employer portion of these taxes and insurance premiums in the form of increased wages. This rule could decrease employers' tax liabilities and increase independent contractors' take-home compensation. However, there are costs to independent contractors if they are out of work or injured or ill on the job because they no longer are protected, unless they purchase their own private insurance. Many of these impacts will depend on the individual risk tolerances of the workers. It is likely that workers who are more comfortable taking risks will be attracted to the potentially higher take-home compensation of independent contractor status, while workers who are risk averse will likely prefer the predictability of traditional employee relationships. It is uncertain how the universe of workers is dispersed, beyond theoretical generalizations. It is further unclear how workers' risk preferences will be distributed across the market for insurance products.
3. Earnings
Potential transfers could also occur through changes to earnings as a result of an increase in independent contracting. These transfers could occur if workers who were employees experience a change in earnings by becoming independent contractors, or if workers who are out of the labor market enter as independent contractors. Although the minimum wage and overtime pay requirements of the FLSA would no longer apply to workers who shift from employee status to independent contractor status, as discussed below, this does not sufficiently explain the potential transfers that could occur as a result of such a shift. As discussed above in section VI.E.3, the Department anticipates an increase in labor force activity, and that each new full-time worker will have the opportunity to earn $51,690 annually.
Several commenters stated that the proposed rule did not take into account the possibility that the proposal would spur widespread job reclassification which would lead to a decrease in wages for reclassified workers. CLASP cited an Economic Policy Institute study showing that “the earnings of independent contractors in poorly-paid occupations lag behind their employee counterparts.”
[
446
]
National Domestic Workers Alliance also commented that independent contractors in low-paid occupations make less than employees, stating: “Misclassification has real-world consequences . . . [S]ome of these so-called independent contractors do not even earn the federal minimum wage.” UBC suggested that “the Proposed Rule fails to address the downward pressure on wages and working conditions that the growing use of dubious independent contractor arrangements is causing in the construction industry.”
Coalition of State Officials challenged the Department's “earnings offset” assumption directly, asserting that the Department's statement that “independent contractors . . . tend to receive higher gross earnings than employees” is unsupported and “contradicts up-to-date findings that independent contractors often earn less than they would have earned if classified as employees.” GFI raised a related concern, citing Economic Policy Institute survey data indicating that “14 percent of gig workers earned less than the federal minimum wage and 29 percent earned less than the applicable state minimum wage,” and that gig workers use the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) at roughly “twice the rate of employee-designated service sector workers,” further citing survey findings that “one in five gig workers could not afford enough to eat and 31 percent could not afford to pay the full amount of their utility bills in the month prior to the survey.”
[
447
]
National Women's Law Center similarly challenged the Department's earnings-offset assumption, citing a study of New York's personal services sector showing that “minimum wage increases helped to raise inflation-adjusted annual earnings of employees by 24.5 percent between 2013 and 2018, compared to
a decline
in earnings of 3.9 percent for independent contractors in the sector.”
If currently unemployed workers or individuals who are out of the labor market enter the market as independent contractors due to this rule, their earnings will increase as they currently have no work-related earnings other than possibly unemployment benefits. The impact on earnings is more ambiguous if employees' classifications
(
printed page 75729)
change to independent contractors. In theory, because independent contractors likely prefer to have at least similar levels of total compensation as they would earn if they were employees, companies would likely have to pay more per hour to independent contractors than to employees because independent contractors generally do not receive company-provided benefits and have higher tax liabilities. Data shows an hourly wage premium for independent contractors when comparing unadjusted mean averages. But as the analysis below illustrates, when controlling for certain differences in worker characteristics, this expected wage premium may not always be observable at a statistically significant level. It should be noted, however, that these estimates do not attempt to incorporate the value of flexibility and satisfaction that many independent contractors cite as key factors in their preference of independent contracting arrangements over being employees.
Furthermore, to attract qualified workers, companies must offer competitive compensation whether they are employees or independent contractors. Therefore, in a competitive labor market, any reduction in benefits and increase in taxes is likely to be offset by higher gross earnings. An Upjohn Institute study of CWS data from 1995 to 2017 finds that independent contractors and contract workers who report being self-employed have weekly earnings of 3 percent and 8 percent more, on average, than wage and salary workers with the same observable job characteristics.
[
448
]
By contrast, some sources warn employers that classifying a worker as an employee can cost between 25 and 40 percent more in hourly terms.
[
449
]
The Department believes this apparent gap reflects at least two dynamics: within a firm, when comparing truly equivalent positions, shifting an employee to independent contractor status is costly because the firm must compensate for lost benefits, payroll taxes, and other expenses. Across the broader economy, however, the Department assumes that the pool of independent contractors skews towards lower-tenure workers who perform qualitatively different tasks from employees, which can compress the measured earnings premium in survey data to only a few percentage points. Such differences in specific job tasks may not be observable in CWS data upon which the Upjohn study relied.
The Department acknowledges that the studies commenters cite for a countervailing earnings effect largely examine gig or platform-based workers, or workers in specific sectors such as New York personal services, populations that may not be representative of the broader independent contractor population from which the Upjohn Institute and Katz and Krueger regression estimates above are drawn. The Department's central estimate is based on economy-wide CWS data controlling for observable worker characteristics, rather than sector-specific survey data; the Department believes this remains the most appropriate basis for an economy-wide analysis but acknowledges that earnings effects may vary meaningfully by industry and that low-wage sectors with high concentrations of independent contractors could see different outcomes than the economy-wide average suggests.
4. Misclassification
Many commenters expressed concern that this rulemaking would exacerbate the misclassification of employees as independent contractors, which occurs when an individual who is economically dependent on an employer for work is wrongly classified by that employer as an independent contractor. FLSA misclassification may be inadvertent or intentional, and its direct effects could include a transfer from the worker to the employer if the employer fails to pay minimum wage and overtime pay to which the worker is entitled. Conversely, reducing misclassification could result in a transfer from employers to workers.
AFSCME and Allegheny County et al. each submitted detailed data on the prevalence of misclassification. For example, AFSCME described a NELP review of state-level task force and audit findings estimating that “10% to 30% of employers (or more) misclassify at least some of their employees as independent contractors,” and a 2000 Department-commissioned study finding that “9% to 42% of employers audited by State Unemployment Insurance Departments misclassified employees as independent contractors with the vast majority of contested claims in some states (up to 95% in some cases) resulting in reclassification of independent contractors as employees.” Allegheny County et al. similarly cited data indicating that “widespread occupational segregation means that workers of color are overrepresented in industries that are especially susceptible to increased misclassification, including construction, trucking, transportation, janitorial services, home care, retail, delivery services, and appl-based work”—and that Black and Latino workers are “already segregated into underpaid jobs”—such that “increased misclassification” would “exacerbate . . . racial income and wealth inequality.” Legal Aid at Work likewise commented that the effects of increased misclassification “will disproportionately harm workers of color who predominate low-paying jobs where misclassification rates are more common.”
The Department has addressed the evidentiary basis for its labor-force-entry assumption at length in section VI.E.3. The Department agrees that misclassification under the applicable legal standard is a proper subject of enforcement and notes that this rule's clarifying purpose is intended to reduce the ambiguity that itself can contribute to inadvertent misclassification. Regarding the misclassification-rate estimates that AFSCME and Allegheny County et al. cite, the Department notes, as it has elsewhere in this analysis, that these figures describe the baseline prevalence of misclassification under existing law rather than a rate attributable to this rule, which does not alter the underlying economic reality test but instead merely clarifies how it should be applied. The Department has not identified data that is attributable to ambiguity in the legal standard that this rule is intended to clarify, as opposed to unlawful conduct that occurs irrespective of the standard's clarity. The Department believes that the enhanced clarity provided by this rule will support the Department's ability to prioritize its enforcement in this area.
5. Job Reclassification
The comments discussed in section VI.D.2 regarding construction industry misclassification and firms' interest in retaining independent contractors are also relevant to potential earnings and job-conversion transfers. GFI commented that the Department's discussion of potential reclassification effects fails to adequately weigh the reliance interests of workers who would lose employee status, citing an Economic Policy Institute estimate that a construction worker reclassified from employee to independent contractor could lose as much as $20,399 annually in income and benefits, and that a truck driver could lose up to $23,266, relative
(
printed page 75730)
to what each would have earned as an employee. GFI further cited the same Economic Policy Institute estimate discussed above in section VI.D.2.a that state and local social insurance systems can lose up to approximately 30 percent of per-worker revenue as a result of misclassification, and stated that this revenue loss compounds the harm to reclassified workers by weakening the social insurance systems on which they might otherwise rely.
The Department has weighed these comments alongside the labor-force-entry evidence discussed in section VI.E.3 and continues to believe the rule's net job-conversion effects would be limited. With respect to GFI's reliance-interest figures specifically, the Department notes that the cited per-worker loss estimates describe the difference between employee and independent contractor compensation generally, rather than an estimate of losses specific to workers who would be reclassified as a result of this particular rule; as discussed in section VI.B above. The Department's central estimate is that reclassification of existing employees attributable to this rule would be minimal, with most growth in independent contracting instead reflecting new labor force entry. To the extent some reclassification does occur, the Department acknowledges that affected individual workers could experience the kind of compensation effects GFI describes, and the Department does not dispute that such effects would be serious for an affected worker.
Additionally as mentioned previously in section VI.B, the Department's position is that businesses would be expected to reclassify workers currently classified as employees into independent contractors only if they determine that the clarity provided by this rule materially shifts the balance of tradeoffs, including legal risk, or to correct a prior classification of a worker's employment status that was mistaken or unnecessary.
G. Alternatives Considered
The Department considered three alternatives to the analysis adopted in this rule, listed below from least to most restrictive of independent contracting:
[
450
]
(1) adoption of the common law control test, which applies in distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under various other federal laws;
(2) adoption of WHD's pre-2021 enforcement policy, which is comprised of sub-regulatory guidance and provides a multifactor “economic reality” balancing test; and
(3) adoption of an “ABC” test (which a number of states have adopted).
The Department previously considered and rejected the first and third alternatives—
i.e.,
a common law control test or an ABC test—on legal viability grounds in the 2021 and 2024 rules.
[
451
]
The Department continues to believe that legal limitations prevent the Department from adopting either of those alternatives, but has included them in this analysis to the extent that it might be helpful in providing greater context on the merits of legislative proposals in Congress.
[
452
]
1. Adopting a Common Law Control Test
The least restrictive (of independent contracting) alternative considered to this rule's streamlined “economic reality” test would be to adopt a common law control test, as is generally used to determine employee or independent contractor classification questions arising under the Internal Revenue Code and various other federal laws.
[
453
]
The overarching focus of the common law control test is “the hiring party's right to control the manner and means by which [work] is accomplished,”
Reid,
490 U.S. at 751, but the Supreme Court has explained that “other factors relevant to the inquiry [include] the skill required; the source of the instrumentalities and tools; the location of the work; the duration of the relationship between the parties; whether the hiring party has the right to assign additional projects to the hired party; the extent of the hired party's discretion over when and how long to work; the method of payment; the hired party's role in hiring and paying assistants; whether the work is part of the regular business of the hiring party; whether the hiring party is in business; the provision of employee benefits; and the tax treatment of the hired party.”
Id.
at 751-52 (footnotes omitted).
Although the common law control test considers many of the same factors as those identified in the proposed rule's “economic reality” test (
e.g.,
skill, duration of the working relationship, investments in equipment and hiring helpers,
etc.
), courts generally recognize that, because of its focus on control, the common law test is more permissive of independent contracting arrangements than the economic reality test, which more broadly examines the economic dependence of the worker.
See, e.g., Diggs
v.
Harris Hospital-Methodist, Inc.,
847 F.2d 270, 272 n.1 (5th Cir. 1988) (observing that “[t]he `economic realities' test is a more expansive standard for determining employee status” than the common law control test). Thus, if a common law control test determined independent contractor status under the FLSA, it is possible that some workers presently classified as employees could be reclassified as independent contractors, increasing the overall number of independent contractors and reducing the overall number of employees. The Department is unable to estimate the exact magnitude of such a reclassification effect, but believes that the vast majority of FLSA employees would remain FLSA employees under a common law control test.
Adopting a common law control test would create a simpler legal regime for regulated entities interested in receiving services from an independent contractor, thereby reducing confusion, compliance costs, and legal risk for entities interested in doing business with independent contractors. Entities would not, for example, have to understand and apply one employment classification analysis for tax purposes and a different employment classification analysis for FLSA purposes. Thus, adopting the common law control test would likely increase perpetual cost savings for regulated entities attributable to improved clarity and reduced litigation as compared to
(
printed page 75731)
the proposed rule. It could, on the other hand, impose burdens on workers who might prefer to be employees subject to FLSA protections.
The Department notes that the Supreme Court has interpreted the “suffer or permit” language in section 3(g) of the FLSA as demanding a broader definition of employment than that which exists under the common law.
See, e.g., Darden,
503 U.S. at 326;
Portland Terminal Co.,
330 U.S. at 150-51. Accordingly, the Department believes it is legally constrained from adopting the common law control test unless the Supreme Court revisits its precedent or Congress passes legislation that alters the applicable analysis under the FLSA.
Commenters disagreed on the policy merits of a common law control test. For example, PayrollOrg expressed concern about “the conflicting definitions of employee and independent contractor between the WHD's proposed rule and the common law definition used by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS),” asserting that the application of different tests will confuse employers and could yield different results for the same individuals. Similarly, while expressing support for the Department's proposed analysis, FedEx remarked that “the optimal solution is federal legislation that establishes a simple, reliable, and objective test for employment status, replacing amorphous, multi-factor tests based on economic dependence.” By contrast, AFSCME asserted that the Congress that enacted the FLSA believed that “[t]o effectively regulate both the longstanding evil of child labor as well as substandard conditions in modern homework, a much broader definition of employment would be required than the narrow common-law test.”
See also
Allegheny County et al. (“By design, the FLSA covers work relationships that exceed the traditional common-law definition of employment—instead including the broad concepts of `suffering' or `permitting' someone to work.”).
Whatever their views on the merits of a common law control test, almost all of the commenters who addressed the alternative agreed with the Department's determination that controlling Supreme Court precedent forecloses its application in FLSA cases. For example, speculating that “[i]t may well be that on a blank slate the best reading of the FLSA's definition `employee' . . . transplants the common law control test from agency law from that old soil to new,” Americans for Prosperity Foundation observed that the Department “is not writing on a blank slate,” concluding that “[t]o minimize litigation risk and maximize the benefits to worker flexibility and innovation, the safest course is the synthesis of existing precedent under the `economic reality' framework DOL has proposed[.]”
See also
Washington Legal Foundation (“The [Department] can't jettison the caselaw requiring a multifactor standard—and it hasn't.”). The Department appreciates that commenters understand the external constraints on its interpretive authority and emphasizes that this rule adopts an analysis which is meaningfully different than the common law control test.
2. Adopting WHD's Pre-2021 Enforcement Policy
On May 1, 2025, WHD issued Field Assistance Bulletin (FAB) No. 2025-1,
[
454
]
directing WHD field staff to no longer apply the analysis from the 2024 Rule when determining employee or independent contractor status in FLSA investigations. Instead, FAB 2025-1 instructed WHD field staff to use the analysis from the July 2008 version of Fact Sheet #13, as further informed by Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2, in WHD enforcement matters. Because Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2 reinstated an opinion letter that was rescinded in early 2021, FAB 2025-1 effectively instructed WHD to enforce its pre-2021 interpretive guidance on FLSA independent contractor or employee status. In relevant part, Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2 applied a six-factor economic reality analysis derived from the July 2008 version of Fact Sheet #13 that focuses on how the factors relate to the worker's economic dependence or independence and emphasizes the degree to which the worker could choose between work opportunities, work for others including competitors, and pursue external economic opportunities. The Department believes that the multifactor balancing test reflected in Fact Sheet #13 (July 2008) and Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2 is neither materially more nor less permissive of independent contractor relationships as compared to the streamlined, core factors analysis adopted in this rule.
[
455
]
Both tests describe the “economic dependence” of the worker at issue as the essential inquiry; both emphasize the “economic reality” of the work arrangement; and both evaluate the same set of underlying factors, notwithstanding an emphasis and consolidation of certain factors under the streamlined test.
While Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2 sought to refine each factor in a focused way, it did not expressly recognize any “core” factors and instead stated that “the appropriate weight to give to each factor depends on the facts.”
[
456
]
In other words, this alternative would not provide specific guidance on how to weigh the factors when applying the multifactor economic reality analysis and would leave stakeholders without clearer guidance to determine independent contractor or employee status under the FLSA, especially in today's modern economy. For these reasons, the Department is not adopting its pre-2021 enforcement policy on independent contractor or employee status.
No commenters specifically addressed the regulatory alternative of replacing the 2024 Rule with the analysis that the Department applied before 2021.
[
457
]
Noting that the Department had already stopped applying the 2024 Rule in its enforcement actions after FAB 2025-1, Flex Association asserted that the proposed rule “therefore codifies the Department's existing interpretive baseline, rather than imposing a disruptive change.” The Department agrees that the analysis adopted in this rule is not a “disruptive change” from its pre-2021 analysis, but notes that there are some meaningful differences. For example, unlike the 2008 version of Fact Sheet #13 or Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2, the analysis adopted in this rule: (1) identifies “control” and “opportunity for profit or loss” as core factors; (2) consolidates “investment” as a consideration within the “opportunity for profit or loss” factor; and (3) advises that the actual practice of the parties involved is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible. As explained in thorough detail in section IV of this rule, these features are refinements to the Department's pre-2021 analysis which the Department believes will bring added clarity and consistency.
3. Adopting an “ABC” Test
The third and most restrictive (of independent contracting) regulatory alternative considered would be to
(
printed page 75732)
adopt an “ABC” test like the ones enacted in a number of states to distinguish between employee and independent contractor status.
[
458
]
Generally, an ABC test presumes an individual is an employee unless the potential employer can satisfy all three requirements to classify the individual as an independent contractor. The three requirements of an ABC test typically are: (A) the individual is free from the potential employer's control or direction in performing his work, both under a contract for the performance of such work and in fact; (B) the work performed by the individual is outside the usual course of the potential employer's business; and (C) the individual is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, or business of the same nature as the work performed for the potential employer.
[
459
]
On its face, an ABC test is more restrictive of independent contracting arrangements than any formulation of an “economic reality” test. Whereas no single factor necessarily disqualifies a worker from independent contractor status under an economic reality test,
each
of an ABC test's three factors may alone disqualify the worker from independent contractor status. The Department believes adopting an ABC test as the FLSA's generally applicable analysis for distinguishing employees from independent contractors would be too restrictive.
In any event, the Department believes it is legally constrained from adopting an ABC test because the Supreme Court has instituted the economic reality test as the relevant standard for determining workers' classification under the FLSA as an employee or independent contractor.
See Tony & Susan Alamo,
471 U.S. at 301 (“The test of employment under the Act is one of `economic reality.'”);
Whitaker House,
366 U.S. at 33 (holding that “`economic reality' rather than `technical concepts' is . . . the test of employment” under the FLSA) (citing
Silk,
331 U.S. at 713;
Rutherford Food,
331 U.S. at 729).
Moreover, the Supreme Court has stated that the existence of employment relationships under the FLSA “does not depend on such isolated factors” as the three independently determinative factors in an ABC test would constitute, “but rather upon the circumstances of the whole activity.”
Rutherford Food,
331 U.S. at 730. Because an ABC test is therefore inconsistent with Supreme Court precedent interpreting the FLSA, the Department concludes it cannot adopt an ABC test unless the Supreme Court revisits its precedent or Congress passes legislation that alters the applicable analysis under the FLSA.
Some labor unions and worker advocacy organizations expressed support for the adoption of an ABC test.
See
NABTU (asserting that the ABC test “protects workers by making it harder for employers to misclassify and offload their responsibilities”); National Domestic Workers Alliance (asserting that a California-style ABC test would be “best suited to address the unique working conditions of domestic workers and other low-pay industries”); SMART and SMACNA (“A clear and concise statement of worker classification through a presumption of employee status in [a construction] industry rife with worker misclassification would both reduce compliance costs borne by employers and ensure that workers receive the FLSA protections to which they are entitled.”). However, the majority of commenters addressing the ABC test were highly critical of it, asserting that its analysis to permit independent contractor arrangements is too rigid and difficult to satisfy. For example, Wisconsin Institute for Liberty commented that “when California implemented the ABC test . . . businesses immediately terminated their contracts with freelancers across industries” and “ride-share companies like Uber and Lyft questioned whether they could continue to operate in the state.”
See also
Truckers Integral to Our Economy (“AB5 swept in approximately 70,000 owner-operators operating in California who had not sought reclassification, who did not want it, and whose actual working relationships reflected genuine independence under any honest application of the economic reality test.”). Researcher Liya Palagashvili commented that “ABC test adoption reduced traditional W-2 employment by 4.73 percent, self-employment by 6.43 percent, and overall employment by 4.79
                        
                         percent.”
[
460
]
See also
Flex Association (citing Dr. Palagashvili's research); Littler WPI (same). Several commenters noted that the California legislature subsequently enacted numerous occupation-specific exemptions to its ABC test,
[
461
]
which they characterized as evidence that the test is not an appropriate or administrable standard.
See
Institute for the American Worker; Manhattan Institute for Policy Research; TechNet; The Transportation Alliance. Finally, CWI and U.S. Chamber of Commerce noted that Supreme Court precedent forecloses the adoption of an ABC test to assess independent contractor status under the FLSA, while a diverse array of commenters emphasized that “no single factor” can determine employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA.
See, e.g.,
Coalition of State Officials; Competitive Enterprise Institute; National Retail Federation; Southern Poverty Law Center.
Having considered the comments, the Department continues to believe that an ABC test would be inconsistent with Supreme Court and federal appellate precedent interpreting and applying the FLSA. As noted above, the Supreme Court has repeatedly explained that “economic reality” is the applicable standard for determining whether a worker is an employee or not under the FLSA. Specific to the distinction between employees and independent contractors, the Supreme Court has explained that “[n]o one [factor] is controlling” of the outcome,
[
462
]
but instead it turns upon “the circumstances of the whole activity.”
[
463
]
Because each of the ABC test's three factors could alone disqualify a worker from independent contractor status, the test would contravene binding Supreme Court precedent. However, even if the ABC test were only a balancing test (instead of a three-pronged checklist), it would still be inappropriate as a regulatory alternative because of its presumption of employee status. As the Department explained in the 2024 Rule, a rebuttable presumption of employee status “would not be consistent with Supreme Court precedent and federal appellate case law interpreting and applying that precedent[.]”
[
464
]
VII. Final Regulatory Flexibility Act Analysis (FRFA)
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.,
as amended by the Small Business Regulatory
(
printed page 75733)
Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996,
Public Law 104-121
(March 29, 1996), requires Federal agencies engaged in rulemaking to consider the impact of their rules on small entities, consider alternatives to minimize that impact, and solicit public comment on their analyses. The RFA requires the assessment of the impact of a regulation on a wide range of small entities, including small businesses, not-for-profit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions. Agencies must perform a review to determine whether a proposed or final rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
This final rule: (1) rescinds a 2024 rule addressing employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA that was published on January 10, 2024; (2) replaces the 2024 Rule with a streamlined analysis very similar to what the Department previously adopted in a 2021 rule published on January 7, 2021; and (3) amends the Department's FMLA and MSPA regulations to clarify that the analysis used to determine employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA should be applied to make that determination under the FMLA and MSPA, which both incorporate the FLSA's scope of employment. By rescinding the 2024 Rule and replacing it with regulations that provide greater clarity and predictable outcomes, the Department believes this rule will likely improve the welfare of both workers and businesses on the whole, including those who wish to work as independent contractors.
Although this rule is not expected to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, the Department provided an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) in the NPRM to explain that determination.
[
465
]
In this FRFA, the Department updates the analysis that it provided in the IRFA and responds to commenter feedback on this rule's potential impact on small entities.
A. Reasons Why Action by the Agency is Being Considered and Statement of Objectives and Legal Basis for the Final Rule
As explained more fully in section III of this rule, the Department is concerned that the 2024 Rule failed to provide an analysis for distinguishing between independent contractors and employees under the FLSA that was sufficiently clear and led to predictable outcomes. The Department is separately concerned that the 2024 Rule's description of several economic reality factors could be viewed as setting a higher bar to find independent contractor status than the law requires. Among other harms, an analysis which is ambiguous or perceived as too restrictive of independent contracting can deter businesses from engaging with bona fide independent contractors or induce them to unnecessarily classify such individuals as employees—concerns emphasized by many self-identified independent contractors who have participated in the Department's recent rulemakings on this topic.
Accordingly, in this rulemaking, the Department is rescinding the 2024 Rule and largely readopting the 2021 Rule,
[
466
]
which provided a sharpened economic reality analysis and did not impede successful enforcement actions by the Department to pursue and remedy misclassification of FLSA-covered employees as independent contractors.
[
467
]
Additionally, the Department is revising the regulations addressing employee or independent contractor status under MSPA and the FMLA so that the analysis in part 795 will apply when determining employee or independent contractor status under those statutes too.
The Department's authority to interpret the FLSA comes with its authority to administer and enforce it.
See
29 U.S.C. 204
;
Fabri-Centers of Am.,
308 F.3d at 592-93 & n.8 (noting that “[t]he Wage and Hour Division of the Department of Labor was created to administer the Act” while agreeing with the Department's interpretation of one of the FLSA's provisions);
Browning-Ferris,
207 F.3d at 267 (“By granting the Secretary of Labor the power to administer the FLSA, Congress implicitly granted him the power to interpret.”);
Sysco Corp.,
1 F.3d at 603 (same). The Department's authority to interpret the FMLA and MSPA is expressly delegated by statute.
29 U.S.C. 2654
(FMLA);
29 U.S.C. 1861
(MSPA).

F. Regulatory Alternatives and Steps Taken To Minimize Economic Impacts on Small Entities
The RFA requires agencies to discuss “any significant alternatives to the proposed rule which accomplish the stated objectives of applicable statutes and which minimize any significant economic impact of the proposed rule on small entities.”

In evaluating regulatory alternatives, the department considered whether alternative approaches would minimize economic burdens on small entities.
As discussed in section VI.G., the Department does not believe that it has the legal authority to adopt either a common law or “ABC” test to determine employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA, foreclosing the consideration of these alternatives for purposes of the RFA.
The Department also considered adopting WHD's prior enforcement policy as a regulatory alternative. As noted in section VI.G.2., beginning May 1, 2025, WHD applied the analysis from the July 2008 version of Fact Sheet #13, as further informed by Opinion Letter FLSA2025-2, in its enforcement matters.
[
488
]
The Department believes that the multifactor balancing test under FAB 2025-1 is neither materially more nor less permissive of independent contractor relationships as compared to the streamlined, core factors analysis set forth in the 2021 Rule,
[
489
]
which the Department is largely readopting. However, FAB 2025-1 lacked specific guidance on how to weigh the factors
(
printed page 75737)
when applying the multifactor economic reality analysis and may have left stakeholders without clearer guidance to determine employee or independent contractor status under the FLSA, especially in today's modern economy.
[
490
]
For these reasons, the Department decided against retaining FAB 2025-1 for determining employee or independent contractor status.
In addition to the alternatives discussed above, section 603(c) of the RFA describes four categories of regulatory alternatives that might be appropriate for consideration in a FRFA analysis. The Department does not believe that the FLSA is best interpreted to encompass these categories of regulatory alternatives or that they are necessarily applicable to this rulemaking.
1. Differing Compliance or Reporting Requirements That Take Into Account the Resources Available to Small Entities
Nothing in the FLSA or the decades of court decisions interpreting it suggest that a worker's status as an employee or independent contractor should turn on the size of the entity that benefits from their labor. As described earlier, one of the primary goals of the FLSA is to curtail “unfair method[s] of competition in commerce” by establishing minimum labor standards that all covered employers must observe.
[
491
]
Providing differing compliance or reporting requirements for small businesses would undermine this important purpose of the FLSA. The Department makes available a variety of resources to employers for understanding their obligations and achieving compliance and has prepared a small entity compliance guide to accompany this rule, as required by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA).
[
492
]
Therefore, the Department has not adopted differing compliance or reporting requirements for small businesses.
2. The Clarification, Consolidation, or Simplification of Compliance and Reporting Requirements for Small Entities
This rule does not impose any new reporting requirements, and the Department makes available a variety of resources to employers for understanding their obligations and achieving compliance.
3. The Use of Performance Rather Than Design Standards
This rule provides guidance regarding the factors that should be considered regarding a worker's employment status under the FLSA, FMLA, and MSPA, consistent with Supreme Court precedent interpreting statutory language which is common to all three laws. It is unclear whether any performance standards could appropriately determine a worker's status as an employee or independent contractor, and such an approach is foreclosed in any event by judicial precedent.
4. An Exemption From Coverage of the Rule, or Any Part Thereof, For Such Small Entities
Creating an exemption from coverage of this rule for businesses with as many as 500 employees, those defined as small businesses under SBA's size standards, would be inconsistent with the FLSA, which, by its statutory terms, applies to all employers that satisfy the enterprise coverage threshold or employ individually covered employees, regardless of the employer's number of employees. Further, as described above, case law interpreting the distinction between employees and independent contractors under the FLSA does not support such an exemption.
VIII. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule that would impose spending costs on State, local, or tribal governments in the aggregate, or on the private sector, in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. That threshold is currently approximately $206 million. State and local government commenters did not quantify alleged unfunded mandate costs. The Department continues to believe that this rule will not result in the expenditure by State, local, or tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, in excess of the threshold. Thus, no written assessment of unfunded mandates is required.
IX. Federalism
This rule will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the National Government and the States, or on distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Therefore, in accordance with
Executive Order 13132
, it is determined that this rule does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant preparation of a Federalism Assessment.
